utterances.text: In addition to freight mobility, we're also taking action to hold third-party delivery companies accountable for their impact on street safety and provide training and resources for delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Roadway safety is important for all New Yorkers, and for delivery workers, the roadway is their workplace.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Our efforts, with support from our strong partnerships with delivery work stakeholders, improve street safety and simultaneously improve the safety and dignity of delivery work.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: For too long, third-party delivery companies have, through algorithmic management and the threat of deactivation, created working conditions that lead to dangerous cycling behavior.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: As such, we're committed to improving street safety in ways that take into account the pressures faced by delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: In this spirit, we continue to build our sustainable delivery unit to address the street safety challenges associated with the rapid growth of on-demand delivery services.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Sustainable Delivery Unit works to strengthen oversight of delivery apps, enhance safety for delivery workers and the public through education and outreach, and analyze the impacts of the delivery industry on our streets.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Through DOT's training portal developed by this team, thousands of delivery workers have already taken the bicycle safety course focused on the rules of the road and safe operation of e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We continue to make strides towards our goal of ensuring all delivery workers have taken our safety training.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Finally, we're also developing policy to ensure that all delivery service companies transition their workforce towards legal and compliant devices.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: As dangerous devices proliferate, these companies must do their part to ensure their deliveries are completed on safe devices.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports Intro 78 requiring trip-level data from delivery platforms, and recommends amending it to grant DOT access and include crash data.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on Intro 78 (delivery data)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Turning to the legislation before the Council today.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: First, Intro 78, sponsored by Council Member Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill would require third-party delivery services licensed by DCWP to share granular travel data for all delivery trips made by their contracted delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We support this bill as requiring trip-level data from delivery platforms will bolster the administration's ability to examine the transportation and street safety impacts of the delivery worker environment.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: With DOT's mission to provide for the safe, equitable, and sustainable movement of people and goods, we also recommend amending the bill to grant DOT access to this travel data to assess the industry's impact on street safety for all street users, not just delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We all

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I also recommend that the bill be amended to include crash data, which would further support our efforts to understand the industry's impact on street safety.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports Intro 95 requiring DCWP to develop materials for moped retailers to distribute at point of sale, and notes DOT already promotes educational materials.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on Intro 95 (moped point-of-sale info)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 95, sponsored by Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill would require DCWP to develop materials containing information related to the registration,

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: inspection, insurance, operation, and traffic safety requirements for mopeds, and would require moped retailers to distribute such materials at the point of sale.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're proud to have supported passage of the state law to require ownership information at moped point of sale and have found it to be effective thus far.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: DOT already promotes a robust suite of educational materials, safety information, and events to help people ride mopeds more safely.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We support this bill and look forward to working with our sister agency, DCWP, and the Council to strengthen ongoing outreach efforts.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports expanding commercial delivery safety and training requirements to cover all two-wheeled devices, including mopeds and motorcycles.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on Intro 110 (commercial delivery safety)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 110, sponsored by Councilmember Brooks Powers.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill would expand commercial delivery safety and training requirements to cover all two-wheeled devices, including mopeds and motorcycles.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Commercial delivery cyclists using bikes, e-bikes, and cargo bikes are already required to receive safety gear and occupational safety training, and we support the need to expand this coverage for workers who use mopeds, motorcycles, and scooters.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Which would further strengthen safety requirements covering more delivery devices used by workers.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We have suggestions for the safety requirements outlined in the proposed legislation, and we look forward to work.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: with council to strengthen safety standards.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports the intent of Intro 214 requiring bike share operators to display rules of the road, but says app platforms are best suited for educating riders.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on Intro 214 (rules of the road)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 214, sponsored by Councilmember Hanif.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill would require bike share operators to display rules of the road on their mobile applications and on physical stations.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: The operators would be required to ensure that users review the rules at least once per year before activating or unlocking a device.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We believe that our bike and micromobility share partners play an important role in educating riders and support the intent of this bill.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Road rules are already posted on every city bike kiosk and inside the basket of every city bike.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Even so, DOT believes that app platforms are best suited for educating riders.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: All of our partners include safety information and road rules within their apps currently, but we look forward to discussing with Council how those can be strengthened.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports prohibiting the sale and rental of Class 3 e-bikes, and says DOT will pursue state legislation for consistent e-bike regulations.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on Intro 244 (banning Class 3 e-bikes)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 244, sponsored by Councilmember Hudson.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill would prohibit the sale and rental of Class 3 bicycles with electric assist.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Class 3 e-bikes can create additional safety challenges compared to lighter and slower e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: In the rest of the state, all vehicles capable of traveling over 20 miles per hour are required to have a license and registration to operate.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We support prohibiting sale and rental of these devices to help reduce their prevalence on the street.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We'll be pursuing state legislation to create e-bike regulations consistent with national and international safety standards.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: To accomplish this, we'll work with advocates in the New York State DMV to advance a regulatory framework that transitions New York

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: and delivery workers away from devices capable of traveling more than 20 miles per hour.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We'll also continue to work with delivery workers through outreach and education efforts to incentivize riders to transition to devices that ride below 20 miles per hour.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We support this bill and look forward to ongoing conversations to strengthen regulations in the e-bike marketplace.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports the intent of Intro 389 requiring third-party delivery services to verify moped registration, while working to mitigate worker protection concerns.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on Intro 389 (moped registration verification)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 389, sponsored by Council Member Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill would require third-party food delivery services to verify the registration of mopeds used by food delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Mopeds are already required to be registered at the point of sale, and we support the intent of this bill as we want to ensure third-party delivery apps are held accountable to also verify registration, while also working with our sister agency, DCWP,

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: to mitigate potential worker protection concerns.

chapters.summary: Flynn says DOT maintains a strong partnership with NYPD on data and defers to NYPD on the details of Intro 787 requiring reporting on targeted traffic enforcement.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on Intro 787 (NYPD enforcement reporting)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 787, sponsored by Councilmember Brooks Powers.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill requires reporting on targeted traffic enforcement operations by the police department.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We maintain a strong partnership with the NYPD on data that supports street safety measures.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We defer to the NYPD on the details of this bill.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports the intent of Intro 950 to create a more level playing field among delivery service companies, but defers to DCWP for details.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on Intro 950 (licensing delivery services)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 950, sponsored by Councilmember Shulman.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill would require delivery services that facilitate or arrange for the delivery of goods in the city to obtain a license.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We support the intent of a more level playing field among delivery service companies, which would include all major third-party delivery services that rely on these devices to obtain a license.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: in an effort to comprehensively address micromobility safety in the delivery industry, but we defer to our sister agency, DCWP, for details.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports the intent of Intro 985 to create a trade-in program for unsafe devices, but has concerns about resource intensity and suggests a narrower approach.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on Intro 985 (trade-in program)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 985, sponsored by Chair Abreu.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill would establish a trade-in program for Class 3 bicycles with electric assist and vehicles that resemble but do not legally qualify as Class 1 or Class 2 e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: While DOT supports the bill's intent to encourage New Yorkers to replace unsafe and illegal vehicles with compliant micromobility devices, we have concerns with the bill as written.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Standing up a program like this is very resource intensive and a narrower approach that targets the most dangerous illegal devices could prove a greater impact on street safety.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: As we finalize a full evaluation of last year's e-bike trade-in program, we look forward to sharing lessons learned to inform a program with council support to best enhance street safety for all road users.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports the intent of Intro 986 requiring dynamometers to test micromobility devices, but notes concerns about equity and implementation, deferring to DCWP.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on Intro 986 (dynamometers)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 986, sponsored by Chair Abreu.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill would require the use of micromobility dynamometers to test micromobility devices operating in the city, followed by a report of data gathered through the testing.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We support the bill's intent to ensure all riders use safe, compliant devices.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're interested in testing any technology that can help increase the use of safe devices on our streets.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: At the same time, we've heard concerns about equity and implementation.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We would defer to DCWP on those concerns.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We look forward to working with Council and the MYP to...

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: to develop best practices for implementation.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports Intro 988 prohibiting misleading advertisements, but recommends expanding it to also prohibit advertising illegal devices as e-bikes.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on Intro 988 (false advertising)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 988, sponsored by Chair Abreu.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill would prohibit the advertisement of vehicles required to be registered with the Department of Motor Vehicles as powered bicycles or powered mobility devices.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We support this bill to prohibit misleading advertisements, but the current draft of the bill only targets the advertisement of legal devices, given that they must be registered with the DMV.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We think it's also important to expand the bill to also prohibit advertising illegal devices as e-bikes or other legal mobility devices, such as in the case of the most recent crash in front of One Center Street.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: These illegal devices cannot be registered with the DMV and therefore would not be captured by the bill as drafted.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports the intent of Intro 989 requiring bike share operators to report safety incidents, but notes operational challenges with self-reported data.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on Intro 989 (bike share safety reporting)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 989, sponsored by Chair Abreu.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill would require that the city's bike share operator report safety incidents involving their devices, followed by a report published to DOT's website every six months.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: City Bike is now an integral part of New York City's transportation system.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Given its growing role in our transportation system, understanding how it contributes to the safety landscape is critical to enhancing safety on our streets.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We support the intent of this bill, but understand there are operational challenges to collecting some of this data for the system operator, such as incident data being self-reported by riders.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: City Bike's existing program agreement already includes robust requirements to report known safety incidents to DOT.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports Intro 994 requiring third-party food delivery services to maintain liability insurance, saying workers and pedestrians should not pay for on-the-job injuries.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on Intro 994 (liability insurance)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 994, sponsored by the

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: sponsored by Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill requires third-party food delivery services to maintain liability insurance.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We support efforts to ensure that delivery services carry appropriate insurance to protect New Yorkers when there are incidents on the job.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Workers and pedestrians should not be left to pay for injuries and damages caused by collisions on the job.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Delivery apps need to acknowledge their role and bear the responsibility for the externalities of their business.

chapters.summary: Flynn says DOT already prioritizes pedestrian safety and supports the intent of Intro 1004 requiring signs reminding pedestrians to look up, but has concerns about fit with existing toolkit.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on Intro 1004 (pedestrian safety signage)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 1004, sponsored by Council Member Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill requires DOT to paint signs on street corners or intersections adjacent to a crosswalk that remind pedestrians to look up at incoming traffic.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: The bill also requires DOT to provide educational materials on street safety to schools.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This is work that we already strive to do and would be happy to collaborate with Council on strengthening our outreach and educational efforts.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Pedestrians are our most vulnerable population.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Everything we do prioritizes pedestrian safety, and we completely understand the need to make sure everyone on the...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can sergeants identify who's interrupting the commissioner?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And please escort them out the chambers.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And we completely understand the need to make sure everyone on the roadway is aware of their surroundings.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We already deploy data-proven interventions, and our efforts are working with research showing that extremely few fatalities are caused by distracted walking.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Although we support the intent of this bill, we have concerns with how this tool fits within our existing street safety toolkit.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We always welcome input from Council.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: members on any suggested locations to explore additional safety enhancements.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports Intro 1021 requiring third-party delivery services to submit annual safety reports and plans, and says DOT's mandatory safety course is proving successful.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on Intro 1021 (safety reports and plans)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 1021, sponsored by Chair Abreu.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill requires third-party delivery services to submit an annual safety report to DCWP, including crash data.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Third-party delivery services will also be required to submit a safety plan with any initial or renewal application.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: New Yorkers deserve a workplace where their safety and dignity is the top priority, including the delivery cyclists who serve our city year-round.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: As mentioned, our mandatory safety course for delivery workers is proving successful, and we continue to empower delivery cyclists to make safe trips through direct outreach.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Along with delivery worker education and outreach, we must continue initiatives strengthening delivery app accountability, and we support this bill as it enhances these efforts.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We look forward to working with Council and our sister agency, DCWP, to ensure meaningful street safety measures.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports the intent of Intro 1052 requiring DOT and NYPD to include micromobility data in crash reporting, and says they already coordinate on open data.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on Intro 1052 (crash reporting data)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 1052, sponsored by Council Member Palladino.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill requires DOT and NYPD to include data on micromobility devices in crash reporting.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We support the intent of this bill as we already coordinate with NYPD to include detailed data on micromobility crashes in open data and look forward to working with Council to ensure our data continues to be reflective of all road users.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports the intent of Intro 1066 requiring traffic calming devices in bike lanes at 50 intersections, and says DOT is already taking steps to install such devices.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on Intro 1066 (traffic calming in bike lanes)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 1066, sponsored by Council Member 1.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill requires DOT to install traffic calming

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: devices in bicycle lanes at no less than 50 intersections throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We share Council's goal to enhance safety through a variety of traffic calming devices and design changes that together make streets safer by encouraging slower speeds for cyclists.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We support the bill's intent as we're already taking unprecedented steps in our safety engineering efforts to install these devices and look forward to discussions with the council to strategize initiatives that meet our shared goal to support safe and accessible cycling practices.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports Intro 1069 requiring delivery services to submit trip data and DCWP to study and set safe delivery standards, but suggests placing it with DOT.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on Intro 1069 (safe delivery time standards)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Intro 1069 sponsored by Chair Abreu.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill requires delivery services to submit data to DCWP for each trip, followed by a study to determine the street safety impacts.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: DCWP would then promulgate rules establishing safe delivery standards based on those findings.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: With street safety as our priority, we support the bill, but find more value if this bill is placed with DOT.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We look forward to ongoing conversations to strengthen our understanding of delivery worker travel patterns based on trip level data.

chapters.summary: Flynn says the administration needs more time to analyze the bill banning Class 3 e-bike use, and is pursuing state legislation for consistent regulations.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on pre-considered 2361 (banning Class 3 use)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, pre-considered 2361 sponsored by Councilmember Hudson.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill would prohibit the use of Class 3 e-bikes in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're always thinking critically about how regulatory efforts could mitigate street safety concerns.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: As previously stated, we're pursuing state legislation to create e-bike regulations consistent with national and international safety standards.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: The administration needs more time to analyze the bill and connect with stakeholders.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: before we formalize our position.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We look forward to working with the Council on how best to partner together on these efforts to ensure appropriate safeguards are in place for workers.

chapters.summary: Flynn says DOT is interested in new technologies but wants to hold delivery apps accountable for incentivizing unsafe riding, and defers to DCWP on details.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on pre-considered 2587 (tracking unsafe behaviors)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Next, Pre-Considered 2587, sponsored by Council Member Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill requires the installation of traffic safety tracking technology on the

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: devices used by delivery workers with a progressive penalty structure.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Safety is our North Star, and we're always interested in exploring new technologies that support our mission, but as previously mentioned, we want to hold delivery apps accountable for incentivizing unsafe riding behavior.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We defer to our sister agency, DCWP, on the details and look forward to future conversations on how best to promote safe riding behavior.

chapters.summary: Flynn supports the intent of requiring sidewalk riding detection technology, but says existing technology cannot effectively distinguish sidewalk from roadbed and may cause safety issues.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn testifies on pre-considered 2590 (sidewalk detection)

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Lastly, pre-considered 2590, sponsored by Chair Abreu.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: This bill requires the installation of sidewalk riding detection technology on e-bikes and e-scooters that are part of self-service share systems, with violators facing a progressive penalty structure.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: E-bike and e-scooter riders must abide by the same traffic laws, rules, and regulations applicable to drivers.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Riders are permitted on arterial and local streets throughout the city and must use designated bike lanes when available, and riding is prohibited on certain bridges, expressways, and highways unless a designated bicycle path exists.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: In general, riders are not permitted to operate on sidewalks, but we do have locations across the city that allow for sidewalk riding, as indicated by official signage.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We support the bill's intent so riders abide by these rules, but based on our research, existing technology cannot effectively distinguish

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: between sidewalk and roadbed and can cause safety issues for riders in the road if the technology mistakes them for sidewalk riders, slowing the device while in traffic.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We share the council's concern with unsafety.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: safe riding behavior, and look forward to working with the sponsor to discuss existing and reliable safety tools to address this concern.

chapters.summary: Flynn concludes by emphasizing every death is avoidable, notes Vision Zero has reduced traffic deaths by nearly 30%, and says DOT is committed to preventing future tragedies.
chapters.title: Commissioner Flynn concludes testimony with Vision Zero reflections

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: In conclusion, every death or serious injury on our streets is an avoidable tragedy, affecting not only the victim, but their families, friends, and colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Since I began serving as commissioner, I've met many New Yorkers who lost loved ones to traffic violence or were themselves injured in a crash.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Hearing their stories and understanding the long-term pain and trauma that never really go away, it makes these issues not just academic, but so very tangible.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And it underscores the importance of our work together here today towards Vision Zero.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Likewise, every member of our team that works on Vision Zero and street safety projects carries with them

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: a profound sense of responsibility to not only honor the memory of those who've been lost with aggressive data-driven action, but to prevent the next tragedy from happening.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Vision Zero works.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It's saving lives.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Compared to the same point in the year before Vision Zero was implemented, traffic deaths are down nearly 30%.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But this is about more than numbers and percentages.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: These are real people, real families.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: That 30% reduction in traffic deaths means more than 50 individuals are alive this year alone compared to the year before Vision Zero began.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: That's 50 individuals, 50 families, and many more times, many times more neighbors, coworkers, and classmates of those individuals, all of whom will be

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: spared from tragedy.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're encouraged by the progress we're making at DOT, but acknowledge that there's much more to be done.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I would like to thank the Council for the opportunity to testify before you today, and I look forward to partnering together on meaningful legislation to help shape evolving micromobility trends in a safe and impactful way.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We would now be happy to pass to DCWP for testimony.

chapters.summary: Sam Levine, Commissioner of DCWP, introduces himself and his staff, and thanks the council for the opportunity to testify on micromobility.
chapters.title: DCWP Commissioner Sam Levine introduces himself and thanks the council

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner Flynn, and good morning, Chairs Epstein, Abreu, Felice, and members of the Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Public Safety.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: I'm Sam Levine, Commissioner of the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: I'm joined this morning by our Chief of Staff and Deputy Commissioner for External Affairs, Carlos Ortiz.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today before the committee on micromobility in New York City and related legislation.

chapters.summary: Levine says DCWP is the nation's leading municipal enforcement agency, has secured over $1 billion for New Yorkers in 2026, and conducted nearly 800 outreach events.
chapters.title: Commissioner Levine discusses DCWP mission and recent accomplishments

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: The New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection is the nation's leading municipal enforcement agency charged with delivering economic justice.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: In the last nine months, the Mamdani administration has demonstrated New York City's commitment to refuse to allow multi-billion dollar corporations to rake in record profits on the backs of New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: DCWP has been at the forefront of this all-hands-on-deck effort, protecting New Yorkers from corporate tricks and traps that make their lives more difficult.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: And I am proud to report that through our programs, protections, and policies, we have secured more than $1 billion on behalf of New Yorkers,

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: thus far in 2026.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: During this administration, I have made engaging New Yorkers a priority across all of DCWP's services and programs, ensuring that we as an agency hear directly from New Yorkers on the issues that matter most to them.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: This includes direct outreach to consumers, to small businesses, to workers, and partnerships with our sister agencies, such as my colleagues at the Department of Transportation.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: In 2026, we've conducted nearly 800 outreach events and have engaged with nearly 200,000 New Yorkers through direct public awareness efforts and financial empowerment programming.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: We remain committed and steadfast in our promise to the communities of our city that we are here as a partner and ally and stand ready to champion their rights.

chapters.summary: Levine highlights new tipping protections, a $131.5 million enforcement action against DoorDash, and efforts to protect workers from arbitrary deactivation.
chapters.title: Commissioner Levine discusses delivery worker protections and enforcement

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Now turning to the topic of today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: At the start of this year, we celebrated the passage of laws to advance protections for delivery workers, including tipping protections and an expansion of the minimum pay rate to more workers.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Our tipping report, which showed two major apps, engineered design tricks to make it harder for consumers to tip and drove down worker pay by more than half a billion dollars, exemplified the need for these laws.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: More recent reports show that these new tipping protections have lifted workers'total earnings on the delivery apps by more than $100 million and on course to hit $184 million by the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Earlier this year, we secured more than $5 million from three major delivery apps and reinstatement for up to 10,000 wrongful

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: We terminated workers.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: This work is only accelerating.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Just last week, we announced a historic $131.5 million enforcement action against DoorDash, the largest worker protection enforcement in the history of New York City, for systemic violations of New York City's delivery worker laws.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: More than $115 million will go directly to over 260,000 delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: And by arming workers with tools to report trip data directly to DCWP, we are both investing in worker power and ensuring that these massive violations will not recur in our five boroughs.

chapters.summary: Levine argues that worker safety and street safety are not in conflict, and that deactivation protections are critical to any street safety agenda.
chapters.title: Commissioner Levine says worker safety and street safety are complementary

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Now, a common tactic by app companies, often to distract from their track record of mistreating workers, is to pit workers'rights against street safety.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Nothing could be further from the truth.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: I speak with delivery workers all the time, and they consistently describe the pressure to complete more orders in less time or risk deactivation.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: As Councilmember Hudson said earlier, no worker should have to choose between their safety and their livelihood.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: That is why the Mondani administration was proud to support and will be vigorously enforcing Local Law 34 of 2026, which puts an end to arbitrary deactivations in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Today the Council is considering numerous bills aimed at strengthening street safety and we look forward to a thoughtful discussion of each.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: But our administration, and I speak for all the agencies here, believes strongly

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: strongly that the basic deactivation protections provided by Local Law 34 are a critical part of any street safety agenda.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: No amount of training, equipment requirements, or monitoring can make our streets meaningfully safer if workers are still operating under constant pressure to race against the clock or risk losing their jobs.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Street safety requires not only addressing how delivery workers ride, but the incentives and pressures that shape how they are required to work.

chapters.summary: Levine says DCWP enforces laws against unsafe and illegal micromobility devices, conducting nearly 1,000 inspections and issuing over 460 summonses since 2023.
chapters.title: Commissioner Levine discusses enforcement against illegal devices

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Turning now to our enforcement efforts, we enforce various laws that protect consumers from the sale of unsafe and illegal micromobility devices, and we aim to keep our city free from these devices.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: DCWP is a lead enforcement agency for local laws 39, 49, and 50, and we also actively enforce against the sale of oversized and overpowered motorized scooters and illegal mopeds.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Following the passage of these laws, DCWP sprang into action, conducting enforcement suites of retailers across the five boroughs and working to swiftly bring them into compliance.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: DCWP continues to conduct regular proactive enforcement in this space.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Just this past summer, our inspectors and attorneys conducted a comprehensive sweep of micromobility retailers across the city, working to ensure continued compliance with our laws.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: And since we began enforcing these laws in 2023, the ECWP has conducted nearly 1,000 inspections and issued more

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: than 460 summonses to brick-and-mortar businesses for violations of Local Law 39, Local Law 49, and the Motorized Scooter Law.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: In 2026, we issued over 85 cease and desist orders and 41 summonses to online sellers for violations of Local Law 39.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: We have also targeted eight locations for sealing, sealed three of them, and brought five into compliance prior to having to seal them.

chapters.summary: Levine supports Intro 78 requiring delivery services to submit trip data, but says the bill should be placed with DOT, which is best positioned to oversee street safety.
chapters.title: Commissioner Levine testifies on Intro 78 (delivery data)

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Turning to today's legislation and starting with Introduction 78.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Intro 78 requires licensed delivery services to submit data for each trip made in the city to DCWP.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Our administration supports this legislation to require third-party food delivery services to submit data regularly.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: However, and we, our agencies are aligned in believing that this bill should be placed with DOT, which is best positioned to oversee the city's street safety laws, and indeed already does.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: The administration looks forward to working with council on this legislation.

chapters.summary: Levine supports Intro 244 banning the sale and rental of Class 3 e-bikes, but has operational concerns about online and field enforcement challenges.
chapters.title: Commissioner Levine testifies on Intro 244 (banning Class 3 sales)

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Turning to Intro 244, which would prohibit the sale and rental of Class 3 e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: DCWP supports this bill, which would ban the sale and rental of certain throttle e-bikes with a higher speed capacity.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: However, we have operational concerns related to online and field enforcement challenges.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: As not all products accurately post or specify speed information.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: We look forward to hearing from stakeholders today and working with council and our

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: agencies on this bill.

chapters.summary: Levine supports the intent of Intro 389 requiring delivery services to verify moped registration, but recommends guardrails to prevent unfair deactivations.
chapters.title: Commissioner Levine testifies on Intro 389 (moped registration verification)

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Turning to Intro 389, this would prohibit third-party food delivery services for permitting any food delivery worker

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: hired, retained, or engaged by the third-party food delivery service to utilize a moped unless the delivery service has verified registration of the moped.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Our administration supports the intent of this legislation to require third-party food delivery services to verify moped registration.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: However, we have concerns that the bill as written could result in delivery workers being unfairly deactivated by delivery apps unless there are reasonable guardrails in place.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Workers should be given notice and opportunity to address any issues with their vehicle registration and the chance to get back to work once this is addressed.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: We recommend adding in language requiring warnings and other progressive discipline measures to ensure workers are not permanently deactivated arbitrarily and providing for an extended effective date.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: We look forward to working with council and our sister agencies to establish a balanced approach that tackles both street safety priorities and workers'rights and needs to earn a living.

chapters.summary: Levine supports the intent of Intro 950 to expand licensing of delivery services, but recommends tailoring it to companies engaging independent contractors.
chapters.title: Commissioner Levine testifies on Intro 950 (licensing delivery services)

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Turning to Intro 250, this bill would require delivery services that facilitate or arrange for the delivery of goods in the city to obtain a business license from DCWP and would set forth conditions on such a license and enforcement options.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: DCWP supports the intent of this bill to expand the coverage of its third-party food delivery service license.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: However, we

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: recommend that we tailor this bill to require licensure for companies that engage contracted delivery workers as independent contractors so that we focus on appropriate companies and not unintentionally burden small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: We have started off 2026 with aggressive enforcement against powerful corporations and we look forward to continue that are exploiting workers and we stand ready to continue that fight.

chapters.summary: Levine supports Intro 988 prohibiting misleading advertisements, but has policy and fiscal concerns about the breadth of outreach required.
chapters.title: Commissioner Levine testifies on Intro 988 (false advertising)

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Turning to Intro 988, which would prohibit the advertisement for sale, lease, rent, or distribution of any vehicle that can be registered with the New York State DMV as a street legal e-bike or e-scooter.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: The bill requires DCWP and DOT to develop and distribute informational materials on unauthorized e-bikes and e-scooters to retailers to post and offer to consumers.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: DCWP supports this bill, which prohibits the advertisement for sale, lease, or registration.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: However, DCWP has policy and fiscal concerns about the breadth of outreach contemplated by this bill and the significant investment that would be required to conduct it.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: We look forward to working to ensure that any new campaign is coordinated with the appropriate agencies who have similar campaigns and may have additional subject matter expertise.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: We look forward to working with the council on further refinements on this bill.

chapters.summary: Levine supports the intent of Intro 994 requiring third-party food delivery services to maintain liability insurance for accidents involving delivery workers.
chapters.title: Commissioner Levine testifies on Intro 994 (liability insurance)

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Turning to Intro 994, this bill would require certain third-party food delivery services to maintain insurance to cover liability that arises from accidents involving a delivery worker on an e-bike scooter.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: e-bike, e-scooter, or illegal moped while the delivery worker is making a delivery or is available to make a delivery for the third-party food delivery service.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: DCWP supports the intent of this bill to require apps to maintain liability for insurance for accidents involving a delivery worker on micromobility devices.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: We look forward to hearing more from stakeholders on this bill today.

chapters.summary: Levine supports Intro 1021 requiring annual safety reports, but believes they should be provided to DOT, which is best positioned to use the information.
chapters.title: Commissioner Levine testifies on Intro 1021 (safety reports)

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Turning to Intro 1021, which would require third-party food delivery services to submit an annual safety report to DCWP.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: The administration supports this bill but believes these reports and plans should be provided to DOT, who is best positioned to leverage that information for the street safety enforcement and overall strategic planning efforts.

chapters.summary: Levine shares the goal of removing unsafe devices but has significant concerns about unintended consequences for delivery workers, including loss of livelihood.
chapters.title: Commissioner Levine testifies on pre-considered 2361 (banning Class 3 use)

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Turning now to pre-considered bill 2026-2361, this would prohibit the operation of class 3 e-bikes and require the violators receive a warning for the first violations and escalating civil penalties for subsequent violations.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: We share council's goal to rid our streets of unsafe micromobility devices.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: However, we have significant concerns of unintended consequences that would most heavily impact delivery workers, many of whom are immigrants with limited English proficiency and other vulnerabilities.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Delivery workers could face losing their livelihoods as well as increased interactions with law enforcement at a time when many are especially fearful of such interactions.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: And could also lead to confiscation of the device they use every day to earn a living.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: We look forward to a

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: working with the council to improve street safety while balancing the needs of some of our city's most essential yet vulnerable workers.

chapters.summary: Levine has concerns about constant electronic surveillance of workers and potential unfair deactivations, and looks forward to working with the council.
chapters.title: Commissioner Levine testifies on pre-considered 2587 (tracking unsafe behaviors)

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Turning now to pre-considered 2587, this would require third-party delivery services to use tracking technology to detect when certain delivery workers engage in unsafe traffic behaviors while making a delivery or when available to make a delivery.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Generally, we have concerns about the idea of requiring constant electronic surveillance of their workers, who are primarily immigrants.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: We also have concerns that as drafted, this bill could lead to delivery workers being unfairly deactivated by delivery apps.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: We look forward to working with Council to further street safety and worker safety goals while limiting unintended consequences that may flow from this legislation.

chapters.summary: Levine thanks the council, says the administration looks forward to collaborating, and turns things over to the police department.
chapters.title: Commissioner Levine concludes testimony and turns over to NYPD

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: In conclusion, I want to thank the Council sincerely for the opportunity to testify before these committees on today's legislation and to the Council's attention to these vital issues.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Our administration looks forward to hearing from stakeholders today on the impact of these bills, and we look forward to collaborating closely with the Council during the legislative process.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: I welcome any questions you may have for further discussions, and now turn things over to our police department.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We look forward to answering any questions you may have.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We will hear from Speaker Julie Menon.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Let me recognize Council Member's nurse, Mark.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Take a bond, Pierina Sanchez, Banks, Public Advocate, Williams, Palladino, and Aldebar.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Madam Speaker.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin asks why the 2013 law requiring delivery workers to wear identifying vests is not enforced, and asks both DOT and NYPD to commit to enforcing it.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin questions DOT and NYPD on enforcement of vest law

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I want to start with the fact that in 2013, the City Council passed a law that required all delivery workers to wear a vest to identify themselves as commercial workers, among other safety requirements.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The Council updated this law last year with Council Member Brewer's bill.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: To make it clear that the law applies to all delivery workers, including those that work for third-party apps.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yet, if you were to ask the average New Yorker, they would tell you they've never heard of this law, and they've almost never seen a delivery worker wearing the required vests.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That is because there seems to be zero enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So the question is both for the NYPD and DOT, since you're both responsible for enforcement of our micromobility safety laws, why is there no enforcement of this law?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: You know, we very much share the priority of ensuring that delivery workers are operating safely, both for themselves and for others out there.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And, you know, we agree as well that the landscape, the delivery landscape, has continued evolving in terms of

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: workers using different kinds of devices beyond just bicycles, and we're supportive of the legislation to expand that.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're absolutely open to further conversations around the enforcement side and how we can keep improving the delivery worker landscape.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, I just have a question for that, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So when you say you're open to conversations on enforcement, will you then commit now to enforce the council's law on this topic?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're committed to enforcing any laws on the books, and I'm happy to look closer at, you know, if there's gaps and how we can continue partnering with PD on the enforcement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And from the PD's side, with regard to the corporate side enforcement, right, against the, you know, employers, that we very much would defer to DOT.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: With regard to the street-level enforcement, and I do think that the message to the patrol officers on the street is we are prioritizing that conduct that is most dangerous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I understand the concern you're raising, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But again, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I do think that the critical point is identifying dangerous behavior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Officers are seeing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They're directed to take enforcement action.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, so will the agency also then commit to enforcing this council law?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We will certainly look at it and prepare additional training for the officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Again, there's always going to be a question of what we're prioritizing on the street in terms of enforcement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's inescapable, but I understand what you're saying, Speaker, and we will 100% take that back to look at additional training and to make sure our officers understand all the tools available to them.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, the council's now passed several laws on this, and no one knows anything about them.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We passed them for a reason.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So one of the reasons for this hearing is to get the commitment from the agencies to actually enforce the current laws we have in the books that are not being enforced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We are 100% going to take that back.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, and so I'd like a commitment from both agencies in writing to us.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We really want to, I just want to have like more conversations, okay?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I'm sure Councilmember Brewer is going to expand upon that in her questioning as well.

chapters.summary: Menin asks NYPD for the number of ticket citations issued for micromobility infractions this year compared to previous years, and Chief Obey provides moving summons data.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin asks NYPD for ticket citation data

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Secondly, how many ticket citations has NYPD issued regarding micromobility infractions this year, and how does that compare to last year and to the year before that?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So moving summons says year to date 2026 to e-bikes 10,055 versus 5893.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Stand-up scooters, 640 versus 380.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Mopeds, 18,716 versus 9324.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Motorcycles, 18049 versus 36778.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: These are moving violations for what we consider to be the most egregious offenses.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Can you provide all of the data, though, in writing to the committees?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

chapters.summary: Menin asks Commissioner Flynn about implementing age verification for City Bike, referencing a recent fatal accident involving a 15-year-old, and Flynn says discussions with Lyft are ongoing.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin questions DOT on age verification for City Bike

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: To Commissioner Flynn, in August I sent you a letter urging age verification for city bikes.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I made clear there are numerous options on the table.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Obviously, you could use a Muni ID system.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So again, the letter was very clear.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It does not involve utilizing, you don't need to use facial recognition technology.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: There's so many other ways to do this.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We currently have a Muni ID system.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The SAFE Act being passed at the state level on social media companies, both the New York Attorney General and the Governor identify numerous ways for age verification.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Earlier this month, there was a fatal accident involving two teenage girls, one of whom was 15.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Since that accident, I got a response from you in the letter, so I want to understand what is the agency going to do in terms of this issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: The safety of young New Yorkers is our top priority, and certainly at DOT we're most focused on the street safety, but also online safety, as you noted.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We do appreciate Lyft's efforts to protect young riders and to explore age-appropriate access to city bike that preserves data privacy, security, accuracy, and equity.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And as an administration, we're committed to that.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So I know that there's very productive discussions going on right now with Lyft, and we're exploring all possible avenues to achieve both goals, street safety and online safety for young New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, and I mean, I should clarify, we're doing a bill on this.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The bill is not ready to be released today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It will be released in the coming weeks, and that will mandate an age verification system.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So just wanted to make sure that I express that.

chapters.summary: Menin asks the administration to assess its enforcement of micromobility laws, and NYPD and DOT describe stepped-up enforcement and data-driven approaches.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin asks about on-street enforcement success

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: How would the administration assess its on-street enforcement of our micromobility laws thus far this year, and do you think your enforcement efforts have been successful?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I guess PD will start.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I'll speak briefly and then turn it over to Chief Obey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But obviously there's stepped up enforcement and the numbers that Chief Obey described earlier speak to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Obviously there's always more work to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So we're following the data, both in terms of key locations, key corridors, where there's a concentration of accidents, injuries, fatalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're acting in response to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Again, it's a very data-driven approach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We talk about precision policing in other contexts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: This is about precision when it comes to traffic safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Obviously, there's always more work to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And, you know, every accident is one too many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Every fatality, obviously, is one too many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But we are very focused on this issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And with that, I'll turn it over to Chief Obey.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So enforcement decisions are made this way.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: We focus and hive visibly to corridors citywide.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: There are 15 of those corridors.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: In all boroughs and they touch mostly all precincts.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: These corridors were identified in collaboration with the DOT, just reviewing data going back four years prior to 2024.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Nine corridors citywide were identified in 2024.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: That has since expanded to 15 in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: An example of one such corridor is

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Parkway in the confines of the 606166 precincts where we had three fatalities in all of them in March of 2025.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: And this was caused by a speeding operator.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: We typically direct our resources along corridors where we see spikes in fatalities, injuries, and collisions.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: And in this particular case, three fatalities along Ocean Parkway in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: We have zero as we sit here today.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Total collisions are down along that corridor.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Total injuries are down.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Total corridor moving violations are up.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: And vision zero movers are up.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: As it pertains to micromobility devices, the first thing we do, we'll speak about that also at length, point-of-sale initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Point-of-sale initiatives addressing unsafe motorized devices at point-of-sale locations, addressing these...

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Retailers and we started that work in two phases in 2021.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: The initial focus was on mopeds.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: This year we focused on high-powered out-of-class e-bike and e-scooters.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: As of September 21st, we visited 71 storefronts were identified, 63 inspected.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: 90 bikes seized from three locations, three corresponding old summonses.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Inspections for the most part, we found broad compliance and follow-up visits will continue.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: And we work hand-in-hand with the DOT at those locations where we distributed flyings.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I'll jump in.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I would echo everything Chief Obey said.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We have a really great working relationship, both at the staff and leadership level with PD, to use the data and really let the data drive all of our efforts.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Enforcement is one piece of that.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But really, we're taking a comprehensive approach.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: That's enforcement, education, infrastructure, regulation.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And I would, you know, I guess to answer the question, I do believe that it's working.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I believe that we're seeing the trends going in the right direction overall.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Year to date, we've seen 151 traffic fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: That's down nine from this point last year.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And it's down 43 from 2024 at this point.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We have seen an uptick, as was noted, in e-bike and e-scooter fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And that certainly underscores the importance of the work we're all doing here today together.

chapters.summary: Menin asks about data on collisions between pedestrians and e-bikes, and whether NYPD contacts hospitals for missing data, and DOT says they are working on better data integration.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin asks about collision data and hospital reporting

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And what data does NYPD and DOT have on collisions between pedestrians and e-bikes, e-scooters, and mopeds?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Is there any additional data you feel will be important to have that the city currently doesn't have access to?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And then lastly, is NYPD regularly contacting EMS and hospitals to see whether there is data that they're missing on accidents and fatalities?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: To the second point, no, we're not.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: You do not?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: We do not, no.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Is there a reason why you don't do that?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: For the most part, when we have collisions or injuries that should be brought to the police's attention, we get called by the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So someone will reach out for the most part.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So I don't know that there are any misses.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: I can add here, Madeline Labde, Chief of Staff at DOT.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: I think the broader coalition work of all of our sister agencies on the Vision Zero Task Force, we have health and hospitals as well as the Department of Health and working with research institutions and level one trauma centers to engage them both in an

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: educational way as well as in a data way.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: So there are longer term plans that have been mentioned in the Vision Zero Reimagined Report the administration released earlier this month

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: that talk further about our goals for better integration of all the pieces of data from a collision to the streetscape to the hospital data in a more holistic manner.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: So there are lots of goals for linking all this data more fulsomely at each point and rationalizing it as well as ensuring that we are not having misses that are in ERs or other places around the city.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So for health and hospitals, you are collecting that data, but if it's not a health and hospital hospital, you're not?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Because I just want to make sure I understand.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: Yeah, I would have to go back and talk to our colleagues at the Department of Health who lead this coordination work with H&H.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, if you could please get back to the...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: the committees, but I really would urge you to be working with all hospitals because we're hearing from a lot of EMS doctors about this issue, which is something concerning.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I think there really needs to be a real plan here to be working with our hospital system on this so that we're actually getting fulsome data on this.

chapters.summary: Menin asks what the administration is doing about noncompliant retailers selling illegal devices, and DCWP describes inspections, summonses, and sealing orders.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin questions retailer accountability for illegal devices

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Moving along to retailer accountability and illegal high-speed devices.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So the council did an investigation regarding retailers and found that New Yorkers can still readily find and purchase illegal micromobility devices, both through brick and mortar retailers and online.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: What is the administration doing around noncompliance with our laws by those retailers?

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Madam Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: I'm happy to start, and then I imagine Commissioner Flynn will want to jump in, too, given their efforts on online enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: With respect to on-the-street enforcement, I'm pleased to report that just this last September we completed 276 inspections.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: The results are encouraging.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: The number of unique businesses inspected in 2026 is about up already 50% from where we were in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: The number of locations with the violations are down.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: The number of locations in compliance are up.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: None of this is to say we have solved the problem or that we don't have more work to do.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: We absolutely do.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: But our strategy of proactive compliance sweeps, paired with the possibility that these businesses can actually face ceiling orders, eight of which we've issued, some of which we then rescinded.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: after the

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: businesses came into compliance, I think demonstrate that we are making progress in effectively enforcing local laws 39 and 49.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Speaker, I would also add that of the 53 businesses we found not to be in compliance during the most recent sweep, 13 have already moved back into compliance and the other 40 are scheduled for re-inspection as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And how does the 276 inspections compare to the last couple years?

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Let me see.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: I believe in 2025, we were at 192.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: In 2024, we were at 317.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: That was a little bit of a wild west in 2024.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Again, we're going to hit more before the end of the year, but I am encouraged by the trends we are seeing.

utterances.speaker: Sam Levine
utterances.text: Obviously, we still have a lot of work to do.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, I have a lot more questions, but I want to be respectful.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We've got a lot of colleagues that want to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm going to save the rest of mine for second round and turn it back over to Chair Abreu.

chapters.summary: Abreu defines terms like motorized micromobility device, street legal e-bikes, and motorized scooters, and asks everyone to be precise when sharing data.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu clarifies terminology for micromobility devices

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker Menon.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I want to just make a note on terminology.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Before we begin with questions, I want to say a bit about terminology.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This is a complex regulatory space with...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: A mess of terms.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So I'm hoping this will help ensure we're all on the same page before we dive in further.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'll be using the catch-all term motorized micromobility device to refer to any motorized bike, scooter, hoverboard, or other device that is not a moped or motorcycle.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'll be referring to e-bikes that are currently legal to sell and operate in New York City as street legal e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: That includes properly certified Class 1, Class 2, and Class 3 bikes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'll be referring to e-scooters that are currently legal to sell and operate in New York City as street legal e-scooters.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: These are stand-up or sit-down scooters that meet state and city speed, weight, and certification requirements.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'll be using the term motorized scooter to refer to any motorized micromobility device that is not legal for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This includes e-motos, illegal e-bikes, or any illegal micromobility device.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And I'd like to make a request of all of us here today to please be clear and as precise as possible when describing these device categories, especially when sharing statistics or other data.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I know it's challenging and at times that term can be confusing, but let's all try our best.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks what percentage of micromobility ridership is motorized devices and how it has changed, and DOT says they don't have a precise breakdown due to private ownership.
