chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks for ridership breakdown of micromobility devices

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So starting off today, I would like to first get a general overview of the state of micromobility in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What percentage of total micromobility ridership is made up of motorized micromobility devices, including e-bike, e-scooter, and moped ridership?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And how has that ridership of motorized micromobility devices changed over the last five years?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: It's a question for Commissioner Flynn, I believe.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So just to clarify, just an overall synopsis of kind of micromobility in the city.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Well, we'll look up more specific numbers, but I can say, you know, at a general level, what we've seen is certainly a growth.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We know just across the board, and I guess on the point of terminology, I'll say cycling, but I mean really any kind of cycling and micromobility has grown by 60% in the last few years and continues to be the fastest growing mode as a percentage.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: You know, in the actual safety data, what we've seen was there was a spike a few years back.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And on the whole, we've seen the numbers coming in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: In general, this year, and maybe I can get the specific numbers here, but...

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Pedestrian fatalities currently at this point this year are at, I think, an all-time low or maybe tied for an all-time low.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Same for motor vehicle occupants and traditional cyclists.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Where we've seen the spike, as I mentioned earlier, was with e-bikes and e-scooters.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And I think that's a reflection that...

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Some amount, we don't know the exact amount, of traditional cyclists have adopted e-bikes for all the reasons you and others have mentioned, that they're convenient.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: and then a fast way to get around the city.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So at the moment, there's no percentage breakdown of micromobility ridership in terms of e-bike, e-scooter, moped ridership that you have at the moment?

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: No, in terms of ridership or ownership, there isn't considering there's so much private use and private ownership.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: However, we can defer to DCWP to speak to any of the information that they have specifically on delivery workers in that population.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I mean, look, it's important to have that breakdown.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I mean, I guess, you know, speak to the challenges of obtaining that breakdown and maybe a path to getting that breakdown.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I think it's important for us to understand what's actually on our streets.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: If we can't get that basic understanding, I think that poses a larger issue for us.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks if DOT has an estimate of how many Class 3 e-bikes are in the city, and Flynn says they don't have comprehensive numbers, only anecdotal data.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks for estimate of Class 3 e-bikes

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Do you have an estimate of how many Class 3 e-bikes there are and how did you arrive at this estimate?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: No, we don't really have great numbers for that, for the reasons that Maddie mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Many of them are privately owned.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So we have, you know, mostly anecdotal, I would say, based on either DCWP's data with delivery workers or the crash reports we would get from NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But we don't have that type of comprehensive number.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks for an estimate of illegal motorized scooters on city streets, and DOT says without registration requirements there is no single source of truth.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks for estimate of illegal motorized scooters

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And is it the same with respect to an estimate on illegal motorized scooters?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Any breakdown on that on our city streets?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And how did you arrive at that estimate?

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: So, Chair, I think this actually speaks to one of the important reasons for this council hearing today, which is we have a lot of information on car ownership because of all of the registration required at the state level.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: Without that information for these modes, we don't end up having...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please, please, if you would like to express yourself, please use hand gestures.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And again, if you're in violation of that, you will be escorted by the sergeant at arms.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: My apologies for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: But to speak to sort of the tracking of how we reach vehicle numbers, be they commercial, privately owned, or others, often that comes from a state DMV.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: It has a much more accurate data pathway because of the license requirement.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: This class, without any...

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: any license requirement, there isn't a single source of truth where they are captured in terms of the amount that are on the streets or that are sold.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks what percentage of collisions involve illegal devices, and Chief Obey says NYPD does not break down data by legal vs. non-street legal.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks what percentage of collisions involve illegal devices

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Of collisions involving motorized micromobility devices, what percentage involve illegal devices?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I don't know if PD has this information.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So we track very generally.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: I think the difficulty, I think, is one of the reasons why we're here today.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: We don't break down.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: The data and collisions by legal or non-street legal.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: It's just e-bike, stand-up scooter, that type of thing, but we don't do legal versus non-street legal.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Does the admin have a plan to begin collecting that data?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I think having that information, again, is very important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Totally understood, though I will say, and I think this will be coming up over the course of the hearing, right, part of the challenge is that

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: sometimes, particularly with e-bikes, being able to tell on its face whether it's a street legal or street illegal device can be very difficult to determine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Now, when you have a fatality and you have sort of an in-depth CIS investigation, we're going to be able to determine that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But to the extent, you know, talking about an accident, no fatality, no serious injury, and that's a serious matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm not making light of any accident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But I would say different type of investigation is going to go into that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: To the extent in every case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We would have to determine whether a particular e-bike is street legal or street legal on its face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's a complicated matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm not saying it's impossible, but that is very challenging.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks if the determination of illegality was based on max speed capability, and Flynn explains that for fatal crashes they have a breakdown, with roughly two of 17 e-bike fatalities involving illegal devices.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks about mayor's statement on illegal e-bike deaths

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I understand it's complicated, and I have a lot of questions on that later.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The mayor was recently quoted in a press release stating that since 2017, more than 45 people have been killed while riding illegal e-bikes, and more than 14 people have died while riding illegal stand-up scooters.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Is it correct that the determination of whether a given e-bike or e-scooter was illegal was based on its max speed capability?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can you explain in more detail how this analysis was done?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So we have that breakdown for fatal crashes.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And I guess just to go to your earlier question, for this year, what we've seen so far is that roughly two of 17 of the fatalities have involved in illegal e-bike.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Three were unknown, so it's possible.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And then for stand-up scooters, six out of 11 were illegal and four were unknown.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So that gives an idea.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks why the administration hasn't made prior assessments of illegal devices in fatalities public, and Flynn says they work to put crash data on open data and will look closer.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks why prior assessments weren't made public

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Was this the first time that the administration had assessed whether the devices involved in these fatalities were illegal or not?

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: We can speak to that.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: No, I think that any time that there is a fatal crash, the methods by which NYPD and DOT work together on immediate response and investigation and then analysis for

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: future street safety work shows that we're collecting a lot of information, including photo, video, and other information.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: DOT helps partner with NYPD's Chief of Transportation team to review the imagery from these more intense investigations and documentation to help assess the legality or illegality of a given device.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: So that can include reference the chart that we provided in our testimony, some of the pieces there of which category it may fall into based on its manufacturer and other information that the team supports with research.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: If this is not the first time that the administration had assessed whether the devices involved in these fatalities were illegal or not, why hasn't the administration made those prior assessments available to the public?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, so we work really hard and closely with PD to put a lot of crash data on open data.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I'd have to go look closer to see if this is on there, this level of detail, but it's something we're happy to take a closer look at.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks if DOT tracks infrastructural features of locations where serious crashes occur, and Flynn says they do a robust post-crash process and will follow up with specific breakdowns.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks about infrastructure features of crash locations

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Does the administration track the infrastructural features of locations where serious and fatal micromobility-involved crashes occur?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: For example, do you know what percentage of crashes occur on streets without protected bike infrastructure, without adequate street lighting, without traffic calming measures, etc.?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So we do a really robust post-crash process.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We have a team that goes out following NYPD to inspect the scene of a serious or fatal crash.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: They look to identify any immediate fixes that are needed, and then our safety planning team will develop any medium-term improvements that can address either that fatality or crash or just other issues.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We certainly do a series of different kinds of studies looking at different aspects of safety, whether it's correlating it to the type of bike infrastructure or other kinds of infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I don't think I have the numbers here.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So let's first say that you do, but the administration does track infrastructural features of locations.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Where serious and fatal micromobility-involved crashes occur, correct?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Okay, and if you can please follow up with my office with those specific breakdowns.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: That would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Happy to.

chapters.summary: Abreu notes cars have killed 66 pedestrians while e-bikes have killed none, and asks how DOT prioritizes ending road violence caused by cars and trucks.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu highlights cars as leading cause of death and asks about DOT approach

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The micromobility conversation often focuses on the potential risk posed by riders of motorized micromobility devices.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: But the data shows that cars and trucks remain the overwhelming cause of injury and death for our road users.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So far in 2026, cars have killed 66 pedestrians, while e-bikes have killed none.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Cars and trucks result in 95% of deaths and serious injuries on our streets.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Just as Monday, a woman was struck and killed by a truck driver who then left.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This tragedy marks the 10th hit and run by a vehicle driver in two months, and according to some reports, the 17th e-bike rider killed on New York City streets so far this year.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I want to extend my condolences to all these victims and their family members.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This is a real life.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Or death priority for me and all New Yorkers who walk and bike in our city.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And that's why on October 27, I plan to convene a hearing on the city's Vision Zero initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I hope that we can have a fuller conversation at that time, but for now, I want to ask, how does the administration's approach to micromobility policy prioritize ending road violence caused by cars and trucks?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, I would absolutely agree that, you know, this is a really nuanced,

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: traffic safety is a very nuanced topic, and that's why we really try to use the data to help us prioritize our resources, our investments, our policies.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And I would echo what you said about what the data is showing us.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So we want to focus on where the greatest risks are.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We released our Vision Zero reimagined plan a couple weeks ago, and I think you'll see in there really a reflection of that.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I think as you opened today's hearing with, you know, it's a, we need to keep that greater perspective, and micromobility is one piece of the overall puzzle of safety on our streets.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So I know we'll talk in a lot greater detail at that hearing, but.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Certainly our whole toolbox around Vision Zero, whether it's dramatically increasing our output of street safety redesigns,

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: whether it's looking at automated enforcement's role in it, which we found to be extremely effective,

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: whether it's working with the council or pursuing state-level legislation to increase accountability for the most dangerous and high-risk folks on our streets.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: That's all part of our approach.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And before I pivot to effective and equitable on-street enforcement, what more can DOT do to reduce conflicts between micromobility users and large vehicles, particularly in areas like Midtown?

chapters.summary: Abreu asks what DOT can do to reduce conflicts between micromobility users and large vehicles, especially in Midtown, and Flynn discusses bus lanes and systemic reviews.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks about reducing conflicts with large vehicles

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, right.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I think maybe what you're alluding to is that two of the recent fatalities were both on streets with bus lanes.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Well, 14th Street's a busway, 34th Street has the bus lane.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And I think, you know, I mentioned that we always, we look

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: in reaction every time there's a serious or fatal crash, but likewise, we're always looking systemically as well, right?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Are there trends coming up?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Maddie mentioned the Vision Zero Task Force.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: All the members of that, we examine the data, we see kind of what's bubbling to the surface.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So if there's something like a particular issue like that, if it's a bus lane or if it's interactions between

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: trash or other large trucks and cyclists, then that's something we'll home in on and we'll really do a deep dive on it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We'll do a deep dive on October 27.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks how many illegal micromobility devices NYPD has seized this year, and Chief Obey provides numbers for moped and e-bike seizures.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks about NYPD seizures of illegal devices

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How many illegal motorized micromobility devices has NYPD seized or impounded so far this year?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So when we seize motorized micro-lead devices, whether mopeds, e-bikes, or scooters, the decision to seize is based on

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: whether the device itself was used in the commission of a crime, reckless driving of an e-bike or e-scooter, e-bike or e-scooter operator under the influence of alcohol or drugs, or if it's an illegal device.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: That's a motorized scooter that is an illegal e-bike, illegal e-scooter, or an unregisterable, which is a moped, which means a moped that cannot be registered.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So year-to-date 26, moped seizures, 10,080.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: E-bike seizures, 1,206, year-to-date 26.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How does the number of seized illegal micromobility devices compare to the number seized last year?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: I just gave the moped seizures.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: I'm sorry I don't have e-bike seizures for 25, but I do have the year-to-date numbers for 26.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can you share those?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: No, I just share them.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You said you have the year-to-date numbers.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can you share that?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Yeah, so for moped seizures, 10,080, that's year-to-date 26.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: E-bike seizures, 1,206, year-to-date 26.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks what percentage of seized devices were used for commercial purposes, and Chief Obey says NYPD does not track that.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks what percentage of seized devices were commercial

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What percentage were used for commercial purposes?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So we don't track that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Any reason why you do not track that?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: What we do track is when it comes to seizures, again, our seizure reasons are based around this, not around whether that device itself is being used for commercial purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And also, the reality is that sometimes we're just not going to know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sometimes we will, obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You can imagine lots of situations where officers are encountering an unlawful motorized scooter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The user may not even be there, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And it's subject to, they're going to seize it for a variety of reasons, but they may not know when they're creating that voucher, for example, whether it was commercial or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So again, it would be very hard to track that in a systematic, thorough way.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks NYPD to walk through the seizure process from beginning to end, including determination, storage, destruction, and appeal opportunities, and NYPD explains.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks NYPD to describe seizure process

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can you describe NYPD's seizure process from beginning to end?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: For example, how is the determination to confiscate a device made?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I think you were getting into that, Chief Abbe, earlier in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Where is the device taken?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And when and how is the device destroyed?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And does the writer have any opportunity to appeal or retrieve their device?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Walk me through the beginning on the decision-making to confiscate.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Where the device is taken, and when and how the device is destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So, and building off of what Chief Obey was saying a moment ago, So the initial seizure may happen for a variety of reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: different reasons and that will affect a little bit the path this takes, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So it could be because it's being used in connection with a felony or misdemeanor and we do see that sometimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It could be seized pursuant to the administrative code, that's 19-176.2D, as a motorized scooter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: When it's being used in a dangerous manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It also may be seized as an unregistered motor vehicle under the VTL.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So when that happens, the device is going to be taken initially to the precinct of occurrence, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There it's going to be vouchered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Dodger saying, you know, where the device was taken from, and assuming we know who it was taken from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It'll be stored initially at the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: At some point, it may be transported to a property clerk facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That typically would be the pound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the process after that, so the question is going to be if we get a request

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: to return it or we don't get a request for return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That will take different paths.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So let's assume no request is ever made to get the device back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It will be held, if it was taken as arrest evidence in connection with a felony,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: felony or misdemeanor, we'll wait till the termination of the underlying criminal matter, plus 151 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Otherwise, if it was seized pursuant to that admin code provision I mentioned, or essentially pursuant to the VTL, 90 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If after that time period, no one's claimed it, it's gonna be destroyed, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If someone is coming to request the return of a device, so if it was seized as arrest evidence, obviously it's going to wait until the underlying matter is resolved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The person has to bring proof of adjudication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Let's say it was a criminal summons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If it's under the admin code of the VTL,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Again, assuming that there was, you know, you're going to have either an oath summons or it could be a B summons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The summons has to be adjudicated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The person comes to the command with evidence of the adjudication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And then the last point I want to make is that depending on the situation, right, if you have something that is an unauthorized motor vehicle, right, you can't just ride it away because you can't ride it on the streets of New York.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So in that situation, the person either has to get, you know, they have to show up with the relevant license and registration, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Or they come with like a flatbed truck, they can put it on the truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But we can't let someone ride away in a device that's unlawful to ride on the streets of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks what percentage of NYPD enforcement actions target non-UL certified devices, and NYPD says that enforcement is handled by DCWP and FDNY, not NYPD.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks about enforcement targeting non-UL certified devices

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What percentage of NY...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: IPD's on-street micromobility-related enforcement actions target non-UL certified devices compared to devices that exceed legal speed and wattage limits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So the non-UL, the UL issue, right, that enforcement is really not us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So that's in the admin code 20-610, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Is really about points of sale, and that's going to be on the UL piece, that's going to be DCWP or the fire department.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So NYPD does not do enforcement actions that target non-UL certified devices, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I want to be clear, though, because the relevant admin code provision that I believe you're talking about, right, is not about possession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's about selling it, renting it, the things you do at the point of sale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And actually, by statute, actually, PE does not have authority to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It is actually assigned to other agencies.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks what enforcement actions NYPD has done regarding legal speed and wattage limits, and Chief Obey describes point-of-sale inspections and seizures.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks about enforcement on speed and wattage limits

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So what type of enforcement actions have you done with respect to legal speed and wattage limits?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So you're talking about, like, for example, with the e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So there really are two different things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If you're talking about the inspections at points of sale, that'll actually turn it over to Chief Obey to discuss.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So with point of sale inspections, I just want to start by saying that we started these initiatives in 2021.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: And again, combining retail education, working closely with the DOT, inspections, and then enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So in 2021, which was phase one for us,

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: The focus at that time was on motorized two-wheelers, specifically mopeds.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So these are mopeds that are problematic in the sense that they cannot be registered.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So in all of 21-22, 127 inspections, 108 seizures, we issued 108 old summonses.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: In all of 23, 124 inspections, 61 seizures, 67 criminal, and 28 old summonses.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: We did the work through the first quarter of 2024, January through March 24, 263 inspections, 11 seizures, 19 criminal summonses issued, and 11 old summonses.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: In response to the concerns that we started to see with the trends in injuries and

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: collisions and fatalities with e-bikes, especially e-bikes that are, I mean, you know, the motorized tool world, especially devices that were higher powered or out of class e-bikes and e-scooters.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: In January of this year, NYPD and DOT identified 71 storefront locations selling higher powered devices.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: We selected these devices based on...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Commissioner, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I think you've been responsive to my question.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

chapters.summary: Abreu quotes the Vision Zero Reimagined report on removing illegal devices and asks if any agency opposes it, and they say no, and discuss equitable enforcement.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks about Vision Zero report and confiscation proposal

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I will now transition to my next set of questions, which is, first, I want to quote again from the Visions Zero Reimagined report.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: One of the Adamant stated goals is to perform, and quote, removal of illegal and unlicensed micromobility devices from city streets,

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: and quote, conduct targeted street sweeps and confiscation operations in areas with high concentrations of uncertified devices.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Do any of the agencies at this table oppose this part of the mayor's proposal?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: That's in the Vision Zero Management Report.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Just want to just get that on the record.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: No, I think...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Okay, all right.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So will it be implemented equitably?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We look to center equity in the way we approach all of our, whether it's design, enforcement, outreach.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So, yes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What does equitable enforcement look like in terms of the confiscations and the sweeps?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I just want to make sure, and you support, does the PD support the mayor's proposals?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And the key is to do this, right, to your point, in a fair way, in a data-driven way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We can't be everywhere all the time, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There has to be, this isn't half made about resources and deployment, and the key is to do that in a way that is data-driven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Not anecdotal, but where are we seeing concentrations when it comes to enforcement in terms of injuries, crashes, and deaths?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that should drive the decision.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So you're referring to objective measures?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks if a tool to objectively measure device legality would make confiscation more equitable, and NYPD says the idea is interesting but raises procurement and operational questions.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks if dynamometers would make confiscation more equitable

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So would a tool to objectively measure whether a device is legal make the mayor's confiscation proposal more equitable than reliance on visual inspection only?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You're talking about the dynamo.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'm getting towards that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Okay, sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: No, so...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: When it comes to the dynamometer bill,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You know, you are certainly right on the issue, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we think the idea of using this device is very interesting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It certainly speaks to the challenge that we have in terms of identifying street legal versus street illegal devices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So that's, I think, very important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Now, it is new to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It is new.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we do have a lot, a lot of questions about how we would use it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's new, I think, to any, it would be new to any major American city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so that raises a host of questions in terms of procurement and cost and operationally, sort of operational functionality, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: How would this work in practice?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: How would we actually do it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And those are a lot of questions.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And just so you know, I'm sure you know this already, the bill that I'm referring to only refers to the use of the technology.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: It does not speak to how it gets implemented.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And so it gives the agency, your agency, a lot of discretion on how that gets implemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I do think it's important, right, before we are legislatively mandated to do this, that we first work and work with you and your team and the council to explore these questions and the answers to those questions.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Will you join us for a demonstration of the use of the device?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We're certainly open to do that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'll invite you to that.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks how officers verify maximum speed and wattage of a device, and NYPD says they do not have technology to do that in the field.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks how officers verify speed and wattage currently

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How do officers verify the maximum speed and wattage of a device currently that they suspect of being?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Illegal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We do not have technology that allows us to do that in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There are times, right, we have, there are members of service, certain people on.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I got your answer on that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'll move to the next one.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How are enforcement officers instructed to treat devices that are designed to switch between a slower street legal mode and a higher speed unrestricted mode?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How are officers able to identify such devices that can change modes on the field?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: A lot of these devices, they can switch.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And they can be controlled by an app.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: They can be controlled physically.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How can you tell?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Right, and as I was trying to say before, there are members of service who have the expertise and the experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They will sometimes be able to recognize devices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There are times when you can look online, sometimes, and determine, based on how it's advertised, what the capability is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But to your point, it is true that

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: absent the experience and expertise, and given the fact that oftentimes how these things are advertised are not how they actually work in practice, without that, can someone just tell by looking at the e-bike what the maximum speed is?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: No, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And the reason I ask that question is that despite the switching of the mode,

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: a dynamometer can still test for the wattage power of these devices.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So even if they can switch in mode, it can detect the power of the wattage so that folks don't try to circumvent a dynamometer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And just to be clear, the dynamometer as a technology is able to figure out or determine that wattage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There's no question that that could be very useful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We do have, again, like on the front end, the sort of contracting process, which is incredibly important, has to be done with great care, obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But then also, operationally, how would this work?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: How would this actually work on the street?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And that's separate from utility.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And we can figure that out.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks how officers distinguish between Class 1, 2, and 3 e-bikes, and NYPD says in most situations the class is not relevant for enforcement purposes.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks how officers distinguish Class 1, 2, 3 e-bikes

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How do NYPD officers distinguish between Class 1, Class 2, and Class 3 e-bikes when issuing a violation or completing an incident report?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Which specific materials or information do officers rely on?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So in most situations, almost all situations, whether it's a Class 1, Class 2, or Class 3 is not actually relevant for enforcement purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There are some very narrow exceptions to that, but in the vast majority of situations, the question is, is it a legal e-bike or an unlawful motorized scooter?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If it's legal, whether it's Class 1 or Class 2 or Class 3, in most situations, it's not going to matter for us.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Are assessments made on the ground by the officer issuing a violation ever verified or double-checked by NYPD?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So I'm not sure exactly what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Again, if an officer issues a violation, does a supervisor or someone else verify that or you just take it for what it is and you move on?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Well, again, in many situations, right, if you're talking about sort of a random patrol officer on the street, they are...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Rarely going to be making determinations in the field of class one, class two, class three, or about maximum speed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: When we're doing inspections or we're doing an in-depth CIS investigation, that's very different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And there you have individuals who have tremendous expertise and experience with this, and it's going to be a much more in-depth process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But again, I want to emphasize that these determinations, class one, class two, class three, in the vast majority of situations do not bear on our enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Have officers ever made an incorrect assessment about whether a device is legal or illegal that has resulted in a violation being erroneously issued or thrown out?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: For instance, has a Class 3 device that is currently legal to operate, has that been erroneously confiscated by NYPD in the past?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Has that ever happened?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm sure that has happened.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Okay, and then if you had a dynamometer, would a delivery worker have been able to keep their device?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: To be blunt, if you're assuming that every patrol officer has a dynamometer, that's, I mean, I just, just to be, no, to be blunt, I, again, I, I,

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that a worker would have a Class 3 device in their hands today if that officer who erroneously confiscated a device would have that bike in their hands today?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If an officer made a mistake regarding the legality of the device, and if that officer had a dynamometer, that could have potentially, yes, there are scenarios where that would have prevented that from happening.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks if real-time objective verification of wattage and speed would assist officers, and NYPD says in the abstract yes, but practical considerations must be thought through.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks if dynamometers would help officers make determinations

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: My introduction, 986, would require NYPD to use dynamometers, portable devices that are capable of verifying the maximum wattage and motor-assisted speed of micromobility devices.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And finally, I'm just going to ask this question.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Would you agree that having access to a real-time objective verification of a device's maximum wattage and motor-assisted speed would assist officers in making on-the-ground determinations about a device's legality?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And again, in the abstract, the answer to that is yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: There are a host of practical, pragmatic considerations that just have to be thought through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That's all.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So I'm going to show you this photo right here.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I want to take a pause here and I'll show my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right, look at this.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Look at this.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I want to take a pause here and just stress how difficult it can be to distinguish between legal and illegal micromobility devices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: In each of these images, one of the devices is street legal in New York City and the

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The other is not.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can you tell the difference?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: No, answer that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I mean, you can't.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I am not going to ask you on this moment to try and verify which is which because I recognize that it is an unfair question.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: But I think seeing these types of devices side by side, one legal and one not, drives home how nearly impossible it is to tell what kind of device is which by just looking at them.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: If we want to be able to get the fast and dangerous illegal devices off our streets, and to do so without unfairly targeting or confiscating legal devices, we need a way to identify

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: device types accurately, and dynamometers will give us this ability and take the guesswork out of enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks if an eventual ban on Class 3 e-bikes is needed to transition away from devices over 20 mph, and Flynn says the administration supports restricting sale and rental but needs more time on a ban.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks about transition away from >20 mph devices

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I know that the administration shares my goal of getting fast, dangerous devices off our streets.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: According to the recently released Vision Zero Reimagined report, one of the administration's micromobility priorities is to transition New Yorkers and delivery workers away from devices capable of traveling more than 20 miles per hour.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: My first question is, and this is for Department of Transportation, do you think that any citywide effort to transition away from the use of devices capable of going faster than 20 miles per hour would have to involve

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: an eventual ban on the operation of Class 3 e-bikes in New York City?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So I guess I would start by pointing out that there are devices, two-wheel devices capable of going over 20 that already are legal in our city, like mopeds.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: They're regulated differently.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So I think, like I mentioned earlier, we want to look at a more holistic approach to how we classify, and honestly, a simpler and clearer approach, because as you mentioned,

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: visually or even just otherwise, right, even the chart in my testimony, it's complicated.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So as we mentioned in Vision Zero Reimagined, we do want to pursue state legislation that would clarify it.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But in the meantime, we feel that restricting the sale and rental of Class 3 e-bikes makes a lot of sense to help transition.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So an eventual banning on Class 3 is not something that the admin is willing to do.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I mean, I've heard from advocates 20 is plenty.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: These devices go up to 25 miles per hour, the legislation being considered.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Would have an eventual transition away for two years, which is normally the life of a ban.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I understand you're pursuing state legislation, which if we went through state legislation, it would require a class three device to be registered.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: If they were to be changed, yeah, in that way.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So is it fair to say the administration supports registration of Class 3 bikes pursuant to state legislation?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I think there's a lot of discussions.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I mean, that is the movement.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: If you do Class 3, it would have to be registered.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: If I may, there's a lot of discussions with stakeholders, legislators, advocates, and analysis, frankly, to understand what's the best approach.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting a specific approach.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I was just giving the example that Class 3 e-bikes are only one piece of the puzzle.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But, you know, certainly we want an approach that puts safety front and center.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: That would be the number one priority, and that would drive it.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I think we're still, you know...

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: With the specific bill, I think we would need more time to analyze the specifics, connect with stakeholders, and understand the impacts because the impacts would be significant.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And even if we were to assume that these, even if, just for the sake of argument, if the administration did support a class three registration pursuant to state legislation, these devices,

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: cannot be registered because they have no VIN numbers.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Do you recognize that?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, this would be a more comprehensive change to regulatory structures.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So given that difficulty, if we are saying that we need to transition away from devices that are 20 miles per hour, is the administration willing to leave anywhere between 60,000 to 100,000

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: class 3 bikes on our streets even though they're dangerous?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: No, we absolutely support the intent to cycle those out of the market.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Well, the intent is to ban them within an eventual time period that actually works.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: That gives enough workers the time to save for a new bike, but also making sure that we're getting these dangerous devices off our streets.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And if 20 is plenty, is the mayor's position that 25 is plenty?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So I think I think you're gonna say 20 is plenty 20 is plenty we do support the intent I think these are the kinds of discussions we'd like to have with the council and with other stakeholders before I turn over my colleagues for questions I know there have been you know conversations about

chapters.summary: Abreu asks NYPD if they wish to outsource street safety enforcement to DOT, and asks DOT if they have manpower to enforce street safety laws, and both say no.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks NYPD and DOT about enforcement responsibilities

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You know DOT, you know being the person, you know being being in the purview of enforcing street safety laws I just want to ask a question to PD first.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Do you wish to outsource your street safety enforcement to DOT?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And my question to you, Commissioner, is would you like to enforce street safety laws?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I think that's a massive question.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Do you have the manpower to enforce current street safety laws?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I will now turn it over to Councilmember Epstein.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks about the 15 high crash corridors, what data was used to identify them, and where they are located, and Chief Obey describes the data-driven process.
chapters.title: Chair Epstein asks NYPD about high crash corridors

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Bray.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I know it's going to be a long day for all of you, so I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And for the public here, thank you for sticking with us.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I know there are people still waiting outside.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We're still trying to get them in.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So if you're not staying, please get up your seats so someone who's trying to get in can get inside.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Can I first start with PD about the high

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: crash intersections.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You mentioned there are 15 intersections.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What data did you use to come up with those 15 intersections and can you tell us where those intersections are?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So we worked closely with the DOT.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: We could certainly give you what we used at the time, but this 15 corridors we established going back to 2024.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: One such example of a corridor I just mentioned was Ocean Parkway, 606166 precincts, and we maintained data.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Across those corridors.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So where are the 15?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Can you tell us where those 15 intersections locations are?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: It's the entire city, essentially.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: But there's only 15, right?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So we're not talking about 500.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: They cover multiple precincts.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: For instance, I'll give you...

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: I said Ocean Parkway, right?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: That's the 606661 precinct.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So I'm going to go by precincts.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Eastern Parkway, 717377 precincts.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: You look at 6th Avenue in Manhattan, it's the 1st precinct, 6th precinct, Manhattan South, Manhattan, I mean, Midtown North, Midtown South.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So it's essentially the entire city.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: It touches every borough.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And so what data did you use to determine that?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Did you use 311 data, crash data?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What did you use?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So essentially we go where the data takes us, and these are the locations across the city where at the time and even now, naturally the numbers are much better now, but we still maintain them same corridors.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: At the time it was spikes in fatalities, spikes in collisions and injuries.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Going back to Ocean Parkway again last year, March 2025, three fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: We had that horrific accident in March of last year.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: This year, as we said, zero fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, so I'd like the data for all 15 intersections because I appreciate that you're naming one, which is great.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: And we can name more.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: I have the data for all of them.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So it's something that we maintain.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: It's not an issue at all.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm happy.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm sure the public would like to hear it.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: Chair, we're happy to add to this as well from DOT.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: DOT analyzes, we receive NYPD's crash data, and then we process it and do the analysis.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: We help look at what the trends are that help drive our Vision Zero work, as well as DOT-specific work on street redesigns.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: So the corridors are arterial roads, 15 of them, not just intersections, but full corridors across the entire city.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: We can get you the list fully.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: But these are where we have seen the most fatalities and collisions, and they're the highest risk corridors throughout the city.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks if 311 data was used and if the list of corridors is public, and DOT says they use crash data and are happy to share the list.
chapters.title: Chair Epstein asks about data sources and public release of corridors

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And so, and just, so I'm just be clear, did you determine if there's a bus lane there, a bike lane there, to use 311 data on complaints to kind of assess these corridors?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: The data, the data just, we just looked at collisions, injuries, and fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Those, those are the three main factors.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So if, if there's 500 complaints about First Avenue and 14th Street, just an example, by my district and

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Board of Council, my Marlonis district, where we've seen a lot of injuries, but we haven't seen, you know, we did have a fatality a week ago, but like, how would that measure up if there's like hundreds of

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Is that a factor that you're looking at?

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: So I would say that DOT takes in 311 complaints, anything that comes to our correspondence unit or our arts program, which is sort of our in-house 311 for tracking communication from the public.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: We also work closely with all of your offices, with our sister agencies, with the mayor's office, and external stakeholders and institutions.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: That also includes our New York City public school system.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: So we are taking in inputs as it relates to what's on the ground from a street design perspective and reviewing those as well.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: So that would be housed within DOT.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And then that information is that shared out to the public so they know these are the 15 intersections that have high crash data?

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: I'm not sure if there's been a public release of this, but it's something where we've been out visibly.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: The High Visibility Corridors collaboration between NYPD and DOT has gone back several years, and it accounts for both an education and an enforcement component.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: So we are both DOT staff and NYPD officers are out there together on the corridor in sequence to ensure that folks are aware of what their responsibilities are as drivers on the road to be safe and to drive the speed limit

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: and to make sure that we are coupling that with enforcement after the education.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, it'd be great for us to have it too because obviously collaborations across the board.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You know, are there bike lanes at those intersections?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Are there bus lanes on those intersections?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What is the location that kind of why is that intersection you determined to be a higher?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I think there's a fuller information data set that might be helpful for all of us to be helping you ensure that people, you know, these locations are identified and we can help identify those locations to reduce incidents and reduce fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: We're happy to take any information from yourself or your colleagues and absolutely include it in our work.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I would love to see this data be made public because I do think it's important for us to know and the public to know that these are high crash areas.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And if something's not listed on that report, people could be like, hey, you know, this is a tough intersection.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We could look for some redesigns.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Maybe there's a way to, if there's a bike lane or not a bike lane, a bus lane or not a bus lane, what could you do to have a calming measures to help that intersection?

chapters.summary: Epstein asks how the public can get a corridor on the list for review, and DOT says they can reach out through 311, borough commissioners, or council offices.
chapters.title: Chair Epstein asks how public can request corridor review

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: And I would say that that is essentially the bread and butter of the work of the New York City Department of Transportation.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: We are thrilled to work with you on that stuff, and I think that we are happy to explore any sort of particular problematic corridors, intersections, or locations.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And then how would the public or us be able to get...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Concerning corridor on a list for further review?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I mean, we have multiple channels for folks to do that, right?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: They can reach out through 311.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: They can reach out to our borough commissioners'offices.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Obviously, we love to hear from our council partners and things you're hearing.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: from your constituents, community boards, of course.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So there's different ways for things to be elevated.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And as Maddie said, this is at the core of what we do, and we're always interested in refining it.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: But PD basically said they didn't use 301 data in determining these intersections.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It's a, yeah, so for that particular initiative between our agencies, it's really data-driven around crashes because that's the crux of the issue.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: But when we think about safety more broadly at DOT, we're thinking about all these different channels to get both quantitative and qualitative input.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks if data is collected on helmet use and infrastructure in crashes, and Chief Obey says they collect helmet data but not infrastructure data.
chapters.title: Chair Epstein asks about helmet data and infrastructure in crashes

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And just for these intersections, do we have data about whether helmets were used if it was a bicycle crash?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Like, do we have that kind of data?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: There was a fatality.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Do we know if someone had a helmet on or didn't?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Like, it was a car.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And, like, do we, do you, are we collecting that data?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, so if we have a fatality in an intersection and we're determining this high crash area, are we also evaluating whether people, if there was an injury of someone on a bike or a scooter,

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: was a helmet being used, were there safety measures, was it in a bike lane, near a bike lane, a bus lane, kind of what the infrastructure was in those intersections?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So not the infrastructure for sure, but the type of device, whether or not the deceased had a helmet, yes.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks if time of day trends are analyzed and what improvements have been made, and DOT says they look at trends and have made changes like automated speed enforcement.
chapters.title: Chair Epstein asks about time of day and lighting improvements

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: All of that is gathered by our CIS data team.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And you determined that in these areas, the time of day or time of evening,

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: where these incidents are occurring, have you determined that it's happening more like we've seen, you know, the data we've collected is in the evening, is that something you've

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: kind of made the determination, if you have, what improvements on lighting and support have you put into place in those intersections?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So I can speak to just one example, again, going back to Ocean Parkway, because we did a lot of work with the DOT.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: That collision was driven by speed.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So naturally, we reached out to our partners in the DOT, and I don't know if they could speak to automated speed enforcement along that corridor.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So that was one thing that...

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: I don't know if we could speak to that, but this is going back to March of 25.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Just a recommendation as to what we...

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, Chief.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Right, so I guess a couple things there.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: You asked about the infrastructure, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So absolutely at DOT, that's something we look at both in the immediate aftermath of a serious crash, but also obviously as part of our more systemic work across the whole city and prioritizing different corridors and areas.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So yes, and then you mentioned time of day.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Absolutely, we're always looking at trends in the data.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: One thing we've discovered is that with the, as we get to the fall and it gets darker earlier in the day, we do see an uptick.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Or, you know, we know, for example, that Halloween is actually one of the most challenging.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So we're always looking at different kinds of trends and then tailoring our approach and response.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks what modifications have been made on 6th Avenue, and Chief Obey provides collision data and DOT describes street redesign changes including widening bike lanes.
chapters.title: Chair Epstein asks about modifications on 6th Avenue corridor

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So, for example, I know you mentioned 6th Avenue and the 6th Precinct.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What kind of modifications have you made on 6th Avenue to kind of deal with that crash data?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You identified one of the locations was 6th Avenue, right?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So I just want to be clear that these are lengthy corridors that run the entire city.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, sure.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So I just gave an example of a location, again, 6th Avenue in Manhattan, touching on four separate precincts.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: We haven't had anything that I can speak to that I know personally.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Again, we look at what's core for us, which is fatalities, serious injuries, and...

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Serious injuries and collisions.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So if there is something along that corridor that really rises to that level, say we see a series of fatalities, God forbid, we throw everything at it.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: We're pulling our partners at the DOT, put our heads together, again, going back to Brooklyn, speed enforcement, automated speed,

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: enforcement type devices along that corridor.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So there are recommendations that are made after we see a spike, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So when there is something like that, then we get together and...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm asking specifically about the 6th Avenue corridor, because you mentioned the 6th Avenue corridor as a...

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: I could tell you about enforcement, I mean, what we've done, but...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Sure, what have you done in enforcement on 6th Avenue?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Okay, so I will tell you...

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Sixth Avenue corridor, again, the first precinct, sixth precinct, Midtown South, Midtown North.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: In 2026, year to date, 193 collisions.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Last year, 179, so up slightly by 14, but the year is not quite over yet.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Down in total injuries, 87 versus 104 from last year.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Again, year in 25, but this year to date is 87.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: And I will tell you that it's one versus one in terms of fatalities along that corridor, again, touching four precincts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If I may, I think part of what you see here is, you know, and we work very, very closely with DOT, is, you know, we have the enforcement piece.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's only one piece, obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: It's an important piece.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so, you know, we'll do the in-depth work that the CIS team does an incredible job looking in-depth at these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: collisions, we will drive enforcement, working very closely with DOT, who will then, they're looking at this in a more programmatic way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Obviously, they have lots of pieces here that are not the enforcement piece, whether it's education, whether it's structural issues.
