utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So it's very much a collaborative effort between us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We have the enforcement piece and DOT with the broader street safety piece.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And on 6th Ave specifically, just to put a finer point on that, we have been in the process of developing and implementing a range of street redesign changes.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: One thing that we were seeing there is because as the volume of cyclists and micromobility users has increased, the bike lane

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: starts to get congested, right?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And you may have a speed differential between the higher and lower speed micromobility.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So part of our redesign is actually to widen the bike lane to make sure there's enough space for cyclists to safely pass each other.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks about street calming techniques on 6th Avenue, and Flynn describes a holistic approach including geometry, signal timing, and curb extensions.
chapters.title: Chair Epstein asks about street calming techniques on 6th Avenue

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And you mentioned that the crashes are mostly auto-related.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So are there street calming techniques you're using, like on the 6th Avenue corridor?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: To slow that down to avoid additional fatalities on 6th Avenue.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Absolutely, and it's always a very holistic approach.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We're always looking at all the different aspects of the street and how it works and all the users.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So, you know, it's very rarely just like a...

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Here's the hammer.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Here's the nail.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: There's usually a bunch of different pieces.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So on 6th Ave, you know, it's things like the overall geometry, the number of travel lanes, the width of the lanes.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Is there space for curb extensions to slow turning vehicles and improve visibility?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It could be hard in daylighting.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: It could be things like the traffic signal timing, like I mentioned, the bike lane.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: And probably other things I'm forgetting, but it's really a soup-to-nuts approach.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It'd be great to see what those are in these top 15 intersections, what those activities are, so we are educated, so we can educate the public on what you're doing, because if I don't know what you're doing on

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: parts of my district or other people's districts, it's hard to know that the general public would have that information as well to say, hey, this is what's happening.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Is this improving this situation?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And if it's not, what other tools?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: could be available to us all to be able to improve those concerns.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: I'm happy to discuss that with my team.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, if you can get us in writing about what those, you know, in these five top 15 areas, in writing what you guys are actually doing, I think that would be useful for us to have.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks what NYPD does about sidewalk riding, and Chief Obey provides enforcement numbers and notes the three E's: enforcement, education, engineering.
chapters.title: Chair Epstein asks NYPD about sidewalk riding enforcement

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So I do go back to PD.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We've heard a lot from people over the years around people riding on the sidewalk.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And what does PD do about that activity?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: I think it's been mentioned here that enforcement is just one piece of it, right?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: For us in the traffic safety world, we talk about the three E's.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So enforcement, education, and engineering.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Sorry, that's the DOT end, yes.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: So as it pertains to sidewalk...

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Summons says, I'm just going to give you enforcement numbers, 2026 year to date, 711.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: Year end 2025 was 446 for e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: For e-scooters, 164 year to date versus 32 year end 25.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So you're saying you're giving people tickets for riding on the sidewalk?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Is that what you're saying, enforcement?

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: Chief Obey
utterances.text: But that's the enforcement piece of it.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Right.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks about DOT's public education campaigns, and DOT describes working with schools, distributing materials, and multilingual outreach.
chapters.title: Chair Epstein asks DOT about education campaigns

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And how about the education side for DOT?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You're going to kind of public education campaign you're running to kind of talk about that?

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: One thing I want to note, too, to Chief Obey's point about the three E's, because there's also an engineering component, we've actually done a real good amount of data analysis and found when we provide bike lanes, it significantly reduces sidewalk riding.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: So that just underscores kind of that we're taking this comprehensive approach.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: We could talk in a little more depth about just more broadly our education.

utterances.speaker: Mike Flynn
utterances.text: campaigns?

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: So we take public education really seriously.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: We think that, you know, an all-of-the-above approach, as the Commissioner has said, is really a critical piece of the success of Vision Zero.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: Education, you know, at every, you know, potential input, one piece obviously is the importance of educating our New York City school students.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: So we are working closely with the New York City Public Schools team, both in terms of a curriculum approach as well as a broader sort of engaging with the schools around the logistics around their actual facilities as well.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: So from a holistic perspective, ensuring that children have safe routes to school and know the risks of different types of devices in terms of their speed, the legality and all of that.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: We have also done public education campaigns in the recent past, especially as we started to see the increase in the use of micromobility devices on our streets in the recent years to remind people to get smart before you start.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: We distributed those materials widely to brick and mortar bike shops.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: and community facilities to our sister agencies and to the broader public.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: We also worked with stakeholders, including the delivery workers and their representative organizations, to really ensure we are going as far and wide as possible.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: DOT maintains a multilingual staff for engagement purposes out in the field, and we use them regularly.

utterances.speaker: Madeline Labadee
utterances.text: They are some of the same people that are engaging the delivery workers alongside DCWP staff, as well as engaging everyday New Yorkers for the high visibility corridors with Chief Obey's staff.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks if the high visibility corridors can be mapped and shared, and DOT says they are happy to share the list and collaborate.
chapters.title: Chair Epstein asks about mapping high visibility corridors

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, it'd be great to talk more about high visibility corridors and maybe if we can map those out in the city.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I feel like where I represent and live feels like a lot of bike issues are going on and a lot of safety concerns.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So I don't know if it's a high visibility corridor, but it'd be great to know that and then maybe figure out ways to do further collaboration because obviously we want people to be safe.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We want people to be able to work.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I mean, this is a balance we're trying to manage here.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks DCWP what policies they are working on to ensure both public safety and worker protections, and Levine says they are complementary and deactivation protections are key.
chapters.title: Chair Epstein asks DCWP about balancing worker protections and safety

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Can I go to DCWP just around that policy balance around worker protections and safety?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Kind of what policies is DCWP working on now to ensure we have those protections for public safety and worker protections at the same time?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Fundamentally, our administration and certainly our department feels that these goals, worker safety and worker well-being, are not in conflict.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: In fact, they're complementary.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: The points I made at the beginning is that the deactivation protections, for example, are an absolutely critical ingredient to a comprehensive safety strategy.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: At the end of the day, if workers feel that they can be deactivated arbitrarily without cause for, say, not hitting those delivery times, we're never going to have safety on the streets because we're forcing people to choose between their livelihoods and their safety.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We are also strong supporters, as you know, of the council's minimum pay rate, which we've been implementing and enforcing aggressively.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That's part of having a more professional delivery workforce.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You know, I think the apps wanted to have a model where they'd bring in tens of thousands of people to, you know, occasionally do deliveries, maybe not trained on what's safe, maybe not trained on the legal devices.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Our focus is on making sure you can actually earn a living as a delivery worker.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You can afford a safe device, know how to operate a safe device, and know that you're not going to be fired for putting safety first.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Just on the current deactivation protections and due process protections, do you think there are enough protections already within the law for workers to prevent deactivation without due process?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Well, I think when local law 34 takes effect in January, there will be.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Do you think there's additional protections that need to be put in place to protect those workers?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think that's a very good question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think we should have follow-up discussions around it.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I want to see how I want to make sure that the app companies are complying with 34.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I've made clear to them I expect compliance on day one.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But we should have additional discussions about whether that regime protects drugs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: from unjust detention.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And just, sorry, I would like to reiterate the commissioner's point as well about how all these systems or policies from our respective agencies are really working together.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Obviously, the work that PD is going to be doing on on-treat enforcement is critical.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: What we do to ensure that vehicles are affordable for New Yorkers and they have, they're able to keep their jobs and not be fired arbitrarily, that's critical.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: What DOT does on the traffic safety side of the enforcement question of holding, we're hoping to hold these companies accountable.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: This all works in tandem, and I think that coordination is what we're trying to bring to this legislative package today as well.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks if DCWP has a role in ensuring app companies require workers to have appropriate gear, and Levine says they don't enforce that but are concerned about unintended consequences.
chapters.title: Chair Epstein asks DCWP about vest enforcement and worker gear

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, I want to turn back to, I know Councilmember Brewer, Bill, earlier around vests and notices around workers.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Does DCWP have a role into ensuring that the

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: App companies are requiring the workers to have appropriate gear on for making that determination.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What oversight did DCWP provide to make sure that's actually happening on the street?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Well, we don't have a direct role, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That's not what we enforce.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: What I will say, and we're in regular touch with DOT and our other agency partners about this, is we do have concerns, candidly, that we don't want someone losing their job, possibly losing their place in this country because they don't have a vest on.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And again, I don't mean to minimize the importance of wearing these vests.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think it's highly important.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But as you said earlier, I do think it is important to strike a balance and recognize, yes, we need enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yes, we need to monitor this.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: No, we should not have workers losing the job for, say, a first-time infraction.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think an important point that was raised earlier was that

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: For years, the apps skirted compliance to certain laws in previous administrations.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And what Councilman Brewer's bill is going to be able to do is to connect noncompliance now with an implication on the apps license from DCWP.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So we're working closely with our colleagues at DOT.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I've been joining many calls with them and the apps and also with delivery workers as well to ensure that there is a smooth rollout of these requirements that doesn't have an unintended consequence of workers being deactivated.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But we're fully committed to enforcing that once it's in place.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks what role DCWP will play in overseeing app companies to ensure they don't pressure workers to break the law, and Levine says they will enforce deactivation protections and minimum pay.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks DCWP about app company oversight

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I do want to turn our attention to...

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I was just going to add on the commercial bicycling law enforcement that we've had over 5,000 workers taken.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: bicycle safety course so far.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And as Carlos mentioned, we're in active communication with the industry about the laws, including the vests.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So it's happening and we take it seriously.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Yeah, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And I appreciate that more training is always going to be helpful for workers and for the public at large.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: But I do want to turn our attention to the app companies themselves, because I think what we're seeing is pressure on the workers from the app companies.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And what role will DCWP overseeing those app companies to ensure that they are having workers not being pressured to do illegal routes, not going too quickly?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What can DCWP do to kind of make sure those app companies are having workers comply with the law and protect it?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I'm happy to discuss that, Chair, and then I'll also talk about how we're working with DOT on this as well and how we're going to deepen that partnership if this legislation passes.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We're very focused on a vigorous enforcement of deactivation protection starting in January.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Again, I cannot underscore enough that...

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: At the end of the day, all the training in the world, while critical, is not going to be sufficient if a worker goes out on the street and feels that they're going to lose their job if they don't hit these unrealistic times that the delivery apps are insisting on.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That is why we're going to enforce the just cause deactivation law aggressively.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It's why we're fighting for the minimum pay rate and enforce the minimum pay rate.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And it's why our administration is committed and supports the legislation that we're

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: have additional safety data reported to the administration.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Our suggestion on that legislation is that it should go to the Department of Transportation because they have expertise on street safety.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But I can assure you, Chair, that our agencies have been working hand-in-hand and will continue to work hand-in-hand to make sure this is a holistic and coordinated strategy to ensure safety on our streets and prevent arbitrary deactivations.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: If I may add, thanks, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I want to underscore we do appreciate the Council's attention to this because it's really true.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: The industry is dependent on access to our streets, our curb space, our sidewalks, but we have very limited insight into how they're operating and what the implications are.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We don't have the data that we need to really evaluate their impact on these public assets.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So access to that data would really bolster our ability to examine the transportation and street safety impacts of the model, of their delivery worker model, and would inform future investment and policymaking.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Yeah, no, it's really interesting that, you know, this is an industry relying on public.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: space, right?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: It is exclusively relying on public space and they're making money off access to that public space.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And there's some regulatory role, I think, that we are underutilizing to ensure that when they're using it, they're using it appropriately and making sure that they are held accountable.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And I'm wondering,

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: If you feel like, I hear what you're saying about the deactivation, but I'm not sure if you have even

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Once we get the deactivation, do you have enough tools to ensure the app companies are – do you feel like you have enough tools if the deactivation applies, goes into effect next year, to force the app companies to do the right thing in our public spaces?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think we do.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think you're absolutely right on your premise, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: These are companies that have built a business model on purporting to not employ their workers, not paying for the infrastructure they use, which are city streets, raking in tens of billions of dollars from New Yorkers,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: and leaving the responsibility of street safety to the government, to the police, to the DOT, and to others.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It's a broken business model that much of this legislation is going to go a long way toward fixing.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: In terms of our capacity to effectively enforce the law, I do have confidence we're going to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We are already working closely with worker organizations, including thanks to the support that you are providing to nontraditional worker organizations, to ensure workers understand their rights that take effect in January.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And I will add that I think our victory last week over DoorDash, and I was pleased to stand alongside you to announce that, demonstrates that this is a department

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: in this administration that's capable of taking on massive lawbreaking and delivering big wins for the city.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We are not afraid to take these companies to court, and if they violate our deactivation laws, we're going to do just that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Chair, I would also like to share that, just to echo Commissioner Flynn and Commissioner Levine's testimony, there are certainly bills in this package that we can see as adding additional tools to our enforcement mechanisms here.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And then now I'm

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So we certainly want to work with those.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And then additionally, there's a lot of bills here where the intent's there.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We just want to make sure that everyone's had a chance to comment on them, our delivery workers, street safety advocates, because ultimately we're in the first step of this legislative process where we have to hear these voices out if we want to develop good coordinated policy.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks if DOT and DCWP have the resources to analyze new data, and DOT says they have a sustainable delivery unit and safety analytics unit.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks DOT and DCWP about data analysis resources

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And my final question, just for DOT, DCWP, we're potentially going to give you a lot more ability to do that data collection.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You have the resources in-house to be able to analyze and synthesize that data so it will be useful to the public.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So I would say...

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yes, safety analysis is really core to what we do, and we have created this sustainable delivery unit.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We also have a safety analytics unit, but we have resources across.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So I think for this particular analysis, we do.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And, you know, I would just say that the Intro 1069, the bill would basically give us that ability to...

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We need to get the data, but then we can basically study it and promulgate rules based on what we're seeing there.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Abreu recognizes Council Members Krishnan, Brooks-Powers, and others, and notes Public Advocate Reynoso is present, then turns to Chair Feliz.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu recognizes additional members and turns to Chair Feliz

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Before we turn over to Chair Feliz, I'd like to recognize Council Members Krishnan, Brooks Power, Santa Suoso Morano, Ariel Naviles, and we've also been joined by Board President Reynoso, who's in the back.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you for joining us.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Chair Feliz.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks who is in charge of enforcing the vest law and what has been done to achieve compliance, and DOT and NYPD say they will look at training and enforcement.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz follows up on vest law enforcement

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chairs Abreu and Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So two sets of questions, one related to enforcement at the street level and second at the enforcement at the point of sale.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But before that, I just want to ask some follow-up questions to the

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: the questions that our speaker asked about the laws that we passed in 2017 related to the vests and also the IDs that these drivers have to carry.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So who is in charge of enforcing this law?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Is it DOT and DCWP?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So DOT is able to enforce, it's also in NYPD's code, so I believe they are also two folks, but I'll defer to our colleagues at NYPD to speak more on that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Right, so there's the street level piece, and then there's the corporate piece, the corporate regulatory piece.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You know, the corporate regulatory piece is really much more sort of for DOT.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It's not something that a patrol officer is going to do in terms of on the, you know, summonsing on the employer side.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: With regard to the street-level enforcement, as I said earlier in response to the speaker's question, we're going to take that back and look very carefully at that in terms of the training that we're giving to the officers.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: All right, so you're going to look at the training given to the officers.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What, if anything, though, has DLT or any of the administration done so far to get us to compliance with that rule?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So I know that this has been an issue over the course of several administrations.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So the introduction of the law early on over a decade ago started, I think, from a place where we're in a very different economy and use of our streets than we are today in terms of the devices and the companies that are out there.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So for the most part, at that time, DOT was enforcing at brick-and-mortar locations with sort of dedicated employee delivery workers and couriers.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Obviously, the landscape of the city has changed quite a bit since the original introduction of the bill.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Across the last two administrations, the Department of Transportation has sent letters about lack of compliance to the third-party delivery companies that are licensed by DCWP today and have been

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: rebuffed on those in the past in terms of formal compliance.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That is why it is so important to tighten up these laws in the proposed legislation, as well as other legislation that has passed recently affecting the CBL.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: How long does the administration think it'll take to get us to full compliance with that rule, or at least fair compliance?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think we'll need to have discussions with our partners and take a closer look at it.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What steps do you think we have to take to get us to a good amount of compliance with that rule?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Do you think we'll be able to make progress in six months?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: The joint staff of DCWP and DOT in our conversations regularly with the app companies have given them, I believe, a March 2027 timeline to be in full compliance.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks how NYPD prioritizes enforcement of e-bike, scooter, and moped violations, and NYPD says they focus on the most egregious violations and use data.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz asks NYPD about street-level enforcement priorities

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, so a few questions on street-level enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: As we know, micromobility devices provide a lot of benefits to our communities, and that could make enforcement on this issue challenging and complicated.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We obviously want to make sure there's a lot of interests and factors that we have to balance.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We want to encourage their use.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: They're great for our environment, great for congestion.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: They're great for the riders who are able to get from point A to point B very quickly, and we obviously don't want to over-enforce to the point where we'll discourage the use of these devices.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: At the same time, we want to make sure that they're used responsibly and safely.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: When these devices aren't used responsibly, they create foreseeable public safety risks for all of us, including the riders.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: When people drive these devices recklessly,

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: running red lights, speeding, driving on sidewalks, driving on the wrong way of a road, they create foreseeable risks of injury for all of us.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And obviously, people in our city should not have to worry about their safety when navigating our streets.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So a few questions for the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: How does the NYPD prioritize enforcement violations related to e-bikes, bicycles, scooters, and mopeds?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Is it by location, type of violation, history in the region?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Right, so I'll turn it over to Chief Obey in just one second.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think just at a high level, big picture, right, it's data, data we're getting from DOT, crash data, injury data, fatality information, obviously.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We're also getting, of course, we do get, and several council members have said this, right, complaints from the public, 3011 calls, issues raised in the community, and obviously all that has to go into it.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Again, it has to be data-driven.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It can't be anecdotal.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We're looking at the totality of the data we have, both in terms of DOT data, our own data, data regarding community complaints, and sort of looking at that in totality and being responsive to that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So with that, I'll turn it over to Chief Obey.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Okay, so in addition to what Commissioner Garber mentioned, I did touch on the point-of-sale initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: The goal there, again, is to remove unsafe motorized devices at these retailers, and I gave some testimony on that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So with enforcement, we have...

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: The numbers, I could certainly provide the numbers, but I do want to emphasize that we focus on the worst violators and violations.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So essentially, on the most egregious violations, reckless driving, disobey steady red light, disobey traffic control device, wrong way driving, disobey stop sign, fail to yield, that

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Those are the types of summonses that we focus on.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So I just wanted to just mention that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But we do have the data to e-bikes, e-scooters, that type of thing.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And we also have seizures also.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That's on the enforcement end.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks how many illegal mopeds NYPD has seized and about ghost plate operations, and Chief Obey provides seizure numbers and describes joint operations.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz asks about moped seizures and ghost plate operations

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, a few questions on mopeds.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: How many illegal or unregistered mopeds has the NYPD seized so far?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: This year and how do the numbers compare to the past few years?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I know you briefly touched on it earlier, but you just made it clear.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I did, and I just want to be careful with that because we don't make that distinction.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I'll give you the numbers, but we don't do illegal versus non-street, I mean, legal versus non-street device.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We just, you know, when we seize, we seize because it's an e-bike, it's a moped, it's a stand-up scooter, it's a motorcycle, that type of thing.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So there's no distinction that's made.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, so how many this year compared to the previous two years?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So for all the motorized devices, okay.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So for motorcycles this year, year-to-date 26, 46, 55.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: For mopeds, 10,000, 080.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: For e-bikes, 1206 versus 957.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Stand-up scooters for this year, 199.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Total two-wheel device seizures, 16,140.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Talk to us about some of the operations that the police department has in place to help remove illegal mopeds from our communities or mopeds that might be violating our rules.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I know it could be challenging.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'm sure all of us have seen videos.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: They're pulled over and they take off on police officers.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Something that I know you really like is ghost bed operations.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I could talk about that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That's one of the ways that we actually are able to...

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You know, attack the problem of illegal mopeds.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So I'll just talk about ghost plate operations real quick, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So with Ghostbait operations, just as it pertains to the tool with device world, we have conducted 29 joint operations this year.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Again, this is the multi-agency part of it.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: 418 arrests, 17,730 summonses issued.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: More importantly, 63 motorcycles and moped seizures in 2026 year to date.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So that's just one way besides the point of sale seizures and also ghostweight operations, especially for mopeds and motorcycles and mopeds.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks about challenges NYPD faces in enforcing moped rules, and NYPD says mopeds are easier to identify than e-bikes but pursuits are dangerous.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz asks about challenges in moped enforcement

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What are some of the challenges that the NYPD has had when it comes to enforcing the moped-related rules and seizing them if needed?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Well, I think, you know, we were talking before about the challenges with the e-bikes and sort of whether you can see being able to tell whether something is street legal.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So with mopeds, that actually is easier, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Because the mopeds, whether it's class A, class B, class C, those like motor vehicles or motorcycles, it actually is a class of motorcycle, which is a class of motor vehicle.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Has to be licensed, has to be registered, has to have a VIN.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So if you have a moped with no license or a license that's not a legit license, or if there is no VIN, or if it's not registered,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: right, that's subject to, there's going to be enforcement action, you're going to have a summons subject to a seizure.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: The challenge, Chair, which you alluded to, is to the extent you have mopeds taking off on us, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We have to be incredibly careful about that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: As you know, we tightened up our vehicle pursuit policy for all sorts of good reasons.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And so, you know, to the extent you have, you know, mopeds that are unlawful, that are moving or fleeing from us, that presents obviously very significant safety issues.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So, you know, a lot of that enforcement is going to be, you know, you're trying to engage with someone when they're stopped.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Or you have the moped on, you know, it's parked, it's on the street, it's attached to something, and then, you know, the officers are in a position to do the assessment as best they possibly can.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Is this a lawful moped without the danger that would come, obviously, with a pursuit?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, and how heavy would you say, this is something that I actually saw about a year ago, I would see very often police officers driving around with a large van and also driving around looking for mopeds, and generally they would engage when they were parked.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And based on what I saw, they were very professional.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: It was a very successful operation.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: They were able to seize it without any incident.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Obviously, the mopeds were parked, and the owners were sometimes not even around.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: How heavy would you say that operation is today compared to the last two years?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'm not sure I have data right here on the number of such operations.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We certainly do that, and that can be a very safe and effective way to do it, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: If we have a whole bunch of mopeds, for example, that are parked somewhere, we can bring a team there.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: This could be an inspection in a store, obviously, but it could be out on the street.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That can be ideal because you don't have the safety issues with the pursuit, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You just have the Lopez there, it can be assessed.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We can make sure we have the right people there in terms of expertise, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Members of service who have done this before, who know what to look for.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We can have members of the legal bureau actually on scene sometimes to help with those assessments, make sure we're doing it exactly right.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So we certainly do those quite regularly.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And that is actually a very good example of something that can be in response to community complaints, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We hear about community complaints.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Hey, there are a whole bunch of illegal.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: mopeds that are parked out here on the street or you know are here on the street okay we can get a team out there and make that assessment in a very safe and a very fair way

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: and we can look and see if we have data on the number of such operations I just don't have that here

chapters.summary: Feliz asks about data on tickets for illegally parked mopeds, and NYPD says they do enforce and will pull data.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz asks about tickets for illegally parked mopeds

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Yeah, and speaking about parked mopeds, do you have any data on the number of tickets that you've given for illegally parked mopeds that are registered?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: There certainly is enforcement activity there.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I know that's a big issue.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: You generally see that in commercial areas, 20, 30 mopeds parked in the fire lane, which is obviously illegal.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And to be clear, we're going to summons and seize those devices, irrespective of whether the device itself is legal or illegal, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: If you've parked a moped in a place where it is not lawfully allowed to be, like if you have a legal moped, but you just parked it on the street, that's subject to summons and to seizure.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So, look, we'll see what data we have on that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We certainly issue summonses for motor vehicles that are, you know, that are, let's say, partially on a sidewalk, for example.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We have to go back and see how granular the data gets and how much we break it down.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks about NYPD's strategy for addressing sidewalk riding, wrong-way riding, red light violations, speeding, and failure to yield, and NYPD says these are key priorities.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz asks about NYPD strategy for sidewalk riding and red lights

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What is the NYPD's strategy for addressing sidewalk riding, wrong-way riding, red light violations, speeding, and also failure to yield?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I mean, as Chief Obey said, what you've just recited are some of our key priorities in terms of enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You know, there are you've listed some of the key moving violations that go directly to safety, pedestrian safety, cyclist safety, the safety of everyone on the road.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And those that is what is prioritized.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks about the rise in grand larcenies involving vehicles and the role of moped thefts, and NYPD says they will get back with data.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz asks about theft of mopeds and grand larcenies

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, a few questions, and these are questions that we briefly chatted about at our last hearing a few weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: The theft of these devices, and obviously we're talking about rider safety.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: The city, especially compared to the pre-COVID numbers, we've seen a drastic increase in the rise of grand larcenies involving vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: That involves mopeds, correct?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It would include mopeds, yeah, yes.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Though I will say, and I'm not sure if this is where you're going, part of that spike, I'm not saying all of it, part of that has to do actually with issues in four-wheel vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We talked about this a few weeks ago, where there were certain types of cars that, finally, a flaw in the manufacturing that made them very easy to steal.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Criminals figured that out and realized that because of certain problems with certain types of vehicles, they could go steal them in record time.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That's something that we've worked on in a variety of ways, including by working directly with the car manufacturers to identify those problems and get them to actually fix them.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So certainly part of the story there is about deficiencies, I would say, in four-wheel devices, though you're certainly right that part of that is also

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: going to be thefts of mopeds.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: How many GLAs have we had this year, grand larcenies involving vehicles or autos this year compared to 2019?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Do you have that data?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We don't have that here.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We 100% can get that for you.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, so I looked at the data before we started the hearing, and they have more than doubled.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: It's about 4,000 versus over 8,000, so more than doubled compared to the pre-COVID numbers.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Do we think the theft of mopeds has contributed to that drastic increase?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I know you mentioned it's different vehicles that are easier to steal, but I'm wondering the extent that mopeds have played a role.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I got to say, anecdotally, I would think yes, but I don't want to say that definitively without looking at the data.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But that is something that we certainly do have data on that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We can look at it, and I think we can get back to you with a more precise answer.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, yeah, if you could get us data on that, that would be great.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks about enforcement at point of sale for e-bikes and mopeds, and DCWP describes inspections, summonses, and compliance trends.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz asks about point-of-sale enforcement for e-bikes and mopeds

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So a few questions on enforcement at the point of sale related to e-bikes and also mopeds.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: As we know, mopeds have to be registered in order for them to be sold.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: And enforcement of this rule is crucial.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I know the NYPD has done a lot of work to seize the mopeds.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: In our streets, but of course if we seize a thousand mopeds during a summer, and that same summer a thousand new mopeds enter our streets illegally, then we're never going to see any progress.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Enforcement of the rules at the point of sale is crucial if we want to make

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: progress.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We also have rules related to e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: A few years ago we passed my legislation that requires UL certification for e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We know that on certified e-bikes they cause a lot of fire safety problems in our communities.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Can you provide data on these two issues, enforcement at the point of sale of e-bikes and also mopeds?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: E-bikes on the UL certification, but also mopeds, the registration.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I know you briefly touched on it earlier, but if you could just give us a brief summary of the work you've done on that issue.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Sure, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I can start by talking about Local Law 39 with respect to micromobility.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We've had a very active year in terms of our point-of-sale inspections.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We conducted inspections of 294 unique businesses in 2026.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That's more than a 50% increase from what we saw in all of 2025.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And we are seeing encouraging compliance trends.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: About 53 of those businesses were in violation.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: The vast majority were in compliance.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Others that we began to seal came into compliance.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: With respect to motorized scooters, we issued 50 summons for violations of the motorized scooter law in 2026.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So we are encouraged by the trends, but we're going to continue aggressive compliance sweeps to ensure that these noncompliance figures continue to go down.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Does DCWP currently have sufficient authority to prevent illegal devices from being sold online?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think it's harder online, and that's why we've been working with the Department of Transportation.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You saw the announcement by the mayor and I believe by Commissioner Flynn a couple months ago about a pretty significant enforcement sweep.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We certainly issue summons to online businesses.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We do that all the time.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: If they're outside of the city, they can be harder to serve.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But we are working closely with DOT to improve the effectiveness of the enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I don't know if Commissioner, you want to add to that?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think, you know, on the cease and desist for online sales, so far we've been very encouraged.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I don't have the exact number, but I think over a dozen retailers have already complied, and we're in active discussions with most of the remainder.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You know, but we've also learned that some online retailers are more scrupulous than others, and we see things like, you know, not including the specs or other ways to kind of make it harder.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So as Commissioner Levine said, it's definitely more tricky, the online side of it.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And then, of course, there's the secondary sales market too, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So it just underscores the need for a real nuanced approach.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And I think a lot of the bills that are being considered today can help to...

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It can help us keep evolving.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: How many summonses have been given due to unlawful sale of these devices online?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: For online, I believe we've issued 86 cease and desist letters.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And we've issued, what's that for 2026?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And then we've issued 41 summonses to online sellers that don't comply with the cease and desist letters.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think that's cumulative.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks for updates on the trade-in program for uncertified e-bikes, and DCWP says most apps are using rental subscription models and they are working to strengthen access to safe devices.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz asks about trade-in programs for uncertified e-bikes

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, a few final questions on the trade-in programs that we've been working on these past few years.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So a few years ago, we also passed the trade-in.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: legislation requiring that the city create a program wherein riders are able to trade in their uncertified e-bikes or batteries for one that is certified and safe.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Can you talk to us about any, can you provide any updates on that, including how many certified batteries you've been able to provide?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yes, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Well, I think

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You know, that local law from, I think, believe, Local Law 95, if I'm not mistaken, it provided the companies with a lot of flexibility on how they could comply with the law.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: There were different models they could use, whether it was replacing bikes or offering discounts on rental subscriptions, for example.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It gave them a lot of flexibility in how they could comply.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think towards the end of last year, we had worked with our colleagues at City Hall to issue letters to all the companies, letting them know that they were on notice that had to be in compliance.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We followed up earlier this year to ensure that they would map out for us their plans for compliance as well.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thus far, we've received no complaints from a worker about not receiving some type of vehicle, either through the rental subscription model or not.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think most of the apps, if not all, are using the rental subscription model as how to comply with this.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That said, I think there's ways we can strengthen this access to safe devices, and I know our partners at DOT are working on that actively as well.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks about procedures for enforcing rules at point of sale, and Chief Obey describes the phased approach including education, inspections, and enforcement.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz asks about point-of-sale enforcement procedures

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, and going back to the issue related to enforcement at the point of sale, can you talk to us about the procedures and operations to enforce the rules related or at the point of sale?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I know this could be challenging, so just wondering what the procedures are.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Not challenging at all.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It's something that we've done since 2021.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And again, phase one, we do this work in phases.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: At that time, the focus was on mopeds.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We transitioned in 2026, January, to high-powered mopeds.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And out-of-class e-bikes and e-scooters.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So again, we do this work with the DOT.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: First, we tapped into local precincts, 78 of them citywide, to survey their commands and identify retailers that are selling these devices.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So they came back to us with 71 retailers identified citywide selling these illegal devices.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We reach out to the DOT.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: They do the educational outreach part of it, provide a flyer.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That flyer is instrumental to us in the sense that we provide it to our officers just to help again with why we're here today, make that distinction between whether devices legal or non-street legal.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It's helpful, just some of that language around it.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And also, we also provided that to the retailer.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So there has to be an education point.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You have to give notice to these retailers.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So after we do that with the flyers, then inspections, we start, and then enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So those are the steps that we've taken.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And again, like I mentioned, working again with the DOT.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: 63 stores were inspected as of September 21.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: From those 63 retail stores, nine e-bikes were seized from three locations.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And again, this is citywide.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Nine old summonses were issued for motorized scooter noncompliance.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: 57 criminal summonses were issued for other retail violations.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: For the most part, repeat, we go to the same locations.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: If we have to expand this, we'll do so.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But again, we work hand-in-hand with the DOT on this.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks if e-bikes can legally ride in bus lanes and whether it should be explored, and DOT says they will look into it and consider safety tradeoffs.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz asks about e-bike infrastructure and bus lanes

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, some final questions related to e-bike infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Are riders able to legally ride an e-bike or a micromobility device in a bus lane?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Happens all the time, by the way, and I think it's a great idea.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: But of course, we've got to make sure it's safe.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I don't want to speak out of turn, so let me just confirm that with the team and circle back to that question.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Chair.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, so you're not sure about the legality.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Do you think it would be a good idea to explore that idea, allowing micro-mobility device users to drive?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I think some cities have started doing that, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think it's definitely a question that we're asking.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I mentioned earlier that we're obviously aware that two of the recent crashes were in bus lanes or busways.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And I mean, we'll have to see to what extent, as NYPD does their investigation, that was a factor.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It's something we look at, right, and we have to.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So for sure, you know, it's something that we're going to be thinking about, especially as we expand the mileage of bus lanes and busways across the city.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Everything we do with streets is a tradeoff, right, because we have limited space, so we always have to think about how to maximize safety, accessibility, and mobility for all users.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But we can't always do everything on every street, so that's something we'll be looking at closely.

chapters.summary: Feliz asks what steps NYPD takes when bike lanes are blocked by garbage, cars, or encampments, and NYPD says they respond to 311 complaints and address conditions.
chapters.title: Chair Feliz asks about steps when bike lanes are blocked

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, and what are steps that the NYPD or any other agency takes when bike lanes are blocked?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Let's say by garbage, by cars, or by a representative.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Park Avenue in the Bronx, the area that has a lot of car mechanics.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Generally, you see very large car pieces completely blocking the bike lanes.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Also, I know we've had a lot of conversations about even homeless encampments.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: What are steps that we take on each of those issues when they're blocking a bike lane?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So again, garbage, cars, car pieces, homeless encampments, anything else that could potentially block.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Well, certainly, for example, like on the car piece, if we get a report, it could be a 311 call or otherwise of, let's say, a vehicle blocking a bike lane or something like that, officers are going to respond.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We're going to address the condition, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It's going to get removed and seized.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We'll summons the individual responsible.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Again, it's going to be sort of case by case, but this is actually a big part of what the Q team, or part of what the Q teams do, right, is responding to community complaints.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think that's the guy that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Someone calls 311 and says, hey, you know, the bike lane that I use every day is obstructed by someone has their vehicle there.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You know, we're going to, officers are going to respond and address the condition.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Do you have any data on that?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: How many tickets you've provided, you've given out due to blocked bike lanes?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I don't think we have it here.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Well, yeah, certainly we'll pull the data we have and we're happy to provide that.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Okay, and what are steps that the NYPD takes when it's blocked by other things?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Garbage.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: That's a homeless encampment, car pieces, anything that could potentially block a bike lane.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I would put the homeless encampments to the side because that's something that's really for the Department of Homeless Services and DHS to handle.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: In terms of other things, again, 311, we got a call like that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: If it gets referred to us, assuming it comes to us, the Q teams are going to respond, and their responsibility is to address the condition.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: If the NYPD sees a homeless encampment in a bike lane, are you guys able to refer the case to DSS, give them information about it so they could...

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We would certainly make the appropriate notifications.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But again, you're asking about clearing homeless encampments.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That's really going to be DHS.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I don't have any more questions for now.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Abreu says he will give the panel a five-minute restroom break.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu announces a short break

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And I promise within the next 10 minutes, I'm going to give the panel a restroom break really quickly.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Krishnan has a question, then followed by Public Advocate Jumaane Williams.

chapters.summary: Krishnan describes mopeds speeding on 34th Avenue Open Street and asks DOT to work with him on a micromobility lane on Northern Boulevard, and DOT commits to conversations.
chapters.title: Council Member Krishnan asks DOT about micromobility lane on Northern Boulevard

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs, very much for this important hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It's good to see you all, Commissioners and teams.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I just have one question in particular for Commissioner Flynn.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I know this is an issue we've talked about a bunch.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And, you know, just taking a step back for a second, you know, it's very clear in why this hearing is so important is that our streets are being used in so many different ways.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Those uses are proliferating, and they're outpacing our current efforts to address them.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so that gap is what we as a city need to address.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And there are different ways to do it.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: do so.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We've talked a lot about enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: There's also design, and I want to talk about design in particular.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: As you know, Commissioner Flynn, I've been a big champion on public spaces and safe streets.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We've got in Jackson Heights our 34th Avenue Open Street Paseo Park, which is the longest and most successful open street in the city.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I wanted to address the fact that we've seen a large number of mopeds speeding down our open street.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We've got six public schools there.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'm hearing repeatedly of children being hit or almost hit by mopeds, seniors.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Just last week, a constituent let me know that his five-year-old child was hit by a moped on the way to pre-K.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And the design solution that I think works very effectively is mopeds are using the bike lane on our Paseo Park, even though they're a class three motor vehicle.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Because they'd rather go on a street for pedestrians than go on a street with cars, and that's what we need to address.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Northern Boulevard presents a really important opportunity for a micromobility lane, one that will

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: allow mopeds that are vehicles to go where they should go and not in a pedestrianized space like our open street, and would make the open street and the neighborhood a lot safer.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I know that there is a bus lane on Northern Boulevard too, but I maintain that there are creative ways to ensure we have public transit like buses and a micromobility lane as well, and we can figure that out together.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So I just wanted to get a sense, and this is a solution, by the way, a micromobility lane on Northern Boulevard that's supported.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: by Safe Street Advocates, my constituents, the Deliverist does, because it gives them safe passage too as they go.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It's an all-around winning solution.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So I know we've talked about it a bunch, and I'd just like to know your willingness and openness to work with me as an agency to create a micro-mobility lane on Northern Boulevard and make the street safer for all users.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Council Member, and I appreciate your thoughtful framing of the issue.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It's interesting, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We have kind of two things that have been evolving rapidly in parallel since COVID.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You know, we've really seen an expansion and continues to be a priority of pedestrian space and, you know, more higher and better use of some of our streets and 34th Avenue is a great example.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: At the same time, we've seen this evolution in the micromobility space that we're talking about today that comes with challenges.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: 34Th Ave and Northern Boulevard are a really interesting case study, right, in terms of how we approach these issues, how, like I mentioned a moment ago, every street can't always do everything, and so we have to look at a network level as well, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: There's challenges with that, too.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We've identified Northern Boulevard as one of our bus priority corridors in our bus action plan, so there's a question of how, you know, we try to do all of these things.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And so to your last question, I would absolutely commit to having those conversations and trying to find the best possible solution.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I'll say in terms of the infrastructure side more broadly, we're really excited and proud that the mayor's made a history.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: level of investment in DOT, in our resources to ramp up our output, and we're definitely on track for a record level this year of bus and bike and other improvements like that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I do want to clarify one thing, which is, and I guess it gets back to Chair Abreu's point earlier about nomenclature,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: mopeds specifically are actually not allowed to be in bike lanes, so we would have to think about a solution, if we really mean mopeds specifically, you know, that works in that regard.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Class, you know, e-bikes, legal e-bikes can.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So it's just about those nuances.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And if you could just follow up with the council member's district-specific request, that would be great.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Public Advocate Jumaane Williams.

chapters.summary: Williams notes over 15,000 vehicle collisions and 90 deaths in 2026, says micromobility vehicles are involved in only 16% of injury collisions, and calls for a balanced approach.
chapters.title: Public Advocate Jumaane Williams gives opening statement

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: First, this chair still fits very well, so it's been a while since I've been here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Morning, as mentioned, my name is Jermaine Williams, Papa Garrett for the City of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I want to thank Speaker Menon, Majority Leader Abreu, Chair Epstein, Chair Felice, and the members of this community for holding this important hearing and allowing me to give this opening statement in the middle of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Our city is in the midst of a major transportation transition as more and more New Yorkers utilize electric bikes and similar vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
