utterances.text: We are responsible as lawmakers to update the regulations that shape the operation of our streets accordingly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Unfortunately, despite legal reforms and significant infrastructure investments, including roadway redesigns in recent years, our streets are still unacceptably dangerous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: City data indicates that there have been over 15,000 vehicle collisions in 2026 so far, resulting in over 90 deaths.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: One of these horrific incidences took the life of a teenage boy riding an electric bicycle right in front of my office this summer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I commend the Council for spotlighting this issue and for the many pieces of legislation that members have introduced to improve this dire situation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: It is vital that the city appropriately regulate electric bicycles and similar vehicles as their popularity continues to grow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: At the same time, I do want to highlight that only 16% of the vehicle collisions causing injuries or death this year so far have involved micro-mobility vehicles in any capacity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In 2025, New York will be 42 times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: more likely to be injured by a car than by a micro-mobility vehicle, and 35 times more likely to be killed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I mention that not because any harm is more than the other.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I want to recognize all of the harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I only mention that because any time we try to do any kind of change to car culture, the pushback is severe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And so I just want to make sure we're clear about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: My office has reviewed the administration's recently released Vision Zero reimagined report, and I believe it provides a foundation for further opportunities to strengthen the city's Vision Zero efforts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And I thank the Council for the Vision Zero data analysis released in August and Speaker Menon and Majority Leader O'Brien for their commitment to holding a Vision Zero hearing this fall.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I hope that the Council will pass the micro-mobility legislation and many of the legislations here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I know there's not a lot of time, but I'm going to submit this into the record of feelings that we have on many of the pieces of legislation that is here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I do want to highlight Councilwoman Wan's universal daylighting bill, Intro 511, which I think is extremely important for preventing both car and micro-bill vehicle collisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I do want to say, having lived and born and bred in this city for 50 years, I just want to be clear, and I say this all the time, when I'm walking as a pedestrian, I'm very angry at the bicycles and the cars.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: When I'm on my bicycle riding around, I'm very angry at the pedestrians and the drivers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And when I'm driving my car, I'm very angry at the bicyclists and the pedestrians.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And so I just say that because it is very true that we are all here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: human and just make sure that we understand that we all have a part to play in keeping everybody safe and that's important without ignoring that there are people who unfortunately violate the laws that includes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: our bicyclists and and people on illegal mopeds that we do have to get off the street so i want to work with everyone here to make sure that we're doing this with a lens

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: of humanity, of everyone, and preventing everybody from being harmed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: And so I appreciate the opportunity to speak.

chapters.summary: Williams asks how the city determines when e-bikes are speeding, and NYPD explains they use LIDAR and officer experience, but cannot assess maximum speed of a device.
chapters.title: Public Advocate Williams asks about speed enforcement technology

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I did have one question as I end this, and this may have been answered where I was going, but I know there is an issue that we don't have the technology to know when folks are speeding on mopeds and bicycles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So how do we determine that when we want to enforce

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: speeding regulations.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So I think we're referring to is the dynamometer issue we were talking about earlier.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: To be clear, the challenge is being able to determine what the maximum speed is of, let's say, an e-bike.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I want to be clear about the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So if I think someone is

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: speeding on a, well a moped, many of them shouldn't be on it, but like an electric bike that's going too fast, how do we know that if it's going too fast?

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I believe you don't know.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Okay, so on the speed end, how we currently enforce speeding, there's two ways.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: First, we have a device called LIDAR, that's L-I-D-A-R.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I apologize, I don't, it's acronym, I don't have the whole,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That is used just like the high, it's similar to what the highway officers use on the highway.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It's pointed towards the device itself and it's able to record speed.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: The other way is that officer has to tickle it, essentially saying,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Based on my own professional experience, I can determine that this vehicle, this particular device was going at a certain speed because near misses.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You know, we had pedestrians jump out of the way, that type of thing, or I was in my...

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Just to be clear, right, so you have situations where there's reckless driving.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: The person may well, in fact, be going way over the speed limit.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We may not be able to capture that in terms of a number, but to the extent they're operating their device, again, this is true for anyone, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: This would be true for a driver of a four-wheeled vehicle, traditional bicycle, micromobility device, whatever it may be.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: If someone is driving recklessly, irrespective of the speed, right, they're subject to a summons.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And then separately, there are circumstances where we have the technology to assess the speed at which a device...

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Actually is operating.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: What we cannot do, we do not have technology to

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: to assess what is the maximum speed of a particular device.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Just for clarity, there is a device now that you can use, and then you use the experience of officers to see if someone is speeding.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Carl Wilson asks what research informed DOT's determination that sidewalk detection technology is ineffective, and DOT says it is based on observation and industry conversations.
chapters.title: Council Member Wilson asks DOT about sidewalk detection technology research

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Hi, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: In your testimony, you said that the sidewalk detection technology is ineffective or doesn't work very well.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I was wondering if you could tell me a little bit about what research informed that decision or that determination.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So I'll need to check with the team on specifics of the research we did, but I know that we're constantly monitoring what's out there and tracking the industry and seeing what's available.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think it's based on observation and awareness of what products are out there.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And we're involved with various industry groups where we trade information and things like that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We're always trying to stay at the forefront.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We've had conversations with some of the operators as well and some peer cities.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So, I mean, at a high level, that's sort of what it's based on.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I mean, I would want to reiterate that we're certainly strongly in support of the goal.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So it's really just about trying to identify the specific tools that can get us there.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Just in conversations like that I've had with folks in the industry, they tell us that technology does exist and that it can work.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So, like, how often is that?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: reviewed?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: How often are you checking?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: You said all the time, but what does that really mean?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can quantify it, but we have a pretty large team devoted to Vision Zero policy research, analysis.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: They're involved with different groups.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We talk to the manufacturers.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: As you can imagine, the manufacturers come to us a lot.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Everybody has a product.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Everybody says their product can do everything and is great.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We have to try to unpack it a bit.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So, I mean, we're hopeful that the technology can get there, but at this moment, we're not confident.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks what benchmarks DOT would need to see to consider the technology accurate, and DOT says the main concern is distinguishing between curbside bike lanes and sidewalks.
chapters.title: Council Member Wilson asks about benchmarks for sidewalk detection technology

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Are there certain benchmarks that you would be looking to meet in order to say that this technology is accurate and could work?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yeah, I think our biggest concern is where you have, let's say, a curbside bike lane that's right next to the sidewalk.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Is the, you know, like the geofencing or the tracking, basically, of the location, is it sensitive enough to be able to distinguish that, such that if you are in the roadway on a device,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: and it thinks you're on the sidewalk, and so it starts to slow you down, what might the consequences of that be?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That's our concern.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think as a general rule, we always want to explore new things, but because of the scale of New York and the implications, legal liability costs, whatever they may be in a city this big,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We want to do pilot projects.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We want to kind of see something.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We want to learn from other places before we commit to large-scale adoption here.

utterances.text: I mean, we certainly like to have follow-up conversations on that because we, to your point, I do believe that technology can get there and should be getting there.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: But once big operators like Joko, they have 5,000 fleet, obviously not as big as some other actors, but if they're able to do that,

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: it's important that we also regulate the ride share ecosystem as a whole because you don't want to create an incentive for people to not do Joko because it slows them down on the sidewalk.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: It would have to be evenly applied.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So assuming the technology is there, would you be in support of this legislation?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a great point about the overall market.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You know, again, we're very supportive of the intent and would be eager to sit down and look at it with you and work through some of these questions.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: If the technology is there, I think we should be requiring bikes to slow down on sidewalks as part of ride share systems.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: That's my position.

chapters.summary: Phil Wong says hearings and legislation mean nothing without enforcement, cites victims like Priscilla Locke and Teresa Valenti, and calls for serious enforcement and safer street design.
chapters.title: Council Member Phil Wong criticizes lack of enforcement and street design

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Council Member Wong.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Much of our...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I had a set of questions, but they were already asked, so I was just going to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We have held multiple hearings on e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We have introduced legislation on e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We have held press conferences, rallies, and written op-eds.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We can keep doing that until the cows come home or until they ride down the bike lane the wrong way.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: But none of it means much if the city is reluctant or refuses to enforce the laws already on the books.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My predecessor, Robert Holden, advanced Priscilla's law after Priscilla Locke was killed while legally crossing the street with the light.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: The e-bike rider ran a red light, struck her, and tried to flee.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Too often, victims and their families

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: are left without accountability because these vehicles have no license plates.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Riders cannot be identified.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And enforcement is simply not taken seriously because there's no way to locate them.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I'm also thinking about my constituent, Teresa Valenti.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Who was killed near the Brooklyn Navy Yard by two people riding a souped-up e-bike.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Her death was not only a failure of enforcement, it was also a failure of street design.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: In fact, these souped-up kits are still available.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: When I checked this morning, you can still go into T-Mobile and buy them.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And we have to talk about how we're going to close that loop because...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Nobody, there's no system in place to stop any bike rider to order these kids and soup up their bikes.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Now she got off, Teresa Valenti got off a bus and was forced to cross a bike lane on the sidewalk just to reach the pedestrian path.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And that is dangerous, nonsensical design.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: But DOT approved it.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And in fact, even today, that lane, the bike lane is still there in the same location, waiting for the next accident to happen.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And I can name many other streets with that design in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So this is a two-part problem.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Weak enforcement against reckless and illegal behavior.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: that too often design streets without basic common sense or adequate regard for pedestrian safety.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We do not need another glossy announcement, but we need serious enforcement, real accountability,

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: safer street design, and a willingness to make clear that pedestrians, not reckless riders, not illegal high-speed devices, and not corporate delivery platforms come first.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Do you have a question, Council Member?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: No, that's just a statement.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right, please keep it down in the chambers if you can.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right, Council Member Palladino.

chapters.summary: Paladino says the city has allowed the bike industry to take over streets, criticizes lack of enforcement and accountability, and calls for pulling back on bike infrastructure.
chapters.title: Council Member Vickie Paladino criticizes bike culture and lack of enforcement

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let me echo what my colleague in council just said, Phil Wong.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: 100% Phil, you are on spot on, as was Bob Holden when he introduced Priscilla's Law two years ago.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Again, like we talked about earlier, Phil had just said, about how nothing is going to work unless something is reinforced.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This is absolutely cellophane.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This is nothing.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: You know, I'm looking at this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This is again and again and again and again.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: We have allowed, we have allowed, this city has allowed the bike industry to take over our streets.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And all we're hearing about here today is how people are getting hurt, how they're supposed to be on safe streets.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: There are no safe streets.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: So long as these bike riders own the streets and drive on the streets as if they own it.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Then you go to the cops here and you talk to the police officers as if, what are you doing to enforce the law?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: What are they supposed to do if the law isn't even being enforced?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: None of these people are licensed, registered, or insured.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: They pursue chase, and what happens to the police officer when they pursue chase?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: They get in trouble.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Enough is enough.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: We are sitting here in city council today to try to rectify a situation that you have allowed to get out of control.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Also, GOP, let me ask you this.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Please keep it down.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Let the council member speak, please.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This is what the bike culture has become in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And we have the bike lobby led by the lobbying group, otherwise known as Transportation Alternatives, and their propaganda outlet known as Street Blogs to thank for it.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Does anybody know about the young guy, 41 years old, that was killed in Central Park yesterday by a bike rider?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Okay, 41 years old in Central Park.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Because they're using Central Park as if it's some sort of Tour de France.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Enough is enough.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: You want to pull this in?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Get these bikes.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: You've got to start from scratch to tell you the God's honest truth.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This has got to all be pulled back.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: I know I'm speaking in terms that you don't want to hear, but the reality is we let this go wild.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: With no accountability.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And now here we sit, three years later, I'm sitting in this chair, four years and six months, and you know what?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Nothing has changed.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: It's only gotten worse.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: You show me a street design that works.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: We had Shaker up here talking about how his safe streets, now all of a sudden,

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: The bike riders are taking over his safe streets.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Oh, my goodness.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Is that new to anybody?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Fix the problem.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: The problem lies right here.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: We've got laws.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: We've got to get them enforced.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: But I mean enforced.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This is ridiculous now.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please keep it down.

chapters.summary: Shirley Aldebol says underage children are riding e-bikes and e-scooters unsafely without helmets, and asks what data or enforcement exists, and DOT says they are working on age verification.
chapters.title: Council Member Aldebol asks about underage riders and e-scooter companies

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Aldebar, followed by Brooks Powers.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: We're in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you for speaking today.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I have a, the issue in my district, I don't have e-bikes, share e-bikes in my district.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: We have scooters and e-gliders, which I saw recently.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The big issue is that a lot of kids, underage children, are riding the e-bikes, e-scooters, riding them on the sidewalks, unsafely, without helmets.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Even your 16 and 17 year olds who

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: you know, are allowed to ride the e-scooters.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: None of this is being enforced.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The age requirement is not being enforced.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Riding on the sidewalks is not being enforced.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: It's a serious problem.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: People are, you know, we get a tremendous number of complaints

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: through my office at every meeting that I go to, complaints about kids riding the e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'm not blaming all the issues on the kids, but it is a problem that is increasing and not being enforced.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You have two, sometimes three kids riding on a scooter at a time, weaving in and out of traffic, weaving in and out of pedestrian traffic on the sidewalks.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: It's a serious problem.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you have any data or any way that we can have the e-scooter companies ensure that underage children are not riding

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: e-bikes or any way that...

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: We can enforce safety for these rideshare companies.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Because I blame the rideshare companies.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Somehow it's being allowed, and the rideshare companies are not doing anything about it.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And they don't care as long as they're making money.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: So any recommendations or any data on this?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So I think there's a couple of dimensions to that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We've seen an increase in both privately owned as well as the shared micromobility.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Obviously, those have two kind of different...

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: solution, right, different approaches to how we might solve, if it's privately owned devices and parents are letting their kids do it, that's one thing.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Education for us would be a big piece.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: For the shared programs, like the shared scooters, I'll just note, you know, that for City Bike you have to be 16 or older, and for the scooters share, you need to be 18 or older.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We talked earlier about the age verification, and as I mentioned then,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We're committed to finding a solution that can both ensure safety of young New Yorkers on our streets as well as their privacy.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So it's something we're certainly committed to, and we're actively working through some of those.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Sorry, Council Member, your time is up.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Brooks Powers, she's going to give her opening and then start the clock when she starts the questions, please.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So not yet.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Selvena Brooks-Powers introduces Intro 110 expanding commercial bicycle laws to all electric devices, and Intro 787 requiring NYPD quarterly reporting on targeted traffic enforcement.
chapters.title: Council Member Brooks-Powers introduces Intros 110 and 787

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And to all of the chairs and members of the committees for hearing my legislation a part of today's package.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Our streets are changing faster than our laws.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: E-bikes and scooters.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Scooters serve as an essential mode of transportation for New Yorkers every day and a key source of income for thousands of delivery workers, but illegally operated and uncertified vehicles have raised

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Real and urgent public safety concerns.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The two bills I am sponsoring today, Intro 110 and Intro 787, help hold accountable the businesses that profit from the delivery system and increase reporting and transparency on how the city conducts

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: traffic enforcement on these vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Intro 110 would expand the city's commercial bicycle laws to cover all electric bicycles, mopeds, and motorcycles.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: This places responsibility for the safety and oversight on these vehicles where it belongs, on the businesses and apps that profit from delivery.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Businesses that use such delivery services for commercial purposes would be required to provide safety equipment, identification, and safety information to their delivery workers, as well as maintain records of their delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Intro 787 would require the NYPD to report quarterly on its targeted traffic enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Where these operations occur, how the decision to conduct them is made, the number of summonses issued, and specifically, enforcement directed at e-bike and e-scooter riders, with a year-over-year comparison.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: As part of this,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: full package, the city will work to enforce safer streets, and this bill allows the public and this council to know how it is happening and who is being targeted to do so.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: In previous hearings of the Transportation Infrastructure Committee, we were unable to get clear data on where e-bike and e-scooter violations were most prevalent.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So this bill aims to bring that data forward.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Together, these bills and this full package help bring solutions that don't just criminalize delivery workers, delivery drivers, but make us safer by addressing and understanding the real dangers for all e-bike and scooter operations.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: We can do that while protecting the New Yorkers who depend on these vehicles to make a living or just to get around.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I want to thank the advocates, the workers, my colleagues, and everyday New Yorkers who continue to inform this work.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I look forward to working with the chairs and the committees to move Intro 110 and 787 forward and to hearing from all stakeholders today.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how DOT enforces existing commercial bicycle requirements and if it can extend to mopeds and motorcycles, and DOT says it supports the bill and will work on refinements.
chapters.title: Council Member Brooks-Powers asks DOT about Intro 110 enforcement capacity

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I wanted to ask a couple of questions on my legislation.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So I will just ask them and I can repeat whatever needs to be repeated in the interest of time.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So particularly regarding Intro 110.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: For DOT, Intro 110 would extend the commercial bicycle laws to mopeds, motorcycles, and e-bikes used commercially.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How is the department currently enforcing the existing commercial bicycle requirements, and does it have the capacity to extend that enforcement to these additional device types?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What would the department need to require and verify that businesses provide safety equipment, identification, and safety information to their delivery workers under Intro 110?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And then for Intro 787 for NYPD, hi Chief Obey, it's good to see you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Intro 787 would require quarterly reporting on targeted traffic enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Does NYPD currently track its targeted enforcement operations in a way that would let it produce this report?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And if not, what is the gap that exists?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And then how does PD currently decide where and when to implement targeted traffic enforcement directed at e-bike and e-scooter riders?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And for both agencies under Intro 787.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Several bills today, Intro 787, 989, 1052, create new reporting.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How will the administration make that data consistent and shared across agencies rather than siloed?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So generally, how do the relevant agencies here today, DOT, NYPD, DCWP, coordinate their data?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And needs to one another so that we can really use it and see what we're trying to find through the data.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: There were a few questions there, so I'll maybe start higher level and then happy to dive in if I missed anything.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So I just want to be clear for Intro 110.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We support the bills in 10 and look forward to working with the Council to strengthen and modernize the commercial bicycle law to reflect today's landscape.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We agree the requirements and protections of the CBL should apply to delivery workers regardless of what device they use.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And that this bill would help modernize the section of the law to ensure workers on devices other than e-bikes are also covered by the law, most urgently moped users, which we know are currently excluded, and this bill would close that loophole.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We're looking forward to talking more about any specific recommendations we have.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please keep it down in the chamber.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Let the commissioner speak.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please keep it down in the chambers.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So, yeah, we know the landscape has changed a lot, and we're looking forward to working with you on exactly how to refine it.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think you asked about resources, council member.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You know, we're always evaluating that, and we collaborate a lot with our partner agencies as well.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So, you know, I think that's something we're comfortable with.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yeah, I guess if there were specific other questions.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks if NYPD can produce the quarterly reporting required by Intro 787, and NYPD says they have no objection but want to discuss reporting obligations.
chapters.title: Council Member Brooks-Powers asks NYPD about Intro 787 reporting

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Majority whip, Hanks.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Sorry, if Petey could just answer their question.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So there are a number of questions there for us.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I'm going to try to answer some of them, and then I think Chief Obey is going to take the question about the factors that go into deployment decisions.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: With regard to interest 787,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: totally understand what's behind the bill and understand that you're looking for data about outcomes, the different types of enforcement being taken, where it's happening.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Understand that and no objection to that and happy to work with you on a bill that gets you what you need.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: You know, the one place where we do want to have a conversation with you, Council Member, in your office is, I'm not sure if this is intentional, but there's a way to read the bill that would seem potentially to require imposed disclosure obligations or reporting obligations, you know.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Like every time Chief Obey is making a decision about the deployment of resources and explaining what's going into that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And I'm not sure that's what's intended, but to the extent, you know, we would have to report every time Chief Obey is making deployment decisions and what's behind that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I mean, that happens every day, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Sometimes it happens multiple times a day.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That would be very challenging.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It would.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And then in particular, to the extent the bill would require us to explain

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: potentially every shift in deployment and what's behind that, that'd be very challenging.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It's not typically what we see in reporting bills, but I do wanna emphasize that in terms of where we're doing enforcement, the types of enforcement, how that looks geographically, no objection to

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: getting you that information in the form that will make it most useful to you and to other city agencies and to the public.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And we do share data with DOT all the time.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Just as to your question regarding kind of how the department thinks about deployment in this space, I want to turn it over to Chief Obey.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I just want to put it simply by saying we go where the data is.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But one of the things that we do is we focus on high visibility to corridors.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I mentioned that earlier, and I'll go through it very quickly.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Fifteen corridors identified citywide.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Again, the decision behind the identification process for those corridors were really based on spikes in fatalities, collisions, and injuries where we saw.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Spikes in those criteria.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: One such corridor I mentioned prior to getting here was Ocean Parkway last year.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: One of the things we do, we see a horrible incident like that, horrific collision, three fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We get together with the DOT, throw everything we have at it.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: resources, all of that, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Again, that corridor covers three commands, so that's how we, but essentially all 15 corridors touch the entire city.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So,

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We threw everything at it.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Year-to-date 26, there's zero fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Year-to-date 26, total collisions are down along the Ocean Parkway Corridor.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Total injuries are down, moving violations are up, and vision zero movers are up.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: When you look broadly along all 15 corridors, there's a decrease in fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That's always our number one goal is to drive down the numbers.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Along those 15 corridors, it's 11 versus 17.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We're down six fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Again, every life lost is one too many.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: There's a decrease in injuries, decrease in total collisions.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Vision zero movers overall for all 15 corridors year to date, 74,272 vision zero movers were issued along the 15 corridors.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So this is the type of attention we put along, you know.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So that's one strategy.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Another thing also is ghost plate operations.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We kind of hit that two ways very quickly.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We work with law enforcement partners, PAPD, MTA, just to name a few, TBTA, PAPD.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We have had this year, year to date, 26, 29 joint operations.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And again, ghost plates are cars that display fraudulent, expired, mismatched, no plates, all of that, that world.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: 418 arrests, 17,000 plus summonses issued, 1,817 vehicles seized, and 63 motorcycle and moped seizures.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And then also locally responding to community complaints, we'll see a parked vehicle that is a ghost plate.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: This is one.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: where our traffic agents come in, and for obstructed plate parking summonses.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: They've written 166, 236 summonses.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: This is, again, by our TEAs.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: When it's on the street by uniformed personnel, this is obstructed plate moving summonses, 20,719.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Arrest made for temp tag fraudulent arrest, 1,833 year to date.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So we have that just broken down.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I also wanted to mention a third thing that we see.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Which helps us move from spot to spot.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Again, just looking at spikes.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: One thing we've seen recently is two things.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Lack of seatbelt compliance, when you see that, it means occupants have been ejected out of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We'll attack that by PSAs, reaching out to our partners, New York City, New York State DOT.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So when you look on the highways, you'll see buckle up and that type of...

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Information on there.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But we have short-term initiatives to address that along certain corridors.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So speed is one of the things that we'll do in this particular case after a rash of a tragic incident, speed and seatbelts.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: As it pertains to the micromobility world, we mentioned this earlier, point of sale initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We started that in 2021.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We've continued this year.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I would say great success.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: The work has not ended.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We're identifying additional retailers, and we'll continue to do so.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Again, our enforcement, we have the enforcement numbers.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We do target a number of violations, the worst of the worst, and that's reckless.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Driving, disobey steady red light, disobey traffic control device, speeding, because we know speed kills.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Chief Obey.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I see you have a very responsive answer there.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

chapters.summary: Kamillah Hanks asks for data on e-bike, scooter, and moped injuries and seizures in Staten Island precincts, and NYPD says they will get back to her.
chapters.title: Council Member Hanks asks for Staten Island data on injuries and seizures

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'm now going to turn it over to Majority Whip Hanks.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair, and thank you all for coming here today.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: It's a long hearing.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: And yes, that response was very thorough.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: I learned a few things.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So, of course, I'm always going to go with the Staten Island enforcement and results and questions that really relate to our outer boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So the report gives citywide injury and death tolls, but no Staten Island or precinct breakdown.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So Intro 787 would require reports on targeted...

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Traffic enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many, you know, for the same period, can you tell us how many e-bike, scooter, moped riders were injured or killed in Staten Island's 120 and 121 precincts compared to last year?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So I don't have that on me, but we can get that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We'll get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: That's great.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: I actually own a Vespa.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: All transparency.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: And just as a follow-up, what seizures or summonses occurred in those precincts, and will NYPD work with the out-of-borough local elected officials to make sure that these figures are published regularly?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We'll get you the data on seizures and also run, you know, what you asked for.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: No wishes at all.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hanks asks how Staten Island workers would access the trade-in program and how DCWP would enforce the Class 3 ban against online sellers, and DCWP describes its enforcement strategy.
chapters.title: Council Member Hanks asks about Class 3 ban and trade-in access

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So how, this is regarding to the Class 3 ban and how that would work.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Intro 244 would ban sales and rentals of Class 3 e-bikes with civil penalties up to $2,000.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: It addresses sellers.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: A separate proposal on the agenda addresses riding these bikes.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: How would Staten Island workers access the trade-in program proposed by Intro 985A, and how would the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection enforce 244 against online sellers serving New York City?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Maybe I'll start and then turn it over to Commissioner Flynn.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So in terms of enforcement, we'll pursue the same strategy we've been pursuing, which is really a four-part strategy.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We want to get out and educate the businesses.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We then do inspections.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: If we see violations, we issue summons.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: If we see repeated violations, we'll actually go ahead and seal the business.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Online, as I testified earlier, can be a little harder.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We've been partnering closely with DOT on this.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We've been issuing a number of summons to online businesses.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: DOT, I believe, sent some cease and desist and demands to online businesses.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I expect the pace of that is only going to increase.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And we're really going to encourage members of the public who encounter these devices illegally, let us know about them so we can take follow-up action.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And you are going to see a whole-of-government approach to enforcement there.

chapters.summary: Hanks asks what the public and council can do to help with enforcement, especially regarding ATVs, and NYPD says they do targeted enforcement and want to work with her office.
chapters.title: Council Member Hanks asks what the public can do to help enforcement

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So one second.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So that would lead me to the follow-up is what do you need from the public?

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: What do you need from us to help?

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Help us help you because

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: In Staten Island, we have those ATV four-wheelers that we now know that law enforcement will not give chase.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: They will not try to accost any person riding these ATV four-wheelers.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: But the public also doesn't really understand or know how to report these.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: It's become a big trend where there'll be 20, 30 ATV or riders in a particular neighborhood will call NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: NYPD will say, well, we can't give chase.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: We have to kind of like figure out where they're going to park and then we can go after them after that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So a few points.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: First, I just want to, I mean, with regard to the vehicle pursuit policy, it is true that we tightened that up substantially.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: There are, of course, times when we do give pursuit for felonies and certain types of misdemeanors.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: But you are right that to the extent we're not talking about that class of crimes, you know, otherwise we're not going to be engaged in what can be very dangerous vehicle pursuit.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So in terms of ATV enforcement, this is something that's very important for the department.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: For any ATV, you can't ride on the streets of New York City, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Period.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And as we were saying earlier, often those operations, and we do do targeted enforcement on ATVs, and we'll send teams out.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: For example, if we know there are a number of ATVs that are parked somewhere, that's an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: As long as we're going to try to engage with people when the ATV is stationary.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So to the extent the concern you're expressing is that in your district, we're not being responsive in that regard.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We want to be responsive.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: This is something that's actually very important.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And we collectively are happy to work with you in your office and identifying these issues and working with the commands there to be responsive.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks if DCWP has examined whether trips per hour per worker have increased since Local Law 15, and Levine says they need more data and support the legislation for trip-level data.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks DCWP about Local Law 15 and trips per hour

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We are, I know the public testimony is.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I know you guys are getting a little impatient.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'm getting messages, but we have the admin here, and we have still a few more important questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: In response to Local Law 15 of 2021, DCWP set minimum hourly pay rates for app-based delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: As of April 1, 2026, the hourly pay rate is $22.13 per hour.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Based on basic microeconomics, in order to lower operating costs, the new pay structure might incentivize companies to try to squeeze as many trips per hour out of each worker.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Has the administration...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Potentially DCWP, examine whether trips per hour per worker has increased since Local Law 15 of 2021 was enacted?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Well, I think that observation is spot on, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I was just having conversations during the break with some of the delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: or in the audience about the immense pressure they feel to hit these deliveries on time or face deactivation or worse.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I think the reality is that is our inference, but we do need to see more data on it.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That is why we do support the legislation for the app companies to provide additional

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: traffic data, safety data, trip time data.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: As both of us have expressed, we think that data should go to DOT, but I can assure you once again that our departments are going to be working very closely together

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: to ensure that we have a framework that is holistic, that addresses these app company incentives that are putting all of us at risk.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks why trip-level data is vital for understanding unsafe delivery times, and DOT says it is critical to correlate incentives with safety outcomes.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks about Intro 1069 and trip-level data importance

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: My bill, Intro 1069, will directly address this issue by requiring app-based delivery companies to share trip-level data and requiring DCWP to use that information to set rules around safe delivery time standards.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We need to make sure that in the transition from trip-based to time-based,

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: pay for delivery workers, we are not giving companies license to push delivery workers to make unsafe decisions in a race to keep up with unrealistic timeframes and expectations.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I was pleased to see in the recent Vision Zero Reimagined report that obtaining trip-level data from delivery companies is also one of the administration's priorities.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can you speak to why trip-level data compared to more high-level data is so vital for understanding and addressing unsafe delivery time conditions?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And how does this data differ from the data that you already collect from third-party delivery companies?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yeah, it's really critical for us because right now we, as Commissioner Levine said, we have little to no insight into exactly how the incentives of these delivery algorithms basically

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: play out.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And in order to correlate how do different incentives or number of trips or length of trips or time of trips or location of trips relate to the safety outcomes, we need that trip level data.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We need to disaggregate it, right?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We want to preserve privacy, obviously, but we really need that.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And ideally, we need it connected to the crash data, like trip to crash level, so we can directly correlate it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks about the Parks Department pilot allowing e-bikes on park drives, and DOT says they work with Parks and NYPD but defers to Parks on the pilot's future.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks about Parks Department pilot program for e-bikes

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Now my next set of questions are actually

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Since I have you now, Commissioner Flynn, and then I'll go to DCWP, and then I'll be hopefully done soon.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: In June 2023, the Parks Department launched a pilot program to allow the use of street legal e-bikes and e-scooters on park drives and greenways, which is expected to end on December 31, 2026.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: While the Parks Department isn't one of the agencies represented here today, DOT and NYPD both play a role in the regulation of and enforcement against the operation of micromobility devices on park drives and greenways.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And so I have a few questions about the pilot program that I'm hoping you can provide some insights on.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: To start, can you please describe how DOT and NYPD works with the Parks Department to enforce the laws governing the operation of micro mobility devices in parks and greenways, including with respect to the ongoing pilot?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We work closely with the Parks Department and obviously with our colleagues at the NYPD to assess any sort of bike network.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Park drives are an important piece of the bike network citywide in terms of where people have a safe place to bike.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That in particular includes...

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Folks who are less skilled, newer bikers, children, and more casual riders can often find more safety where there's no risk of cars.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: We obviously have looked at the potential situations both in the collisions that have been mentioned today in the parks as well as in the past

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: and on park drives and work closely with the Parks Department and NYPD to assess if there are interventions needed, be they design or from NYPD site enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I'll pass to my colleagues at MIPD if they'd like to add anything else.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: As I mentioned, the pilot program is currently scheduled to end on December 31st, 2026.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can you please confirm whether that is still the plan?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I'd have to defer to my colleagues at Parks.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I know I'm aware of the pilot program.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I'm aware of that date.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I have to assume it's being actively looked at, but I honestly can't speak to that today.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether extending the durations on the table, or is there anything else the administration is considering with respect to this effort?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yeah, I can't.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: That's not our...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So it's a parks-related question.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Is that your position?

chapters.summary: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps is administered the oath and states his name for the record.
chapters.title: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps is sworn in

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can I please take administrative oath of our deputy chief?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Can you please raise your right hand?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before these committees and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: And if you could just state your name for the record, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps, Executive Officer to Patrol Services Bureau.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks about the lenient penalty structure under Section 20-610, and DCWP says they are open to changing the first-time penalty structure and are seeing more compliance.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks DCWP about enforcement against retailers under Section 20-610

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: My last set of questions are against, sorry, not against, are enforcement against retailers by DCWP.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: According to previous statements from DCWP, Department of Consumer Worker Protection, one issue the agency has encountered regarding enforcement against retailers is that Section 20-610 of the Administrative Code,

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: which prohibits the sale and rental of uncertified e-bikes and batteries, is too forgiving.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This is because when a business first violates such prohibition, DCWP can actually issue a penalty, as Section 20-610 provides that the first violation carries a civil penalty of $0.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Only after catching the business violating 20-610 a second time,

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Within two years of the first violation, can DCWP issue a fine, and even then the fine is only $250.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: However, despite these issues, it appears the city's enforcement efforts continue to rely primarily on Section 2610.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can you explain the issues DCWP...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: W.P.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Has faced in enforcing Section 2610 and whether DCWP still feels that its penalty structure and particularly the inability to find a business for their first violation makes it harder to achieve compliance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think it does, Chair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: As a general matter, we're a law enforcement agency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I believe strongly in the importance of deterrence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And when you get a get-out-of-jail-free, so to speak, for your first violation, that doesn't deter the worst conduct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I will say that our enforcement is having results.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We are seeing more compliance by businesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: A lot of these businesses quickly do come into compliance, and I want to recognize that maybe they were not aware of their legal obligations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But given the very serious issues that the council and our city are confronting around safety, I think we'd be very open to a conversation about changing the first-time penalty structure for these laws.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks why DCWP primarily charges under 20-610 despite its issues, and DCWP says they look at violations across the board and most enforcement is on the street.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks DCWP about enforcement under Section 20-762

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: As you know, the penalty structure under Section 20-762, which contains the city's ban on the sale of motorized scooters, is much less lenient.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: If DCWP finds a business to be in violation of the motorized scooter ban, a civil penalty of $1,000 must be imposed, which increases to $2,000 for any subsequent violation within one year.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: However, we see much fewer fines issued by DCWP for violations of 20-762.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This is surprising as it seems that most devices that would be illegal to sell under 2610 would also be illegal.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: to sell under 2762.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can you please explain why DCWP continues to primarily charge businesses with violations of 2610 despite its penalty structure issues?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And does DCWP have a policy to always assess whether a business could be charged with a violation of 2762 when conducting investigations for violations for 2610?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: On the last part, Chair, yes, when we do an inspection of one of these businesses, either online or in person, we're going to look at violations across the board and issue summons accordingly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We've issued 50 summons against illegal motorized scooters over the last nine months of 2026.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think what that number doesn't capture, though, is the very large number of citations and tickets that NYPD, and confiscations, I should say, that NYPD has issued, which is part of the administration's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So most of the enforcement, I would say, Chair, is on the street rather than point of sale.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So regarding 2610, you're open to changing the penalty structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I believe, yes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And with respect to 20-762, should we expect more enforcement on that statute for...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The sale of these devices that we believe can also be just as captured, you know, equally captured under 2610?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, let me respond in two parts, Chair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: With respect to the changing the penalty structure, I think we would be open to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: My understanding, though, is that Local Law 39 does set the first-time violation at $0.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That was done by legislation, not by rulemaking, so we would need to work with the council in order to change that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: With respect to motorized scooters,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I think our enforcement approach reflects the fact that when we do an inspection, we're looking for violations across the board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The fact that we have 50 summons for motorized scooters versus a lot more for other violations suggests to me that most of the violations are not happening at the point of sale and that most of the confiscations NYPD is engaging in, it is likely, and again, I don't want to swear by this,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: it is likely that many of those folks got those devices from outside the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But certainly we would be open to conversations with the council about how to strengthen point-of-sale enforcement.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks about DCWP's policy of returning to businesses after violations, and DCWP describes their escalation process including re-inspections and sealing orders.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu asks DCWP about re-inspection policy

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Yeah, let's have continued conversations on both sections, talking about what the offense should be for the first offense and the amounts.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: That can be an active conversation.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: That would be greatly appreciated.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: When DCWP charges a business for a micromobility-related violation, do you have a policy of returning to the business some period?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Of time after the violation to see if they are in compliance.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I understand that Mr.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Ortiz says there's re-inspections that will be happening, but just curious to learn more about that policy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely, and this speaks to the escalation

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: process I described earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If we see violations, we're absolutely going to issue summons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're going to do re-inspections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If we see recidivism, we will issue sealing orders, which we have done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Some of these sealing orders we can pull back if the business then does come into compliance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But what you've seen just in our most recent sweep, which was

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I guess it's this month, September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We found 53 businesses not in compliance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: 13 came into compliance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The other 40 we're going to be following up.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I would add to Chair that, or sorry, Majority Leader, that...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Both is fine.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: You can just call me Carlos, too.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: That, you know, when we encounter, if we go into business and we see a lot of Local Law 39 issues or conditions that reflect perhaps a fire safety issue, we will notify FDNY immediately.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And they also have sealing authority under the newest amendments of Local Law 39.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Relatedly, if we see a vast amount of motorized scooters, while we're not able to confiscate, we will notify the NYPD of the presence of motorized scooters so they can confiscate.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: So again, that speaks to the coordination that has to happen between our agencies.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And Chief Obey, Commissioner Obey, I just want to apologize.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I think I pronounced your name Ebe earlier.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I meant to say Obey.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Santosu also, followed by Hanif, and then we'll switch over to public testimony.
