chapters.summary: Kayla Santosuosso describes recurring issues with micromobility devices in parks, including a child hit by an e-bike, and asks how NYPD enforces in parks, and Deputy Chief Alps explains their approach.
chapters.title: Council Member Santosuosso asks NYPD about park enforcement

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I will try to make this brief.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: My question is for the NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: You know, we're talking about pedestrian.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: in safety in a lot of ways today when we're talking about micromobility safety and regulating micromobility devices.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And the chair touched on issues in parks specifically.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I know parks is not before us.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: But I think one of the things that we haven't talked about as much today is pedestrian safety within parks and the enforcement of micromobility devices where they do not belong already in parks.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So the laws are already there, but enforcement is what we're relying upon.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I'm bringing this up because in addition to the numerous recurring issues that we have in my district with micromobility devices in parks, we have a park with an outdoor track next to Fort Hamilton High School, if anybody's aware of this.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: It's Russell Peterson, next to Russell Peterson.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And this is a place where children and families go to walk and run along this circular track.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: The micromobility devices are not permitted on the track.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: It's very clear.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: There's signage.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: This is a recurring issue.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And weeks ago, a child was actually hit and taken in an ambulance to a hospital, hit by a micromobility device.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So we have a persistent problem of a lack of enforcement, which on what is technically parks grounds.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And so my question to you is, when there is a recurring issue within parks, which admittedly parks probably doesn't have the enforcement capacity to,

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: the capacity to enforce, what does that pipeline look like to the precincts and to the NYPD so we can make sure that there's a regular enforcement presence somewhere like that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So this goes through the patrol service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I'm going to ask Chief Alps to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: So the average officer on patrol reports up to my office, and we give direction on how to do that type of enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: Very challenging situation, parks, in that individuals sometimes do not stop when we try to stop these individuals.

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: And it's a very congested area.

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: There's a lot of pedestrians and people enjoying the parks.

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: So do that type of enforcement inside a park is risky.

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: What we like to do is do that type of enforcement on the outskirts to address those.

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: Unregistrable vehicles on the outskirts so they don't make their way into the park.

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: But there are times that we do go into the park and we do that type of enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: And we like to do it when the vehicle is stopped.

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: For instance, Central Park is a challenging environment to do that type of enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: For the most part,

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: Officers step out, they stop any bike or bicyclist in some case if they're operating in the wrong direction of travel or they're operating on a pedestrian path.

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: The conversation starts, they introduce themselves, they ask them why they're stopped, they're told that their body-worn camera is activated.

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: And everything's being recorded audio and video on video and they ask them do you understand why you're stopping them and they understand they understand why they're being stopped and we do enforcement when it's necessary

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: So we are successful in addressing these behaviors inside the park.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Can I ask how that approach would change if the individuals on the bike were minors under the age of 18?

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: So we wouldn't allow them to drive away with that bike because they can't be operating that bike.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: That appears to not be happening because the same group of young people continue to operate within that park.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So we can follow up on details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I was going to say, we'd very much appreciate, you know, following the hearing, following up with you in your office, please.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I guess I would just say we've spent a lot of time today talking about delivery workers, and I understand that, but there is also an issue of youth improperly using these devices that I think deserves its own discussion.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: But thank you for answering the question.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I have one quick thank you to give to DOT while we're talking about pedestrians.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Last time you were here, I bothered you about the 17th Avenue Pedestrian Bridge, which there was no work for seven years, and you have surprised me, and there has been lots of progress in the 17th Avenue Pedestrian Bridge, so thank you so much for all of your work in making that possible.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Hanif, and then we'll transition to public testimony.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks what reforms are underway to improve street safety and working conditions for delivery workers, and DCWP and DOT describe deactivation protections and the Sustainable Delivery Unit.
chapters.title: Council Member Hanif asks DCWP and DOT about reforms for delivery workers

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader, and thank you all for being here.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What specific reforms or rulemaking are currently underway at DCWP and DOT to improve street safety and working conditions for delivery workers?

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Deputy Chief Thomas Alps
utterances.text: I think the most important rule that we're implementing right now with the

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: the street safety is our deactivation protections that the council passed last year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: As I've testified earlier and throughout this hearing, we are never going to have safety on New York City streets if our delivery workers feel they need to choose between their livelihood and their safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: If they feel, as Chair Breyer said, that the app companies are imposing unrealistic delivery times on them such that they have to cut corners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We are committed to vigorous enforcement of the deactivation rules, and I should add, we are also committed to vigorous enforcement, as we saw with the lawsuit against DoorDash, of our minimum pay rate, which is going to ensure that delivery workers can earn a decent pay

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: without having to put their lives and the lives of other New Yorkers at risk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So as I've said throughout this hearing, I think it's a theme from this administration, street safety and worker rights are not in tension.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They are complementary, and we're going to take a whole-of-government approach to making safer New York City streets a reality.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then you're from?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Yeah, so I think two main points.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: One is obviously the Vision Zero Reimagined report, which across the board is looking to improve safety for all street users, including delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: For delivery workers specifically, we launched the Sustainable Delivery Unit in July of last year.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: And, you know, their whole mission is to address street safety challenges associated with on-demand delivery services and commercial cycling.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: So they work to address the impacts of on-demand delivery industry through collaborative, innovative approaches that are...

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Advance the responsible.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Who leads that unit and how much people?

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It's called the Sustainable Delivery Unit, SDU.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Sustainable Delivery Unit, and that's within DOT.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And is there, who runs it?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: What's the frequency of meetings?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Is there a report?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I don't have a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: The head of the unit right now is Irene Figueroa-Ortiz.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: She is on leave.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: It reports into the commissioner's office, though, so it is very close to our leadership decision-making and collaboration across the agency at large.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I will follow up with some more questions about that unit.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how frequently delivery workers interact with officers and what prompts those encounters, and NYPD says enforcement is not tied to whether someone is a delivery worker.
chapters.title: Council Member Hanif asks NYPD about interactions with delivery workers

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then for the PD, how frequently would you say delivery workers are interacting with officers, and what is prompting those encounters?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And if you could be brief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: You know, it's a very hard question to answer, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Because when we are taking enforcement action, let's say a patrol officer sees someone on a bike or on an e-bike or in a car, right, driving recklessly, engaging in dangerous behavior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Chief Obey said, you know, there are certain traffic rules that we emphasize.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They go directly to safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: That entire interaction, right, they may not know if the person's a delivery star or not, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: They may just not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: At times, the person may say something, or it may be clear, or it may not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So, in other words, enforcement action is not in any way tied to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so that's not the kind of thing that we would really be...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: quantifying in our data, if that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then just finally, what types of e-bikes are delivery workers typically using?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And how fast can they go?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Is that a question for DCWP, PD?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Councilor.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I don't know if we have that data accessible right now in terms of what workers, the specific types of vehicles workers are using.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But I think that's also why the administration is looking for additional tools, such as Instruction 78, Instruction 1069, that would help us understand, DOT specifically, receive data that would help them understand what vehicles the workers are using.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Abreu excuses the panel and announces a sharp three-minute break before public testimony.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu excuses the administration panel and calls a break

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This panel is hereby excused.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We're taking a sharp three-minute break.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please keep it down in the chambers.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'll be here in three minutes.

chapters.summary: Staff ask attendees to find their seats and announce that the hearing will open for public testimony.
chapters.title: Hearing prepares for public testimony

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Actually, keep it down in the chambers.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please keep it down.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We're starting right now.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Find your seats, guys.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Find your seats.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: So if we can keep it down in the chamber.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Guys, keep it down.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: I know we have a lot of people who want to come testify.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We have a lot of people signed up.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please find your seats.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: So now we're going to open the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Guys, find your seats, please.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please find your seats.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Make some room in the middle.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Hey guys, if we want to get through the public testimony, we're going to get kicked out of the chamber today because there's an event happening tonight.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: So we really got to go through this quickly.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We have to move to another room.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: So the more delays we have, the more issues it's going to be.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Okay, so now this hearing is open for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: I remind members of the public this is a formal government proceeding and the quorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recording as testimony, but submit transcripts of such recording to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: When you are recognized, you have two minutes to speak on the oversight topic.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Our legislation is being heard today.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you have written testimony and additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please submit it to the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to testimony at council at nyc.gov within 72 hours of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We'll now call the first panel.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I would also like to add that we have about 100, more than 170 people testifying today, so I will be consistent on the two-minute cutoff.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Just want you to know I'm going to be very, very fair with it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: But at two minutes, I'm going to ask that you end your remarks.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Staff call the first panel of public witnesses to the table.
chapters.title: First public testimony panel is called

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: So first, Santis, Sardillo, Rene, Baruch, Akari, Michaels, Wendy, Peace, and...

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Pamela Maneske.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Maneske.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you all here, please come to the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And you can choose.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

chapters.summary: Renee Baruch describes being hospitalized for a week after being run over by an e-bike in 2023, and calls for passage of Priscilla's Law for accountability.
chapters.title: Renee Baruch testifies about being run over by an e-bike

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Renee Baruch
utterances.text: My name is Renee Baruch, and although she's not present, I would thank the speaker for this opportunity to be heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Renee Baruch
utterances.text: In May 2023, I was run over by an e-bike.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Renee Baruch
utterances.text: This was the result.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Renee Baruch
utterances.text: The photograph you see was taken after surgery was performed on, which closed several cuts on my face.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Renee Baruch
utterances.text: The fractures had to heal on their own.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Renee Baruch
utterances.text: I was hospitalized for a total of a week, and I later had surgery to fix the damage to my cervical spine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Renee Baruch
utterances.text: I was told that it was a delivery worker, but of course I don't know the identity, and I only regained consciousness once I was in the ambulance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Renee Baruch
utterances.text: We have no means of identifying the driver of any motorized bike.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Renee Baruch
utterances.text: I was recently in Europe with a huge bicycle culture where there was no infrastructure, just a painted line.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Renee Baruch
utterances.text: And there were bike racks at all the railroad stations and outside of buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Renee Baruch
utterances.text: But they all stopped for red lights and stop signs, and they obeyed the traffic rules.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Renee Baruch
utterances.text: Even as a casual observer, you know that it is not safe to cross a New York City street if you're in the crosswalk, if you have a green light.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Renee Baruch
utterances.text: Unless you first look both ways to make sure that something isn't still coming at you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Renee Baruch
utterances.text: Thank God my vision remains intact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Renee Baruch
utterances.text: No enforcement of any traffic laws is taking place, and you must pass Priscilla's Law Intro 802 as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

chapters.summary: Wendy Peace reads a statement from her sister Jean Kotler's family, describing how Jean was hit from behind by an e-bike going the wrong way in Central Park and remains hospitalized.
chapters.title: Wendy Peace testifies about her sister hit by an e-bike in Central Park

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Wendy Peace.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: I'm also a victim of being hit by an e-bike while I was on my regular bike, the person going the wrong way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: But I'm not going to talk about myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: I'm going to talk about Jean Kotler, and this is a statement from her family as she remains hospitalized.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: On July 7th, my sister Jean was jogging in Central Park, as she did most of the days for the past 10 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: An e-bike going in the wrong direction, in the wrong lane, in the pedestrian lane, in the park, hit her from behind.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: She never saw it coming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: As Jean lay unconscious, bleeding on the ground, this e-bike driver attempted to flee the scene.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: But some wonderful New York City angels made sure he stayed until the cops arrived.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: Not that it mattered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: Can you imagine that three months later, Jean would still be in the hospital and the e-bike driver that ran her down?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: He was questioned briefly at the scene by the police and then let go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: How is that even possible?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: Jean has endured multiple surgeries to fix the damage this e-bike rider caused her body, and most severely her brain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: And she still has a long journey ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: It's incredibly disheartening that nearly three months later, our family has still no meaningful support or accountability from the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: We're not asking for e-bikes to be banned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: We're asking for reasonable laws that provide accountability when someone is seriously injured by one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: Our family strongly supports Priscilla's law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: Priscilla's law would require every e-bike and e-scooter in New York City to carry a license plate and DMV registration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: No other family should have to go through this heartbreak.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: And after three months, we are still asking the same questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: When will there be accountability?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: So also, Parks Department needs to account for this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: We need no e-bikes in the parks and on the pathways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: And please, please, please pass Priscilla's law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Wendy Peace
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your time and consideration.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Pamela Manasse, co-founder of EVSA, describes being hit by an e-vehicle in 2022, suffering a traumatic brain injury and paralysis, and calls for Priscilla's Law.
chapters.title: Pamela Manasse testifies about being paralyzed by an e-vehicle

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: Hello, and thank you, Speaker Menon, for allowing me to tell my story on behalf of all victims of e-vehicle crashes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: My name is Pamela Manassi.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: I am EPSA's co-founder and its first victim.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: Four years ago, in 2022, as I crossed the street legally with my husband, I was brutally hit head-on by an e-vehicle traveling illegally off a sidewalk and into the crosswalk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: I suffered a severe traumatic brain injury and partially paralyzed and lost my career as a cellist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: There was zero accountability for the man who hit me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: He tried to flee, but my husband detained him.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: He got no summons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: He wasn't given a breathalyzer or drug test.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: Instead, he was allowed to walk away freely as seen by witnesses getting a coffee and croissant while I was taken away in an ambulance, paralyzed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: Priscilla's Law Intro 802 that requires license and registration through the use of red light cameras was introduced three years ago, and yet it is not one of the bills brought before the City Council today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: We don't know why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: Each of the 24 bills that are on the list represents only small pieces of solutions, but none will solve the larger safety issues running rampant in the city we love except

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: Priscilla's Law, who, as you already have been told, passed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: away because she took one step out and got hit by a city bike.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: Priscilla's law addresses everything needed for real safety, just license and registration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: So simple.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: License anyone operating a motorized vehicle,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: and hold the individual accountable, individual accountable, for illegal, egregious behavior.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: I don't care what they do for a living.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: These are not bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: These are silent motorcycles, and they are killers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: You may as well just put a gun to my head.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: Oh, by the way, I am still paralyzed.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pamela Manasse
utterances.text: Oh, and that's me, right?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We're now going to, this panel is excused.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The next panel is Brooklyn Bar President Antonio Reynoso.

chapters.summary: Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso notes that zero pedestrians have been killed by e-bikes this year, and argues the council should focus on ending car culture and regulating app companies.
chapters.title: Antonio Reynoso testifies on micromobility safety and car culture

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: I thought I was going to have more people in the panel, but it's all right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: I am Antonio Reynoso, and I'm currently the president of the greatest borough in the city of New York, which is Brooklyn, and I'm happy to be here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: To those that don't agree, you're welcome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: This is a very serious day, and I don't mean to open it up in jest, but this year about 149 people have died in crashes in New York City streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: Zero of those people have been killed by e-bikes or e-scooters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: Generally, e-bikes and e-scooters and mopeds are responsible for 5% of pedestrian injuries and 5% of pedestrian fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: That means 95% of pedestrian injuries and fatalities are caused by cars.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: Yet, here we are, have a hearing with 21 bills aimed at regulating e-bikes and e-scooters, as well as mopeds, which are already illegal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: None are about regulating dangerous driving, and only two are about infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: Meanwhile, important safety bills like universal daylighting still haven't been passed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: When was the last time the City Council held a hearing with 21 bills aimed at improving street safety and curbing dangerous driving?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: Some of the bills being heard today will be helpful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: We should focus regulating on businesses that sell e-bikes and app companies that incentivize unsafe practices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: But instead, too many of the bills rely on enforcement that will absolutely be carried out in a discriminatory way that punishes people of color and workers who are just trying to get around the city to do their jobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: Every major city has tried to pass bike licensing bills, has either repealed it or decided not to try it in the first place because it has failed so often.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: It's unwielding, it's expensive, and it gives police another excuse to target people of color.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: The idea of getting police to report on targeted traffic enforcement is a joke and half-stepping measures like writing look up on streets just blame pedestrians for getting themselves hit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: What we need instead is to end car culture.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: The council should support the admin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: in actually implementing the streets plan and making real infrastructure improvements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: Your time is up, our president.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Antonio Reynoso
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your time.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please keep it down in the chambers.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right, our next panel is Jonathan Cohen, Ben Furness, Griffin Schnitzner, or Griffel, my apologies, Andrew Bonamedi, and Ali Azumro.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Ben, you may begin.

chapters.summary: Ben Furnas says 17 New Yorkers have been killed on e-bikes or illegal devices this year, mostly by cars, and supports bills to get high-speed devices off streets and regulate delivery apps.
chapters.title: Ben Furnas of Transportation Alternatives testifies

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today and for calling today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: My name is Ben Furness, and I'm the Executive Director of Transportation Alternatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: We're here today because a 17-year-old boy is not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: A few weeks ago, just a block from where we're sitting, a boy was killed riding an illegal high-speed device.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: A terrible crash on the Queensborough Bridge path earlier this year left two New Yorkers dead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: So far this year, 17 New Yorkers, some as young as 15 years old, have been killed while riding e-bikes or illegal high-speed devices sold as e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: Almost everyone was killed by a car or a truck driver.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: Like you,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: I hear a lot of complaints about devices that are just too fast for our bike lanes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: As a person who rides a bike and a parent of a six-year-old bike rider, I'm very proud of her, I feel it too.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: To be clear, pedal assist and low-speed e-bikes are miraculous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: They're important, helpful, safe mobility devices that enable countless New Yorkers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: to move around the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: But high-speed illegal devices are different.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: These are illegal to ride in New York City, but they're marketed and sold as legal to young people and unsuspecting New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: Many can travel at speeds exceeding 25 miles per hour or as high as 50 or 60 miles per hour or more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: This is too fast for dense urban environments like New York City, where 20 is plenty on our streets and in our bike lanes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: We need to get high-speed devices off our streets, help people transition to safe devices, and regulate the delivery app companies that have transformed the conditions on our streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: I'd like to highlight a few bills in particular.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: Councilmember Shulman's Intro 950 and Committee Chair Abreu's Intro 1069 empowers the city to revoke licenses of companies that pressure delivery workers to go too fast, and analyze delivery app provided trip data to establish rules around mandated delivery times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: Councilmember Hudson's Intro 244 will get high-speed devices off our streets by banning the sale of the fastest currently legal e-bikes capable of exceeding 20 miles per hour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: Chair Abreu's 985 will help New Yorkers transition away from unsafe devices onto safe, slow ones by creating a trade-in program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: We want thoughtful transition to 20-mile-per-hour streets and bike lanes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Furnas
utterances.text: We're honored to be part of this work.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Johnny?

chapters.summary: Jonathan Cohen, co-founder of JOCO, supports banning Class 3 e-bikes, the trade-in program, dynamometers, and sidewalk detection technology, and offers to demonstrate their sensor technology.
chapters.title: Jonathan Cohen of JOCO testifies on sidewalk detection and safe bikes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: My name is Jonathan Cohen, and together with my co-founder, also Jonathan Cohen, a bit confusing, we co-founded JoCo here in the best city in the world, in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: You know, as Ben mentioned and many others have mentioned, there have been many people who have

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: who have been killed and injured by trucks and cars.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: One this week, unfortunately, she was actually just packing her bag and was hit by a truck on 34th Street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: You know, this was a kind of a really consistent reminder to us that infrastructure and safer streets protect cyclists from much larger vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: I wanted to hone in on four particular proposals that we really support from the bills that were announced today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: First, banning Class 3 e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: 20 is plenty, as everyone has mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: I don't see why anyone should or would be against that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: Second, the trade-in program is an amazing idea.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: People should be able to trade for compliant bikes or rentals towards safer bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: Third, dynamometers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: Same thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: Game changer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: There are too many modified or Frankenstein bikes that are difficult to identify without the right testing equipment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: Safe riding starts with safe bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And lastly, sidewalk detection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: Again, New York is the best city in the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: We'd be happy to sit down with the relevant agencies and show them this proprietary sensor technology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: We've already been working on it and are very excited to roll it out to our entire fleet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: We think this can be a really important tool across the entire industry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And with that, you know, we're really excited to see the city continue to move in the right direction from when we started our company five years ago to today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: You know, riding a bike is, you know, a million times easier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: I believe being a pedestrian is as important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: So thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Alia.

chapters.summary: Alia Soomro says NYLCV supports safe and legal e-mobility devices to reduce emissions and congestion, and supports a multi-pronged approach including infrastructure and app accountability.
chapters.title: Alia Soomro of NYLCV testifies on e-mobility and safety

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: My name is Alia Sumro, and I'm the Deputy Director for New York City Policy at the New York League of Conservation Voters, a statewide environmental organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: Thank you to the chairs and committee members for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: I've submitted longer written comments, so I'm going to focus on the high level today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: NYLCV continues to be a steadfast supporter of safe and legal e-mobility devices, such as low-speed and pedal-assist e-bikes, cargo bikes, and e-scooters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: This helps us to reduce the amount of fossil fuel-based cars on our streets, which can decrease greenhouse gas emissions, air pollution, and vehicle congestion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: These devices offer a more affordable and accessible mode of transportation, and it helps a large portion of the city who live in transit deserts access where they need to go, and it also helps a lot of residents with their employment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: We are saddened by the cyclist deaths and injuries, and we support equitable policy solutions to ensure that all New Yorkers are safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: While our city has made a lot of strides on street improvements, there are still many dangerous, illegal, and high-speed devices out there, and their proliferation is a serious concern, whether you're a driver, pedestrian, or cyclist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: NYLCV is pleased that the admin has released Vision Zero reimagined, and we want to underscore that for this to be successfully implemented, we need to implement, allocate the right capital and expense funding for safety improvement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: and DOT staffing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: And so ultimately to improve safety for all residents, NYLCV strongly supports a multi-pronged approach, such as improving street safety education, street infrastructure,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: requiring more accountability from app-based companies, stopping businesses that sell illegally or falsely advertise high-speed devices, and developing a phased approach to remove illegal and uncertified high-speed devices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: So my written comments go in a lot more depth, but there are a few bills that we support that I just want to quickly highlight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: We support Intro 244.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: We strongly recommend that we...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Alia.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please submit your written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We'll make sure to read it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I don't have any questions, but I believe my co-chair does.

chapters.summary: Menin asks JOCO about their tracking technology for red lights and wrong-way riding, and Cohen says they are working on it and have a zero-tolerance policy with warnings and bans.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin questions JOCO on sidewalk tracking and rider accountability

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Quick question for Joko.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Johnny, just on this tracking that you have for sidewalks, we've seen a lot of Joko bikes go through red lights, wrong way down one-way streets.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That tracking technology you have is available for that as well?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: We're working on it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: We'd love to apply it to anything, to going the wrong way down the street, going against traffic, going red lights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: That's the goal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: All of our vehicles are only class one, and we think it should be applied across the board to everybody.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And so what are you doing now if these issues are brought to your attention around, you know, obviously we talk about safety, making sure people are following the rules of the road, people are on your bikes, you guys own them, and you're renting them out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: So if someone brings it to our attention, if they don't bring it to the, you know, the delivery.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: company that the person's working for, we right away give the person a significant warning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And if they get a couple of strikes, two strikes, they're basically banned from the service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: So we, you know, I have to check if it's two or three.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: I want to double check that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: But we, you know, we have a zero tolerance policy for, you know.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And then it's have the public at large know that this is the JOCO policy.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Is there something available on your website or?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: Yes, it's available on our website and available to all riders.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And the last question, just around training for riders, what kind of ensuring that, you know, people understand, I know you give helmets.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: So we give free helmets and vests to all riders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: We require that you fill out, you know, take a training, take a, you know, an entire training course.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: We also require that you take the DOT training course.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And we're constantly updating, you know, these kind of what's being done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: And we're very supportive of, you know, the right training.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And so if the public had concerns, how would they reach out to JOCO about that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: Support at ridejoco.com or you can contact me directly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jonathan Cohen
utterances.text: But I'm happy to answer.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Abreu excuses the panel and calls the next set of public witnesses.
chapters.title: Panel is excused and next panel called

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This panel is excused.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: On the next panel, we have Yvette Massoudi, Robert Polchinski, Mary Lou Kinlan, Harvey Goldberg, and Roshi Gavechi.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And my apologies if I'm mispronouncing your names.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: If you're the only one from this panel, I'm going to ask a few more names to join you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Just give me one second.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Patty Myers, Janet Schroeder, Andrew Fine, and Thomas Lowy.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And Carol Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Just get them out, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You may begin.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Yeah, Janet, you may begin.

chapters.summary: Janet Schroeder, director of EVSA, says DOT and NYPD injury stats are inaccurate, cites 147 EVSA victims with only 8 police reports, and calls for Priscilla's Law.
chapters.title: Janet Schroeder testifies on e-vehicle violence and inaccurate data

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: Hello, I'm Janet Schroeder, director of EVSA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: We much appreciate Julie Menon holding this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: But what about the tens of thousands of pedestrians and cyclists who have been hit by e-vehicles in the last six years?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: We ask you to stop deflecting from the e-vehicle violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: On pedestrians and bicyclists to talk about cars.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: This is a crisis that ER doctors call a public health crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: Accountability for e-bike riders doesn't make cars more dangerous, but it will change rider behavior and therefore will absolutely save lives and lessen injuries of e-vehicle riders

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: pedestrians and cyclists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: DOT NYPD stats for e-vehicle injuries are gravely inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: Public advocate, your stats are dead wrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: Of 147 seriously maimed EFSA victims, eight have police reports.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: Police usually arrive after the ambulance takes away the victim, and if police are there, they often don't report, citing rider fled, I didn't witness it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: Angela Pfaff at Bellevue ER reports over 300 e-vehicle trauma admissions caused in the last year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: This is one of 54 ER hospitals in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: Council must start pulling and using all ER injury stats.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: Bike lanes don't keep a rider from speeding, running lights, leaving the scene of an accident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: And in all but six of EFSA's 147 crashes, the rider fled.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: Some of the bills we like, thank you for this hearing, yes to ban class three.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: The geofencing bill 2590 is great if it takes the bike down to zero miles per hour so that bikes can't ride on the sidewalk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: But then how will Lincoln Ressler and Cheo say get around the city?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: Resolution 44, calling on New York State legislators to increase penalties for e-vehicles leaving the scene of the crash, only works if all riders can be identified by a registered plate, and that is Intro 802 Priscilla's Law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: Sean, you asked how to tell the difference between legal and illegal e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: How about a license plate for the legal ones?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: We are asking a resolution for City Council to NY State legislators to pass Priscilla's Law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Janet Schroeder
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Next up.

chapters.summary: Andrew Fine criticizes the long wait for public testimony, notes 17 e-bike rider deaths this year, and calls for licensing and registration to distinguish legal from illegal devices.
chapters.title: Andrew Fine testifies on e-bike deaths and need for licensing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Fine
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Fine
utterances.text: I just want to take a moment ahead of my testimony here to register the outrage that I actually found common ground with transportation alternatives today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Fine
utterances.text: We're all ticked off that it takes four and a half hours to get the public's input on this important legislation on street safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Fine
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please keep it down.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please keep it down.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Fine
utterances.text: And I'd like to thank the three city council members who managed to actually stick around to listen to the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Fine
utterances.text: I think it's outrageous that we don't have a full panel here when we've all survived half the day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Fine
utterances.text: I want to thank Speaker Menon for bringing attention to this important public safety issue and holding this historic hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Fine
utterances.text: The body count on our streets continues to rise unabated, and it must stop with this city council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Fine
utterances.text: This includes e-bike riders, 17 of which are dead this year so far, and that's an old count,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Fine
utterances.text: pedestrians throughout New York City and Central Park, and city bike riders, including the heartbreaking death of a 15-year-old doubled up on a city bike on East 14th Street just this month.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Fine
utterances.text: As a parent of three, two former teenage girls and one still teenage girl, this scares the living, you know what, out of me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Fine
utterances.text: I want to say that the bike lobby, which is heavily funded by Uber, DoorDash, Lyft, we see many of them today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Fine
utterances.text: They may wear T-shirts, they might be bearded, they might play the role of activists, but at the end of the day, I'd love you to ask them, are they paid for their appearance today?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Fine
utterances.text: Are they drawing a salary?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Fine
utterances.text: I can tell you one thing, that New York City E-Vehicle Safety Alliance is pure grassroots, all volunteer, and we love the city council to take this more seriously,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Fine
utterances.text: pass licensing and registration, because as Janet just said, that's the way to actually tell legal from illegal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Fine
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Robert Polchinski, 67, describes being struck by a fat-tired e-bike in Hudson River Park, suffering a broken arm, ribs, and leg, and says the offender was never held accountable.
chapters.title: Robert Polchinski testifies about being struck by an e-bike

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: This is on, okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: I'd like to thank both Speaker Menon and of course the three chairs of the committees today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: My name is Robert Polchinski.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: I'm a 67-year-old resident of 14th Street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: Last December, I was struck by a large, fat-tired e-bike.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: Not one of those cute little ones you showed the pictures of before, but...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: Much bigger.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: Over in Hudson River Park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: I've been running and about to begin my trip home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: Leaving the park, however, requires that you cross West Street, a major thoroughfare.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: As I approached the crosswalk at Horatio and West Street, the walk sign was illuminated in my favor, so I headed on my way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: The only problem is getting there requires crossing a two-way bike path.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: Despite signs telling cyclists to yield to pedestrians at the location, the rider did not yield nor attempt to slow down.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: Instead, there was a collective, oh shit, as my right side and his front wheel collided.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: At the moment of impact, I felt like my heart stopped and I was a goner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: If I had hit my head, there may have been one more obituary written.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: 20 hours, first in an ER and later in a trauma center, revealed emergent injuries including a broken arm, three broken ribs, a broken leg, and internal bleeding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: Recovery included surgery, months of therapy, and trauma for both me and my family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: The e-bike operator in my case had stayed at the scene and I'm told was given a summons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: I think for failing to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: although e-bikes are also not allowed in that park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: I was able to obtain a copy of the police report from the precinct and the name and address of the offender.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: I attempted to serve the offender with a notice of claim, but the letter was returned undeliverable, no forwarding address.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: There ended any chance I had of recovering even a portion of the expenses incurred.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: Are you aware that current police reporting procedures do not differentiate between a pedal bike and an e-bike?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: The machine that hit me was essentially an electric motorcycle, not a bicycle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: We register and insure motorcycles and Teslas, but not e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: This makes no sense.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Remind me of your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Robert Polchinski
utterances.text: Robert Polchinski.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Paul Polchinski.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And just a reminder to please state your name before you speak.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Carol Wilson describes being hit by a bike twice while crossing with the walk signal, suffering a skull fracture and concussion, and calls for Priscilla's Law to identify riders.
chapters.title: Carol Wilson testifies about being hit by bikes twice

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: Hi, my name's Carol Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: I have been hit, knocked down, and injured by a bike in New York, not once, but twice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: Both times, the rider disregarded the basic rules of the road and went through a red light.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: Both times, the rider was not in the clearly marked bike lane.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: And both times I was crossing the street in the designated pedestrian walkway with the walk signal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: But this did not protect me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: The first time, a woman was on a city bike.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: I was knocked down, passed out, woke up and dragged myself to the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: She fled the scene.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: I called the ambulance myself and was diagnosed with a skull fracture.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: This could have been deadly as I was on a blood thinner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: After three and a half years, I am still going to rehab to retrain my eyes to work with my brain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: The second time I was hit, knocked down, and again hit my head on the pavement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: I had a concussion and an injured leg muscle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: I'm glad the city is finally focusing on the dangers of e-vehicles on our streets, on our sidewalks, and in our parks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: However, I must say that several of the bills you are now concerning

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: considering will accomplish nothing to change or punish the rider behavior.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: Because there's no way to identify the people who run a red light, hit a person, or leave the scene.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: The common sense remedy is Intro 802 Priscilla's Law, which requires a license plate so that that person can be identified and held responsible for their actions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carol Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity for me to tell my story.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Patty Myers describes being struck by an e-bike in 2024, fracturing her hip and requiring two surgeries, and says the rider fled and could not be identified without a license plate.
chapters.title: Patty Myers testifies about being struck by an e-bike and needing hip surgery

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: Thank you for giving me this opportunity today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: My name is Patty Myers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: I'm a New York City resident and have lived in Manhattan for 21 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: I strongly...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: support in show 0802, known as Priscilla's Law, because New York City needs clear accountability for e-bikes and other electric vehicles to better protect pedestrians.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: September 9, 2024, I was entering a taxi when an e-bike struck me with significant force and knocked me to the ground.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: The rider did not stop.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: Although traffic camera footage captured the incident and the police did come to my home, there was no license plate, registration, or other means to identify the rider and hold them accountable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: Had I been struck by a car, the driver would have faced serious consequences and would have been found from their license plate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: Because this was an e-bike, the rider was able to leave without accountability or responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: I was rushed to the emergency room.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: I stayed there until 3 in the morning and then transferred to NYU Orthopedic Hospital for emergency hip surgery.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: I had a fractured hip.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: It took many, many months for me to recover.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: I was on a walker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: I was on a, then I was on a cane.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: And in May 2025, I underwent a second surgery because the first procedure did not do what it needed to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: I see I'm running out of time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: Even now, when I walk through the streets, I am nervous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: It's not the same.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: I moved here from the suburbs, especially to be able to walk around, have that freedom and excitement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: And now it's taken away from me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: I'm nervous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: I'm scared.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: I'm always looking around.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: So in conclusion, please take into consideration Priscilla's rule.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: It will really make a difference.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: We don't want to have more people harmed and get hurt.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patty Myers
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Thomas Lowy describes being hit from behind by a delivery e-bike in Riverside Park, breaking his clavicle and ribs, and calls for extending automobile insurance rules to e-bikes.
chapters.title: Thomas Lowy testifies about being hit by an e-bike in Riverside Park

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thomas Lowy
utterances.text: Is this on?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thomas Lowy
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thomas Lowy
utterances.text: Well, I consider myself lucky after hearing the previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thomas Lowy
utterances.text: This is what I looked like after I was hit by a e-bike.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thomas Lowy
utterances.text: I'm a lifelong New Yorker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thomas Lowy
utterances.text: I was badly hurt by an e-bike in Riverside Park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thomas Lowy
utterances.text: On the bike lane.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thomas Lowy
utterances.text: Even though the bike lane was marked in those days as prohibited for e-bikes, it was rampant with them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thomas Lowy
utterances.text: And a delivery driver hit me from behind, knocked me down, broke my clavicle, couple of ribs, and of course these horrible bruises.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thomas Lowy
utterances.text: I believe that New York and indeed America developed a system in response to auto accidents at the beginning of the 20th century.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thomas Lowy
utterances.text: Insurance companies in cooperation with the states made mandatory insurance ubiquitous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thomas Lowy
utterances.text: There's no reason to not extend the automobile and truck rules to e-bikes and delivery vans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thomas Lowy
utterances.text: The cost is enormous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thomas Lowy
utterances.text: The hospital charges were, if I didn't have insurance, would have been devastating, and I'm sure for many people they are devastating.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thomas Lowy
utterances.text: Without insurance, we can't go on this way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Thomas Lowy
utterances.text: That's what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This panel is excused.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The next panel, we have Ligia Gualpa.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We have April Herms, Gustavo H.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Sejon Bald, my apologies if I mispronounce your name.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And Mohamed Riaz.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So we have Lihia, April, Gustavo, Ceylon, Sejon.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Oh, you're here.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And Mohamed Riaz.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And we'll begin from my right to your left.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And you may begin when you're ready.

chapters.summary: April Herms supports removing unsafe devices but says banning Class 3 e-bikes without a feasible trade-in program will leave workers without legal devices, and proposes motor alterations instead.
chapters.title: April Herms of Workers' Justice Project testifies on Class 3 ban and trade-in

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: Hi, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: I'm April Herms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
