utterances.text: I'm the Deputy Director at the Workers'Justice Project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: We organize and advocate for the more than 70,000 delivery workers on the streets of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: I'm here today to testify about Intros 244, 985, and 2361, the proposed legislation to ban the sale and use of Class 3 e-bikes, along with a trade-in program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: Workers'Justice Project strongly supports the overall goal of the bills before the Council today of removing unsafe and illegal devices from our streets, slowing down the top speeds of illegal e-bikes, banning the sale of Class 3 devices, and holding delivery apps accountable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: We estimate that tens of thousands of workers currently use a legal Class 3 device, and banning their use without a feasible trade-in program will leave these workers without a legal device that they can use to make a living.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: Getting Class 3 devices off the streets will require a well-planned, fully-funded program to enable delivery workers and other Class 3 owners to safely and affordably transition to new devices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: We do not believe the trade-in program legislation currently before the Council can feasibly accomplish this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: Last year, we partnered with DOT on the e-bike trade-in program targeting unsafe batteries and the 2 million program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: program traded in a total of 400 bikes at an approximate cost of $5,000 per bike.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: To trade in 20,000 Class 3 e-bikes would cost the city $100 million, assuming it's even feasible to source that many bikes, and convince delivery workers to switch from their trusted bikes to the new ones.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: We faced a lot of skepticism in that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: Our proposed alternative is for the council to fund a transition program that would alter the motors of existing legal Class 3 bikes so they could not go faster than 20 miles per hour and provide speedometers to delivery workers so they know how fast they're going.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: This would cost a fraction of the cost of a full bike trade-in program and will allow delivery workers to keep their trusted bikes they know can withstand the rigors of a 12-hour delivery shift and would also enable the city to fund small businesses, bike shops,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: to provide these alterations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: Instead of banning the tools that delivery workers depend on to work, we should focus on the underlying goal, reducing e-bike speeds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Lihia?

chapters.summary: Ligia Guallpa says the package of bills does not address root causes like infrastructure, worker protections, and corporate accountability, and opposes Intros 2361, 2587, and 986.
chapters.title: Ligia Guallpa of Workers' Justice Project testifies on root causes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Yeah, all right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: My name is Lihia Walp.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: I'm the executive director of the Workers'Justice Project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: And first, let me start by making it clear that we strongly support the goal of making our streets safer, making New Yorkers transition to safe legal micromobility devices, and making delivery work safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: We understand the urgency because it's delivery workers who are losing their lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Just this week, a delivery worker died in Midtown.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: And yesterday I actually brought copies of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: of a recent report for each council member, and also will be submitted online, but this report actually highlights that 53% of delivery workers reported a worker-related injury,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: nearly twice than the 2022 report of DCWP.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: We are submitting copies here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: The package, the reason I'm here is because the current package of bills that I think is 2024 now is being here today, does not address the root causes of a street safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: It leaves out the need for safe infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Street infrastructure, stronger worker protections, and a real transition plan, and real accountability to corporations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: We're ready to work with you to add the missing pieces to this puzzle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: NYPD is already conducting increased e-bike enforcements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: We completely oppose Intro 2361, 2587, 986, because we feel that these bills will actually intensify

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: NYPD enforcement, and we cannot put workers'livelihood in the hands of delivery corporations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: We should not deploy NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: We should actually look at investing in a transition plan, holding corporations accountable, expanding worker protections, and actually on page 9 and 10 will tell you the exact reason why multibillion-dollar corporations are...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: How multi-billion dollar corporations exercise

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: enormous amount of pressure for workers.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Gustavo?

chapters.summary: Gustavo Ajche, a delivery worker for over 10 years, opposes Intros 2361, 2587, and 986, saying they will give NYPD more power to penalize workers and confiscate their tools.
chapters.title: Gustavo Ajche testifies against bills increasing enforcement on workers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gustavo Ajche
utterances.text: Good afternoon, my name is Gustavo Che.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gustavo Ajche
utterances.text: I'm a co-founder of the Libristas Unidos and I'm member leader of the Worker Justice Project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gustavo Ajche
utterances.text: And I'm using the apps for more than 10 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gustavo Ajche
utterances.text: And I'm here today to share my concern about the entire package of bill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gustavo Ajche
utterances.text: I understand that the goal is to make the street safer for everyone, but

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gustavo Ajche
utterances.text: There is some concern about some of the bills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gustavo Ajche
utterances.text: So I express my concern and my opposition to Intro 2361, Intro 2587, and Intro 986.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gustavo Ajche
utterances.text: These bills will be...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gustavo Ajche
utterances.text: Give the power to NYPD to make more hard for delivery workers and I think we have to address this and that's what we're here for today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gustavo Ajche
utterances.text: You have to listen to us and to address all this situation in a good way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gustavo Ajche
utterances.text: Come against delivery workers again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gustavo Ajche
utterances.text: So this is, I see one of the bills says it's going to be fine delivery workers with $2,000 ticket and confiscate his tools to work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gustavo Ajche
utterances.text: So this is not right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gustavo Ajche
utterances.text: So we have to be addressed in a different way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gustavo Ajche
utterances.text: My speech is so longer, but I think I submitted.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gustavo Ajche
utterances.text: So I'm not going to read everything.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gustavo Ajche
utterances.text: This is something that we have to address and we're here to open to sit and discuss in a better way and find the best solution for all delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gustavo Ajche
utterances.text: We are 70,000 delivery workers that who use e-bike to survive, to keep feeding our families.

chapters.summary: Sidiki Soumahoro, a delivery worker and organizer, opposes bills that increase punishment, and calls for safer e-bikes, secure parking, protected bike lanes, and delivery worker hubs.
chapters.title: Sidiki Soumahoro testifies against increased punishment for delivery workers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: Good afternoon, my name is C.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: Lubaldi.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: I've been an app delivery worker for almost three years, and I'm also an organizer with Worker Justice Project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: I'm here today to speak against Intro 2361, Intro 2587, Intro 986, and other bills that would increase punishment and enforcement against delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: I work mainly in the Lower East Side alongside more than 200 delivery workers from West Africa.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: We work hard every day delivering food, medicine, and other essential goods for New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: Recently, we heard about a mayor NRPD sweep and possible e-bike confiscation on October 8th.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: This is very frightening for workers who depend on our bike to make our living.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: Many delivery workers have nowhere safe to park their bike, rest, or eat.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: We are often forced to park wherever we can and eat on the street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: We understand that the street safety is important, but delivery workers are not the problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: We want to be part of the solution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: Instead of more punishment, we need safer e-bike, lower speed, secure e-bike parking, more protective...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: bike lane and more delivery star hub where workers can rest and eat.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: We also need the city to regulate delivery app.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: Apps should not pressure workers to accept multiple delivery at once or rush through the street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: Workers should also be protected where we choose safety over speed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: We are asking the city to listen to delivery workers and bring us to the table.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: We know this street because we work on them every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: Make our e-bike safer, not illegal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: We need safety, not punishment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Mohamed Riyadh describes being given multiple orders with impossible deadlines, leading to reduced on-time performance and deactivation, and asks the council to listen to delivery workers.
chapters.title: Mohamed Riyadh testifies on pressure from delivery apps

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: Good afternoon, council members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: My name is Mohamed Riyadh.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: I am a worker at Delivery in New York City for almost three years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: And I'm organizer and leader, Worker Justice Project and Law Service Unido.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: I'm here to share my concern about into 2361, into 2587,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: Intro 998.6.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: While those bills are processed, it's safely misused.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: Delivery workers are considered those could result more tickets and greater pressure from delivery workers'platform.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: Delivery workers already face significant risks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: For traffic, weather, and unrealistic deliveries and deadlines.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: I experienced those pressure myself last week while working from a grab up in the rain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: I was given multiple orders with the same delivery deadlines, making it physically impossible to meet all of them safely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: As a result,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: My on-time performance was reduced, and I was unable to work next two weeks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: If the council member wants to take some safety for delivery workers, if we needed more protected by clients in area,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: their delivery workers around.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: Responsible delivery platform

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: timeframe and that do not encourage safe riding and more parking area for the bicycle,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: stronger protection against the deactivation, meaningful input from delivery workers than safely policies for double up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: We all want safe streets and safe work conditions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: Delivery workers want to do our jobs, support our family, and return home safely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: I respectfully ask the councils to listen to delivery workers and include our voice in decisions that affect our safety and livelihood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: Thank you for your time and thanks so much.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks WJP what street enforcement they would accept, and Guallpa says enforcement is already happening and the problem is lack of infrastructure and algorithm pressure.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu questions WJP on acceptable street enforcement

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: And before it's closed, I just want to show you the amount of tickets and delivery stackings.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You're speaking out of order.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You're speaking out of order.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I do have questions for you, though, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Do you support any street enforcement whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Of course we support street enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Actually, you have a line of tickets of, actually, this is for one worker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: A worker spends around $4,000 to $5,000 every two months just in tickets, in fines every single day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: And the leveristas, actually, not only that,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: In top of tickets, most of them, they actually have to replace their own device every time they're confiscated, which is anything between $3,000 and $4,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: NYPD is already doing a massive amount of enforcement on delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: The problem is not the enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: The problem is the lack of infrastructure in our streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: We have an algorithm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: that is exercising an enormous amount of pressure, actually page 9 and page 10, will tell you how much the apps actually control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: They control the routes that they take, where do they move, how they move, how many deliveries they have to complete, and the amount of time that they have to complete that delivery.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: That's the actual...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Part of the problem.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So, yeah, no, and we have bills that tackle the app regulation.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: That's Len Shulman's bill on licensing, which hopefully they don't do much.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And so we'll try to make those bills stronger.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: But what street enforcement is acceptable?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: The street enforcement that is already happening on the street.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: No, no, I'm asking what street enforcement is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about 70,000 delivery workers that are already getting a stream amount of enforcement, which is civil summons every day at the delivery center.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'm simply asking, is there an enforcement role that WJP would be okay with?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: It's already happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand what other enforcement you're requiring when you have NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Parking in a corner just to give civil summonses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: And when they're already doing back confiscation, that's already the reality of delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Are you asking me if you want them to go to jail?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Is that what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: That's a straw man argument.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: But what I will say is this, is that NYPD testified today that they're not going to be outsourcing their

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: DOT also testified that they don't want to be enforcing street safety laws, right?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And so given that the enforcement is already here and they are not outsourcing that, dynamometers would actually be helpful for your workers to keep their devices from NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: They won't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: Speedometers would also be helpful so that workers can know how fast they're going.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: And I think removing the ways that apps perversely incentivize workers to have to drive unsafely or do their job will reduce the need for enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: I don't think we have a problem with enforcing the legal speed limits and things like that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: But we also need, on the other side, to regulate the algorithms that are pressuring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And I think we need to do more bike lane infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I think we need to expand the network so that your workers are actually not having to be on sidewalks, not having to be sharing the road with cars.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'm with you on that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The other thing I wanted to ask before I turn it over to Councilmember Hanif and Brewer is the admin testified that there is pending legislation at the state level that would classify anything over 20 miles per hour.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Basically classified as a motorcycle, and that would require registration, the same way that we do for mopeds.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Is that something WGP would support as an alternative to an outright ban?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: So we strongly support reducing the speed of e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: That's something that we have worked very closely with the previous administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: We have made a commitment to this administration that reducing the speed should be the right track.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: That's why we're thinking less.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: figured out a system how to reduce the speed of these e-bikes, right, rather than making them illegal or putting cops to chase workers to identify whether they are legal or not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: We will strongly support the idea of figuring out how we can create a system to reduce the speed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: We have concerns, obviously, with registration for a couple reasons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: One is the operating cost that it takes to that, navigating a complicated DMV bureaucracy where many deliveristas or immigrant workers or workers in general have to navigate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: And then where is the ownership and the responsibility of also delivery companies?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councillor Mahani, followed by Brewer.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks what changes delivery companies should be required to make, and Guallpa says they control routes, speed, hours, and deactivation, and need to be regulated.
chapters.title: Council Member Hanif asks WJP what changes delivery companies should make

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you for testifying.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Could you share what changes delivery companies should be required to make that you guys are talking about so that workers can ride safely without putting their livelihood at risk?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Yeah, so in the report that I just shared with you all in page, I think, 9 and 10, I want to highlight something important for people in the public to understand, particularly on delivery companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: We have multibillion-dollar corporations who are making...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: work-related decisions for delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: They are choosing which routes delivery workers take, the order completion speed of delivery workers, the number of hours they work, the number of deliveries they have to accept,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: within an hour, the amount of hours and days they work on the street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: And on top of that, they are consistently, if a worker does not meet the required intensity that they require to work, workers likely face deactivation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Actually, deactivation is the driving fear that forces workers to make unnecessary choices, which is putting their own safety on the risk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Answering your question,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Workers don't have deactivation protections right now, which means they don't have the tools to fight back the ongoing pressure that these apps are exercising on workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Intro 1332 that we passed last year was watered down to please the corporations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: The bill only protects workers who...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Permanently deactivated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: So now we have Uber, Grubhub, and DoorDash moving to a new model of deactivation, which is temporary locking out, restricting its scheduling, reducing the work hours, the number of deliveries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: We actually have about 4,000 workers that have come to our office that have been unfairly deactivated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: We need to regulate the algorithms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: We need to actually expand not just cost protections, but actually look at how this, if the city find out that DoorDash was stealing about more than $100 million from workers, and they had to admit it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: We want to know what's going on behind the algorithm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Yes, we strongly support legislation about collecting the data, except the personal data of the worker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: But let's...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: find out how they're using the algorithm to profit and put not just worker safety, every New Yorker's safety on the line.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So then on the issue of speeding, I mean, adding these speedometer and the denominator, whatever, are they, I mean, that won't change anything unless...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The corporations are actually...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - April Herms
utterances.text: Until you stop the apps from being able to incentivize the workers to have to deliver...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So that longer-term strategy is what I want to make sure we're really aligned on here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: Yeah, and I think the reality is many delivery workers have to make unnecessary choices to keep their jobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ligia Guallpa
utterances.text: And they are the ones who are dying at the highest rate.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It was already asked.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm concerned about the algorithms, and that's what we have to work on.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This panel is excused.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We thank you so much for testifying.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Really, really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Council members, sorry, not council members.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: It's been a long day.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The next panel will be Abigail Jackson on Zoom, Erica Sofa or Sophia, Josh Gold, Juan Restrepo, and Ben Rosen,

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: and Michael Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please come on up.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: beginning with you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: And please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Sure.

chapters.summary: Michael Sutherland supports point-of-sale regulation and infrastructure, opposes banning Class 3 use, and discourages hyper-focusing on delivery workers as the primary issue.
chapters.title: Michael Sutherland of Open Plans testifies on e-micromobility policy

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: Thank you to the chairs for holding this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: My name is Michael Sutherland, and I'm the Senior Policy and Legislative Analyst at Open Plans, an advocacy organization fighting for a more livable city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: At Open Plans, we believe that our streets should work for all users, ensuring New Yorkers have access to safe, legal e-micromobility is a vital part of that goal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: E-micromobility provides an alternative to car trips, which is especially important in the outer boroughs, like in southern Brooklyn, where I was born and raised.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: At Open Plans, we believe three pillars make up effective e-micromobility policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: Point of sale regulation, enforcement, and infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: We support Intros 95, 244, and 988 to address dangerous devices at the point of sale.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: We have serious concerns about pre-considered introduction 2361, which would ban the sale and use of Class 3 e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: We're supportive of a ban on the sale of Class 3 e-bikes, but such a ban on use concerns us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: Warnings distributed through this bill create an environment for pretextual stops, resulting in a disproportionate impact on undocumented.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: to New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: We're supportive of the concept of Intro 986, though we have thoughts about the mechanisms of the enforcement, which we detail further in our written testimony, which we'll submit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: We support Intro 1066, which would add traffic calming measures to bike lanes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: However, we believe that infrastructure is otherwise sorely missing from the conversation and this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: We encourage the council to pursue other ways we can make the use of e-bikes more safe and convenient, like wider two-way protected bike lanes, and look into lanes dedicated to e-micromobility on our busiest e-micromobility corridors, like Councilmember Krishnan was mentioning earlier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: We support the concept of Intro 985.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: A training program is essential in getting certain devices off the streets without limiting New Yorkers'ability to get around.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: And lastly, we strongly discourage the council from hyper-focusing on delivery workers as the primary issue with e-micromobility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: This does a disservice to the delivery workers who provide an essential service to our city and to the task at hand, making our streets safer for all users.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: To this end, we oppose Resolution 43.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: Our positions on these bills and others in this hearing are expanded further in our written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Sutherland
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Erica Sopha says park visitors feel anxious due to speeding bikes and e-mobility devices, and calls for zero tolerance for illegal devices, routine enforcement, and better bike infrastructure.
chapters.title: Erica Sopha of Central Park Conservancy testifies on park safety

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica Sopha
utterances.text: Hi, thank you for having me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica Sopha
utterances.text: My name is Erica Sofa, and I'm the Vice President for Park Use and Stewardship at the Central Park Conservancy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica Sopha
utterances.text: We are the park's sole caretakers, responsible for all 843 acres of the world's most famous urban park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica Sopha
utterances.text: Central Park sees roughly 42 million visits a year, more than Disney World.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica Sopha
utterances.text: Increasingly, what we hear from visitors is that people feel anxious in the park because of speeding bikes, e-bikes, and a fast-growing fleet of e-mobility devices moving with too much velocity and little regard for anyone else.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica Sopha
utterances.text: There have been too many avoidable incidents and injuries, and we are grateful for the Council's commitment to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica Sopha
utterances.text: Let me outline some goals that the Conservancy would support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica Sopha
utterances.text: First, zero tolerance for illegal devices that don't belong in a park at all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica Sopha
utterances.text: Heavy-duty e-scooters, e-unicycles, and unregistered mopeds routinely exceed 30 miles an hour and are already illegal citywide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica Sopha
utterances.text: We need to remove these dangerous machines from our streets and parks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica Sopha
utterances.text: The dynamometers flagged in Intro 986 could help officers do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica Sopha
utterances.text: Second, real routine enforcement against speeding cyclists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica Sopha
utterances.text: Newer detection technology can help identify a speeding rider and alert an officer stationed farther down the route, a speed trap model adapted for bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica Sopha
utterances.text: We also believe the NYPD bike unit should be substantially increased, putting more officers on wheels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica Sopha
utterances.text: to model good riding and intervene in real time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica Sopha
utterances.text: Third, better bike infrastructure on the streets around the park, including protected bike lanes on the transverses, which DOT already supports, so through traffic has somewhere to go besides our interior drives and pedestrian paths.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica Sopha
utterances.text: This would reduce pressure in a park designed for respite and peacefulness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erica Sopha
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Josh Gold says Uber supports safety regulations but opposes disproportionate liability insurance mandates and overly prescriptive tracking, and calls for stronger enforcement of existing laws.
chapters.title: Josh Gold of Uber testifies on delivery app regulations

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Good morning, my name is Josh Golden.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: I'm testifying today on behalf of Uber.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Uber supports regulations that make our streets safer for all New Yorkers, including delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: But too often when traffic tragedies occur, even when they have nothing to do with third-party delivery, the response is to blame this workforce.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Over the past six years, the council has passed dozens of laws regulating delivery apps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Workers are paid by the minute, have access to battery trade-ins, free safety equipment, low-cost UL-certified e-bikes, and required safety training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Uber alone distributed more than 8,000 helmets and 37,000 safety vests over the past 12 months.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Yet app-based delivery workers represent only a piece of e-device traffic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: City bike users take more than a million trips each week, and DCWP found that 40% of restaurants use their own delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: We need stronger enforcement of the laws already on the books, not simply more regulation of one segment of riders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Let's be clear, none of these bills will work without enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: For example, it's still too easy to purchase and operate unregistered mopeds or devices that lack UL certification.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: I want to comment specifically on three of the bills before you today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Intro 999.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: We strongly oppose the proposed mandate, which we believe is disproportionate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: City Bike has operated under a city contract for more than a decade without this type of third-party liability requirement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: And the bill would require a worker riding a 60-pound bicycle to carry six times the liability coverage required of someone driving a 6,000-pound SUV.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Intro 1069.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Workers are paid for their delivery time, and Uber does not pay them more for riding faster or penalize them for taking longer if other companies do it rather than have a study and more data in perpetuity just ban the practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Pre-considered introduction on tracking workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: While we agree with the underlying safety elements of this proposal, we are highly concerned that this legislation is overly prescriptive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Specifically, it risks...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: It risks taking away workers'ability to earn a living by relying on GPS tracking technology that is frequently problematic in dense parts of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Satellite signals bounce, drop, and miscalculate speeds among high-rises.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Thank you for your time and the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Ben Rosen says battery fires are up 70% this year, many from non-structural causes and end-of-life batteries, and calls for mandated battery lifecycle management.
chapters.title: Ben Rosen of Pop Wheels testifies on battery fire crisis

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Rosen
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Rosen
utterances.text: My name is Ben Rosen, and I serve as the Director of Deployments at Pop Wheels, a Brooklyn-based company building battery-swapping infrastructure across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Rosen
utterances.text: Since completing our successful 2024 pilot with DOT, Popwheel's 50-plus outdoor battery swapping cabinets have provided over half a million safe battery swaps to e-bike riders and workers while reducing the lithium-ion fire risk citywide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Rosen
utterances.text: We support nearly all of the bills before you today, particularly those favoring low-speed Class 1 and Class 2 devices over heavier, higher-speed ones.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Rosen
utterances.text: and those removing illegal unregistered devices from our streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Rosen
utterances.text: But as the Council conducts this holistic review, we urge you, do not lose sight of the lithium-ion battery fire crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Rosen
utterances.text: FDNY data released this July showed battery fires up more than 70% this year, on track for over 500 fires in 2026, including some several recent tragic fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Rosen
utterances.text: Now, the data highlights two things worth paying attention to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Rosen
utterances.text: One, an increasing share of these fires are non-structural, which means that they are occurring outside of charging contexts, igniting on the street after overuse in a trash can or through improper disposal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Rosen
utterances.text: And two, a growing number of these fires are caused by batteries reaching the end of their useful life cycle, even when a battery was UL certified at the point of sale.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Rosen
utterances.text: A UL 2271 certification says that a battery was safe on the day it was sold, but not that it was still safe after months of damage or charging cycles on city streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Rosen
utterances.text: The fix is simple.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Rosen
utterances.text: Regular inspection, maintenance, and safe retirement across a battery's full life, available to every rider and not left to the rider alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Rosen
utterances.text: And this can be done in-house by fleet operators, trained retailers, through a city-run assessment program, or through a third-party provider, of which battery-swapping networks like ours are just one existing option.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Rosen
utterances.text: So we have three specific asks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Rosen
utterances.text: The first is to amend Local Law 95 of 2025 to mandate that ongoing battery lifecycle management, the regular inspection, maintenance, and timely retirement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sidiki Soumahoro
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ben Rosen
utterances.text: No problem.

chapters.summary: Juan Restrepo says Lime's shared scooters are capped at 15 mph, use geofencing, and have good safety records, and urges expansion of e-scooter share with clear safety metrics.
chapters.title: Juan Restrepo of Lime testifies on shared scooter safety

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Majority Leader Abreu, Chairs Epstein and Felice, and Council Members Brewer and Hanif.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: I'm Juan Restrepo, and I lead government relations in New York for Lime, the world's largest shared micromobility company and the largest operator in the city's e-scooter program based out of Eastern Queens and the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: With dozens of bills before you, I want to draw one clear line.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Legal high-speed devices are not the same as regulated shared scooters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Our scooters are capped at 15 miles per hour, and new riders are at 10 miles per hour for their first three rides.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Geofencing keeps them out of sensitive areas and creates slow zones.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Riders who break the rules face warnings, fines, and suspensions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: And our UL-certified batteries are handled only by trained professionals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: These safeguards show up in the safety records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: An NYU Ruden Center report found that more than nine in 10 e-scooter collisions in New York happened outside of the shared scooter zone, and that shared fleet incident rates are comparable to cycling.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Our program is trusted and that's why it's growing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Bronx riders took more than 1.9 million Lime trips in 2025, and 41% of them started or ended near a subway station, showing their use.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Queens ridership nearly doubled between 2024 and 2025 to 648,000 rides for all our operators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: This program also delivers on our city's affordability goals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Through Lime Access, eligible low-income New Yorkers get a free 30-minute ride every day, and Access riders have made up as much as 13%

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: of our ridership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Our Lime Prime subscription program offers longer scooter rides at the cost of a MetroCard swipe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: That's why we're excited that the Vision Zero Reimagined report commits to expanding e-scooter share.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Five years after Local Law 74 passed, service is still limited to two zones.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: We urge the Council to work with DOT on a near-term expansion plan with clear metrics for safety and equitable access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Finally, we share your goal in ending sidewalk riding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Line began piloting sidewalk detention technology in the Bronx in 2023.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: We're open to partnering with Majority Leader Abreu on 2025.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Juan Restrepo
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And I'll turn it over to Council Member Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, my apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: On Zoom, we have Abigail Jackson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mohamed Riyadh
utterances.text: You may begin.

chapters.summary: Abigail Jackson says accurate definitions are key, many devices involved in fatalities are e-motos not e-bikes, and calls for promoting cycling while eliminating high-speed devices.
chapters.title: Abigail Jackson of Regional Plan Association testifies on e-bike definitions

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Jackson
utterances.text: Hello, my name is Abigail Jackson and I'm the Transportation Associate at Regional Plan Association, RPA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Jackson
utterances.text: We're a nonprofit research and advocacy organization that for more than a century has worked to shape the region's transportation future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Jackson
utterances.text: We thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on today's agenda.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Jackson
utterances.text: One of the most important things we can do to accomplish our shared goals for street safety is to be consistent with the accurate definition of an e-bike.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Jackson
utterances.text: In New York, an e-bike or bicycle with electric assist has a motor of less than 750 watts, working pedals, and cannot exceed a max speed of 25 miles per hour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Jackson
utterances.text: Many of the electric devices recently involved in traffic fatalities do not fit this definition and are more accurately described as e-motos or high-speed electric scooters, yet they are often confused with e-bikes or e-scooters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Jackson
utterances.text: Conflating those currently illegal devices with e-bikes or e-scooters leads us to address perceived rather than actual street safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Jackson
utterances.text: And while the greatest threat to cyclists, pedestrians, and other motorists, as many have said today, remains cars and trucks, faster, heavier devices like e-motos are presenting an increasing danger on our streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Jackson
utterances.text: We have provided detailed written testimony covering each bill, but there are overarching goals that we would like the Council to consider.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Jackson
utterances.text: We should promote cycling, including low-speed e-bikes, for people and goods movement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Jackson
utterances.text: We should eliminate e-motos or high-speed scooters from our streets and bike lanes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Jackson
utterances.text: We should regulate third-party delivery services that may encourage unsafe behavior and should not regulate their riders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Jackson
utterances.text: Licensing or registering e-bikes is ineffective at promoting safety and reducing the use of e-motos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Jackson
utterances.text: Rules and targets should avoid...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Jackson
utterances.text: equitable outcomes and have clear attainable goals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Jackson
utterances.text: And perhaps most importantly, we need to improve our street network and street design to support safe micromobility and take the onus for street safety off pedestrians and riders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Jackson
utterances.text: Our PA looks forward to continuing to partner with the council and agencies to make sure the final legislation will truly address street safety while preserving access to micromobility as an accessible and affordable option for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Jackson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Epstein.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks Uber about worker claims of being told to take illegal routes, and Gold says Uber does not pay more for speed or penalize for longer times, and supports banning the practice.
chapters.title: Chair Epstein questions Uber on delivery worker pressures

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: For Uber, we've heard from the last panel just around routes and getting people from point A to point B

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: and drivers feeling, one, their safety's at risk for the e-bike riders, and two, that they're being told to go down illegal paths.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So I just wanted to hear...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You know, obviously, that's concerning to hear that, and seeing that injuries are up to 50% of people who are in this industry.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What do you say in response to those claims that we just heard?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: I agree with you that it is concerning to hear that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: I will say that we do not pay them workers more for driving faster or penalize them for taking longer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: I do believe that my understanding from some of the workers that I talked to today and previously that others may do that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: And, you know, I talked about Councilmember Abreu's bill 1069.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Rather than just studying it and collecting data in perpetuity, ban those practices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: We would be supportive of that.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So, so.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: From your understanding, you're fully supportive of an outright ban of requiring people to go wrong way down one-way streets doing illegal activity and support the workers in their ability to have safe routes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And so with that, and just the final question I have, just to ensure that we're all on the same page.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What are the outcomes that you would look forward to seeing if those behaviors were banned and people were not allowed to encourage people to go down safe routes?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What is the future outcome that you'd be looking to see happen?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Safer streets for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, so it sounds like we're all on the same page and sounds like you're on board with it.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks if Uber recognizes the pressure on workers and can play a role in reducing safety impacts, and Gold says they can and support banning on-time rate penalties.
chapters.title: Chair Abreu questions Uber on app role in safety

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I have a question for you, for Uber.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Do you recognize the pressures you're putting our workers in?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: These are workers who, in many ways, as discussed today, have been, you know, they're incentivized to really...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Move as fast as possible for folks to get their deliveries.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Do you believe that the apps can play a role in reducing those safety impacts on our road and making their livelihoods better?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: I do believe we can play a role.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: I'll say a couple things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: First is, as I said to Councilmember Epstein, we don't pay workers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: for riding faster.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: In fact, the opposite is true.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: The city requires us to pay per minute, and we don't penalize them for taking longer, but my understanding is there's some in the industry who do do that, and one thing you can do is ban that practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: I think we're under pressure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: internally to compete with other companies who do have on-time rates.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I see a lot of heads shaking behind you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: We are under pressure because other companies who those workers may be working for do have on-time rates and do penalize workers for

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: not making certain expectations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: We don't do that for workers who use two wheels here in New York City, but others do, and so there would be a level playing field if you just outright banned that practice.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I think a lot more needs to happen so that our workers are treated with dignity and respect.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks if algorithms are the place to start and how to ban the practice of setting minimum delivery times, and Gold suggests banning the practice outright rather than studying it.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer questions Uber on algorithms and banning practices

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Council Member Brewer, followed by Hanif.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You opened the can of worms.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you for doing that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: I was waiting for you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I know you a very long time.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question is then, would the algorithms be the place to start in order to address and do what you suggest for the other competitors?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How would you go about, it has to be a law, I would assume, but again, getting it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In effect would be differently.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How would you go about doing what you think we should do?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Yeah, I think, you know.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Since you know what to do in general.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: I often do not, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: But Intro 1069 is looking to collect a bunch of data and have DCWP to do a study to then set a minimum amount of time that a worker can do a trip in, is my understanding of 1069.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Why not just ban the practice of setting a minimum amount of time and not have a minimum amount of time that a worker can do a trip in?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And you think you can get your colleagues to go along with that?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Not that they have to.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: If it's a law, it's a law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: They're not here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I appreciate you being here.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: You're welcome.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks how Uber defines and enforces time-length fraud, and Gold describes an example of a worker taking unnecessary bridges and says there is an appeals process.
chapters.title: Council Member Hanif questions Uber on time-length fraud and deactivation

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Hanif.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Can you explain how Uber, the apps, define and enforce time-length fraud and how that policy is used to deactivate delivery workers?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Yeah, so we do look at unusual trips.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: So an example that I cite from last year is a worker who repeatedly went from Greenpoint to Prospect Heights via the Williamsburg Bridge and the Brooklyn Bridge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: So that was an unusual pattern that was extending the amount of trip and extending pay time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: And so, you know, there are cases of clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: fraud and they should be demonstrable and clear and under local law 13 what the law the local law the deactivation protections they would have to be clear examples of fraud

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: like that example of a worker who repeatedly goes across two unnecessary bridges in order to extend the amount of time on a trip and a worker who did that did they have an opportunity to challenge that deactivation yeah so we installed a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: well a there's an opportunity to challenge that deactivation with an internal appeals panel as well as through the workers justice project.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You're hearing the opposition, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: For sure.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And how is...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: For the workers justice project also has opportunity to challenge them directly with me, but the city in passing the local law deactivation review also set up their own policies that take effect in January.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And then have you all designed a time length per delivery?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What's the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: No, we have not.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Is that something you all plan to do?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Well, if 1069 passes, then the city would set up the minimum amount of time for us.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What are you guys thinking in terms of just given that you all are deactivating workers for unusual patterns of delivery time?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: So I would say that if 1069 sets up a system where there was a minimum amount of time, we would utilize the city's set minimum amount of time.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Okay, and then right now it's the deactivation, require workers to appeal, and that's the process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: Right now, if there is demonstrated fraud, there's the activation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josh Gold
utterances.text: but we do not set a delivery expectation or have an on-time rate for two-wheel bike deliveries in New York or devices or anything on two wheels in New York.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And we'll get to the bottom of that in the redlining process with the advocates, who I think share vast disagreements with your position today.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This panel is excused.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Next up we have Anna Humphrey, Christopher Shiler, Jean Ryan, Michael Ring, Lloyd Feng.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please keep it down in the chambers.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Remember to state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You may begin.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And please keep it down in the chambers, please, so we can hear our panelists clearly.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Anna Humphrey supports Intro 950 for delivery service licensing and Intro 389 for moped registration verification, saying disabled pedestrians face hazards from reckless micromobility.
chapters.title: Anna Humphrey of CIDNY testifies on delivery licensing and moped registration

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Humphrey
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Humphrey
utterances.text: Hello, my name is Anna Humphrey, and I'm testifying today on behalf of the Center for Independence of the Disabled, New York, Sydney.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Humphrey
utterances.text: We support Intro 950 because establishing a business licensing framework for delivery services is a critical first step toward accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Humphrey
utterances.text: For disabled pedestrians, navigating city sidewalks has become increasingly hazardous due to reckless micromobility operation and unsafe commercial delivery practices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Humphrey
utterances.text: When reckless or illegal e-bike use leads to serious injuries, app-based delivery companies regularly shirk responsibility, leaving vulnerable victims with trauma and unrecoverable medical expenses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Humphrey
utterances.text: In 2023, NYC DOT recorded 30 cyclist fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Humphrey
utterances.text: 23 of those deaths involved e-bike riders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Humphrey
utterances.text: Most of those 23 were working for app-based delivery platforms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Humphrey
utterances.text: By setting clear conditions for...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Humphrey
utterances.text: for licensure and establishing enforcement, Intro 950 ensures that wealthy delivery platforms can finally be held legally and financially accountable for the dangerous conditions created by their business models.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Humphrey
utterances.text: We support Intro 389, which mandates that third-party food delivery apps verify that mopeds used by their workers are properly registered before allowing them onto the platform.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Humphrey
utterances.text: Unregistered high-speed mopeds frequently travel illegally on sidewalks, pedestrian plazas, and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Humphrey
utterances.text: crosswalks presenting a physical threat to pedestrians with disabilities who cannot react or move out of the way quickly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Humphrey
utterances.text: Without proper registration, hit-and-run incidents involving disabled New Yorkers leave victims with zero recourse or ability to identify those responsible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Humphrey
utterances.text: Intro 389 places the burden directly on the corporations profiting from these deliveries, forcing platforms to ensure that every vehicle operating on their behalf follows basic traffic safety laws before hitting our streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Humphrey
utterances.text: We urge the City Council to implement these safety measures that protect pedestrians with disabilities who want to navigate our streets without fear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anna Humphrey
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Christopher Schuyler calls for including people with disabilities in e-bike policy, collecting data on disabled victims, and ensuring adaptive e-bikes are part of infrastructure design.
chapters.title: Christopher Schuyler of NYLPI testifies on disability access and data

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Schuyler
utterances.text: Good afternoon, council members, chairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Schuyler
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to give testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Schuyler
utterances.text: My name is Christopher Schuyler.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Schuyler
utterances.text: I'm a managing attorney in the Disability Justice Program at New York Lawyers for the Public Interest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Schuyler
utterances.text: People with disabilities must be top of mind as the city develops its safety policies around e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Schuyler
utterances.text: Additionally, the city must include people with disabilities in its e-bike policies, including by providing meaningful access to adaptive e-bikes, which exists in a litany

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Schuyler
utterances.text: of different styles, which can be usable by people with disabilities unable to use conventional e-bikes, and by designing city infrastructure, including street and bike lane improvements, to account for adaptive bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Schuyler
utterances.text: I have three main points I'd like to address.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Schuyler
utterances.text: Community voice must be at the table.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Schuyler
utterances.text: So people with disabilities, disability rights organizations, mayor's office for people with disabilities must be consulted as the city develops its e-bike safety policy and infrastructure improvements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Schuyler
utterances.text: Addressing people with disabilities'needs in the design phase and before policies are implemented will keep more New Yorkers with disabilities safe, will ensure that the city is more accessible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Schuyler
utterances.text: for all and will avoid costly retrofits down the line.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Schuyler
utterances.text: Data collection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Schuyler
utterances.text: The city must specifically collect data capturing people with disabilities who are involved in e-bike related collisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Schuyler
utterances.text: Collecting such data will help identify the extent to which people with disabilities are disproportionately involved in such collisions and will help inform safety policies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Schuyler
utterances.text: To the extent that data is not collected, the city should explore ways of doing so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Schuyler
utterances.text: And lastly, make e-bikes and infrastructure accessible by making sure that adaptive bikes are part of any city policies about e-bikes as well as in infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Schuyler
utterances.text: design.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christopher Schuyler
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Michael Ring, a disabled former cyclist, says he fears his children being hit by cars, not bikes, and calls for education and mutual respect rather than unenforceable punitive laws.
chapters.title: Michael Ring testifies on disability, cycling, and car danger

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Michael Ring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: If anyone needs a verbal description of my appearance, I'm a 63-year-old white guy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: I happen to be wearing a hoodie that says Disabled in Action while I'm an officer of that organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Ring
utterances.text: I'm not speaking for them today.
