chapters.summary: Vladimir Klali says NYPD enforcement is dangerous for immigrant communities, calls for DOT to be the enforcing agency, and opposes several bills including Intros 986, 2361, and 2587.
chapters.title: Vladimir Klali of NYIC testifies on enforcement and immigration fears

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: My name is Vladimir Klali.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: I'm the Senior Policy Strategist at the New York Immigration Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: I want to be direct about why we are here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: Nearly every bill on today's agenda answers the same question the same way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: Who enforces the rules on our streets and the answer?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: answer over and over again is the New York Police Department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: We are here to tell you all that this answer doesn't bring us closer to street or community safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: And in 2026, it is in fact dangerous for our communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: The New York City Department of Transportation should be the agency responsible for regulating, educating, and enforcing mobility rules in this city, not the police.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: Every NYPD stop is at risk for our neighbors cannot afford right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: The council knows firsthand what is happening in each of our neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: Federal immigration agents are operating in our homes and our streets, outside our courthouse, and across our entire city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: For delivery workers, tickets, it's not just a ticket.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: It may be a summons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: It may be a warrant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: It may be falling into the deportation pipeline.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: We've already seen what NYPD do when they can enforce e-bikes, and it's not great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: Give NYPD an opportunity, and they will do the harshest enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: For that, we oppose Intro 9.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: 986, T2361, T2587, T2590, Intro 78, Intro 110, Resolution 43.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: We recommend amending Intro 787 to clarify that reporting should not include communications with federal immigration enforcement without any warrant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: And we support Intro 985 with amendments that guarantee that the funding will be available for all workers that need it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: And we ask the City Council to strike NYPD as the enforcing agency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: I trust this package of bills and the confiscation and impoundment as penalties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: Build a data privacy firewalls for workers and New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: Be safe and fully fund the trading program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vladimir Klali
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Daryl Reardon presents findings that 53% of delivery workers report work-related injuries and 40% have severe psychological distress, and warns that nine bills could have unintended consequences.
chapters.title: Daryl Reardon of CUNY testifies on delivery worker health study

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Daryl Reardon, and I'm speaking on behalf of CUNY's delivery work and health study team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: Ligia actually gave you this paperwork already.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: With the Workers'Justice Project, our team surveyed 561 app delivery workers this spring, and our just-release reef, driven by algorithms that Ligia handed you, is submitted to the committee along with our testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: The findings from our study are stark.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: 53% of workers report a work-related injury, more than five times the national rate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: 40% have severe psychological distress.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: distress five times the rate among adult New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: Algorithms are behind the negative health effects.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: Over 80% say the apps decide their speed, routes, and hours, and 52% fear deactivation if they don't deliver fast enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: For 96%, this is their only job, and the threat of deactivation and shift limits pushes workers to take risks that endanger them and the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: These bills tackle a real problem as e-bikes become a permanent part of our streets, and we support those that improve street design, education, and crash data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: But as drafted, nine of the bills on today's agenda could have serious unintended consequences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: Local Law 34, aimed at preventing unjust deactivations, doesn't cover temporary lockouts, and it exempts deactivations the law would require.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: Some of these bills would mandate lockouts and others would make deactivations easier to justify, giving apps new ways to cut out workers and push them to rush even more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: Our written testimony details our recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: Finally, Local Law 34 should be amended to cover temporary outlooks, login caps, and shift limits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: Safer streets require limiting the app's power to make workers rush.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: We urge the Council to aim at the root causes of unsafe streets, the algorithms and business

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: decisions of platform delivery companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Eric?

chapters.summary: Eric McClure proposes a four-point framework: 20 mph speed limit, stopping sale of illegal devices, holding delivery apps accountable, and improving street design.
chapters.title: Eric McClure of StreetsPAC testifies on four-point framework

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader Abreu and your staff for the opportunity to speak today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: I'd like to, my name is Eric McClure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: I'm the Executive Director of Streets Pack.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: I'd like to talk about a four-point framework for improving micromobility safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: 20 is plenty is number one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Whether someone's operating a device that has one wheel or 18, 20 miles per hour should be the top speed permitted on most city streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Any powered micromobility device capable of speeds exceeding 20 miles per hour should be phased out, shouldn't be operated in bike lanes, and should not be classified or marketed as an e-bike or scooter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Number two, stopping the sale of illegal and noncompliant high-speed devices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: The sale of high-speed devices that masquerade as illegal e-bikes or e-scooters and that do not possess a vehicle identification number necessary for registration with the DMV must be banned at point of sale to prevent their use on city streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Three, holding delivery apps accountable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: App companies must end unreasonable delivery expectations and stop incentivizing unsafe behavior.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: They should be licensed and regulated by the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: They should be required to provide liability insurance for workers making deliveries on their behalf.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: As the Driven by Algorithms report released yesterday by CUNY and the Workers'Justice Project underscored, delivery workers operate under tremendous pressure from the apps and face outsized physical danger and psychological stress in just doing their jobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Four, increasing safety through better street design.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Complete street designs are proven to improve safety for all users.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: In order to improve safety around micromobility use, the city should prioritize...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: implementation of physically protected bike lanes, speed up the installation of hardened daylighting at intersections, and lower speed limits to 20 miles per hour wherever it's allowed by Sammy's law, among other measures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Just really quickly on some of the legislation, I won't take all of them today, but we support Intro 244, Councilmember Hudson's bill which fades out the sale and use of Class 3 e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: We support Intro 985, your bill which would create a trade-in program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: We would work hand-in-hand with hers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Intro 998, we support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Also, your bill that would ban the deceptive marketing of registrable high-speed devices, e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Finally, Councilmember Shulman's Intro 960, we also support.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric McClure
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: The statement says most bills address individual behaviors while ignoring systemic issues, opposes bills that burden workers or expand police stops, and calls for infrastructure investment.
chapters.title: Dharaj Ganjukanta (read by another) testifies for NYC DSA

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Dharaj had to leave.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I'm going to be reading his statement on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Good morning, Chairs Abreu and Epstein, Council Members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: My name is Dharaj Ganjukanta, and I'm offering testimony on behalf of the New York City Democratic Socialists of America.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I co-chair our transit working group, a body chartered this year to expand our organizing around transportation and infrastructure issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We appreciate the spirit of this hearing, particularly the focus on pedestrian worker safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: However, most of the proposed legislative solutions fall short in terms of their potential impact and approach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: The bills in this package, for the most part, address individual behaviors while leaving systemic issues unaddressed and ignoring proven infrastructure solutions to street safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We oppose bills that place an additional burden of responsibility on workers and individual cyclists rather than apps or sellers, or bills that provide additional grounds for police to randomly stop cyclists and workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Unfortunately, there are many bills in this package that fall into both categories.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Alternatively, we urge the Council to call for solutions that address the conditions actually producing unsafe streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: That means investing in protected bike infrastructure and other street redesigns that better organize our streets to keep people safe and meet the needs of users.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Far too often, Council members are opposing projects like these either publicly or behind the scenes or choose not to champion them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Other proven safety treatments along with legislation and funding to support them should be prioritized as well, including daylighting intersections, expanding protected intersections for cyclists, bus boarding islands, curb extensions, low traffic neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: and expanding pedestrian-friendly space across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We urge the Council to more aggressively examine and address the role delivery apps and other platforms play in shaping working conditions on our streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Tech billionaires should not be permitted to gamify the scarce public space on our streets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Delivery workers should not be expected to absorb the risks created by unrealistic delivery times and quotas or any other exploitative mandates imposed by app companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: If the council is serious about worker and pedestrian safety, legislation should place meaningful responsibility on corporations that organize and profit from this labor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We recognize that some progress has been made in this regard.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Gonzalo Mercado says some proposals will adversely impact delivery workers through increased NYPD interactions and confiscations, and calls for regulating algorithms and creating a transition plan.
chapters.title: Gonzalo Mercado of NDLO N testifies on delivery worker concerns

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Mercado
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader Abreu.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Mercado
utterances.text: My name is Gonzalo Mercado with the National Day Labor and Organizing Network, ANDALON.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Mercado
utterances.text: As a network of organizations that represent immigrant workers, ANDALON is encouraged by the New York City Council's commitment to ensure all workers can have a safe workplace and free from exploitation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Mercado
utterances.text: Delivery workers experience difficulties every day with every delivery they complete, such as injuries and fatalities, unjust deactivations, street crime, and e-bike theft.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Mercado
utterances.text: Pressures from the apps to deliver faster, just to name a few.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Mercado
utterances.text: While we strongly support measures to increase street safety, we are concerned that some of these proposals will adversely impact thousands of delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Mercado
utterances.text: We are particularly concerned about the following proposals due to the increased NYPD interaction that could result in widespread bike confiscations, deactivations,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Mercado
utterances.text: and other adverse effects on delivery workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Mercado
utterances.text: In addition, these proposals fail to regulate the algorithms that force workers to make deliveries as quickly as possible and do not create a transition plan for workers to be able to afford to make these changes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Mercado
utterances.text: Creating proposals that truly protect the safety of deliveristas and their workplace, the city streets, require conversations and planning with those workers themselves and the organizations that represent them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Mercado
utterances.text: The list below responds to each bill in more detail, which I have submitted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Mercado
utterances.text: But in the interest of time, we encourage the City Council to meet and discuss these concerns with delivery workers and advocates, such as our member organization, the Workers'Justice Project, along with the Deliveristas Unidos,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Mercado
utterances.text: who have been at the forefront of the struggle to improve the lives of delivery workers exploited by giant multinational corporations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Mercado
utterances.text: We thank the New York City Council for the opportunity to offer this testimony, and we look forward to continuing collaborating to advance protections that can improve the lives of all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gonzalo Mercado
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This panel is excused.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Next, we have Sarah Odea.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Baron Johnson.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Alexander Erdade, Tersa Crisp.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Gerardine Williams and Amy Yafet.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You may begin.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And please press the button, yes.

chapters.summary: Sarah O'Day describes being hit by a motorized bicycle, requiring a hip replacement, and calls for licensing, insurance, and a lower speed limit than 20 mph.
chapters.title: Sarah O'Day testifies about being hit by a motorized bicycle

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: I'm Sarah O'Day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: Late April, I was crossing the street and hit sideways by a bicycle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: And it was a straight out accident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: It wasn't anyone's fault, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: Fortunately, I was in terrific shape.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: But it did cause me to have a complete hip replacement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: The ball was knocked off the bone by the force of the hit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: And I tell you this really for three reasons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: One, I think motorized bicycles, it was motorized, and a very fat wheel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: Motorized bikes, I think, should be required to have a license and insurance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: And I also...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: hear of this proposal to have a 20 mile an hour speed limit, which I think is ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: I don't think this bicycle was going eight miles an hour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: Now when it hit me, but the damage it did was enormous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: So would anybody like to be hit by 20 and see how they survive?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: I just, I think 10 would be normal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: People walk at three miles an hour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: And a regular bicycle rider only pedals probably at five, maybe six, unless they're racing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: But if you're just bicycling in the street, you don't bicycle at 20 miles an hour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: You just don't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: And the other thing is, I think,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: It's fine to have regulations, but if they're not enforced, what's the point?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah O'Day
utterances.text: You're welcome.

chapters.summary: Tirza Crisp says EMTs and paramedics are subsidizing the public health system, and calls for competitive compensation and hospital offload time limits.
chapters.title: Tirza Crisp testifies on EMS system strain

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Tirza Crisp.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: I'm here because I think that we have become far too comfortable asking EMTs and paramedics in our city to personally subsidize a public health system with our time, our bodies, and our financial security.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: In March 2025, New York City changed its 911 destination policy because we could no longer afford to keep scarce ambulances out of service on longer transports.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: I think that tells us something important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: The system is already rationing its time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: But patients do not experience hospitals as interchangeable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: When someone has repeatedly felt dismissed, mistreated, or unsafe at the hospital closest to them, they may refuse care there altogether.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: That leaves both patients and providers in an impossible position.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: A person may delay emergency care, decline transport, or then later rely on private EMS to reach a hospital farther away where they believe they will actually be heard and appropriately treated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: This should make us all feel deeply uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: We tell EMTs, become better clinicians, get more education, and then we hand them tuition bills and hundreds of hours of clinical and field training while they're already working overtime or multiple jobs just to live.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: I work for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: You should not have to give up your life to learn how to save somebody else's.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: And we know this city understands the principle that essential workers deserve economic protection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: Just last week, the Mamdani administration secured a $131.5 million settlement after delivery workers were underpaid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: The city has said clearly that systems cannot be allowed to function by exploiting the workers that they depend on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: Depend upon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: EMS deserves that same urgency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: And this city already knows that there is a problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: The council proposed $50 million in recurring funding to begin addressing EMS pay parity because low wages are contributing to recruitment and retention problems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: Bring that proposal back.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: This year, New York City enacted a law requiring FDNY to how many units are actually available to respond and how many cannot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: So we are measuring this shortage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: Now, I believe it is our job to address one of the conditions creating it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: This is an essential infrastructure, and the city cannot afford to adequately pay, educate, equip, and retain the people providing it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Just a reminder to members of the public that you may speak on legislation and an oversight topic that's being heard today, so try to keep your comments to the hearing topic today.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Amy Effet, an EMT, describes a 45-minute response time to a mental health crisis due to staffing shortages, and urges the council to protect emergency medical infrastructure.
chapters.title: Amy Effet testifies on EMS staffing shortages and response times

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: Testing, can you hear?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We can hear you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: Good afternoon, members of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: My name is Amy Effet, and for the past five years, I've served as an EMT across two private EMS providers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: I'm currently on a break from field service, and taking that step back has given me a very clear view of why so many dedicated, experienced responders are walking away from this profession.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: When a resident calls 911, they expect rapid, high-quality emergency care, but having spent five years on the street, I can tell you that our system is reaching a dangerous breaking point.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: To show you what this looks like in practice, last year I was dispatched to a patient experiencing a severe mental health crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: Because of system-wide staffing shortages and the lack of open units, it took almost 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: Yes, you heard that right, 45.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: Just to arrive on scene.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: By the time we walked through the door, the patient had already injured themselves terribly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: That delay wasn't caused by a lack of effort from our crew, it was caused by a system that routinely leaves entire neighborhoods undercovered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: We are losing qualified EMTs and paramedics to burnout, unlivable wages, and grueling working conditions faster than we can replace them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: On top of that, units are routinely held for hours outside

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: overcrowded emergency departments waiting to transfer care, trapping available ambulances at hospitals when they are needed most on the street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: I urge the City Council to protect our emergency medical infrastructure in the upcoming budget cycle, A, by supporting competitive compensation for all EMS to fix the critical retention crisis, not being paid minimum wage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: To set hospital offload time limits so units can return to service as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: When response times lag, our community faces real preventable harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: Protecting our emergency medical infrastructure isn't just an administrative detail.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: It's a matter of life and death.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Amy Effet
utterances.text: Thank you for your time and leadership.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right, so I think there's a...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We have an EMS panel.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I believe you, probably your intention is to testify at an EMS-related hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: We're here for the management, the worker management oversight.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Yeah, this is a different hearing, which makes sense why we're getting a lot of off topics.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What we'll do is just, if you could just submit your written testimony to the

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I mean, if you would like to testify on the issues before us today, you can, but I think what you're speaking about is related to a different hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: Is this public safety?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: It is not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: This is not public safety.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Sorry, it is public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: It's not fire and EMS.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: But it's not fire and EMS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: Right, but...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tirza Crisp
utterances.text: This is regarding public safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, this is regarding public safety.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Tie it to public safety as much as you can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: Will do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: Proceed.

chapters.summary: Gerardney Williams, a paramedic and veteran, says he has responded to many emergencies involving people hit by bikes, and calls for more ambulances and better response times.
chapters.title: Gerardney Williams testifies on EMS and bike collision injuries

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: So my name is Gerardney Williams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: I'm a veteran, a United States Army veteran.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: I'm a New York City paramedic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: I'm a former New York City correction officer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: I work now in New York City as a paramedic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: And I just want to take time to talk about some things that's going on in the current public safety sphere.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: We have a severe staffing shortage in the EMS crisis in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: Response times are out of control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: I myself have responded to multiple emergencies with people being hit by bikes, people being knocked unconscious by bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: I've seen the injuries that these cause, and I can say that we need EMTs and paramedics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: We need better response times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: We need more ambulances on the street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: As of recently, they've cut.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: The New York City have cut ambulance, which has increased response times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: Also, hospitals participate in the New York City 911 system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: They've determined they want to cut ambulances, which makes response times go up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: So these accidents that people are having when they're being hit by bikes, it'll be longer before an ambulance gets to you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: Unfortunately, hospitals are putting profits over patients, and it's a result of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: Since last year, dozens of units have been taken out of service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: Hospitals are refusing to replace them, making our 911 system less efficient.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: Earlier this summer, I responded to two people stabbed on Upper West Side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: I'm coming from the east side of the hospital, right next to Central Park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: It took me about 10 minutes longer than it would have took me if I had an ambulance on the west side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: So these are critical times, and these times where they're cutting Medicaid, we need more ambulances on the street and not less.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Baron Johnson, a paramedic, asks who protects EMTs and paramedics when they are assaulted, and calls for support so they can go home safely.
chapters.title: Baron Johnson testifies on EMT and paramedic safety

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: Hey, how you doing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: My name is Baron Johnson, also a paramedic in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: I came here today wondering what I could possibly say in such a short amount of time, because the truth is I could speak for days about what EMTs and paramedics experience and how often

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: the very people who dedicate their lives to helping others are left feeling unprotected themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: As I sit here today speaking for the men and women who dedicate their lives to helping others, often putting their lives and safety at risk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: Everyday EMTs and paramedics walk into situations most people could never imagine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: We witness violence, tragedies, and death, yet we are still expected to remain calm, professional, and compassionate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: We sacrifice our bodies, our times, our families, and sometimes our mental health, but we keep coming back because we love what we do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: We want to be a beacon of hope for the people when they're in their

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: Worst moments in their lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: But today I have one question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: Who takes care of us?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: When we are assaulted, when we are threatened, and when we are forced to defend ourselves, who stands up for us?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: No EMT or paramedic should ever have to choose between protecting their own life and protecting their career.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: We took an oath to help people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: But we did not take an oath to become punching bags.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: We deserve protection, we deserve support, and we deserve to go home safely to our families without feeling that defending ourselves could cost us our livelihood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: So today I'm asking our elected officials, healthcare leaders, EMS agencies, unions, and communities to stand with us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: Enough is enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: When society needs us to show up, because someone can't breathe, we show up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Baron Johnson
utterances.text: When someone is dying, we show up.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This panel is excused.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Next up, we have Jareth.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Swayaseya, Mark Tabashnik.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Matthew Brevent.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Jason Framowitz.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please, please make your way up.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We don't have a hard stop.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We're going through the whole night.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Peter Reed?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Ira Gershenhorn.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: See you over here.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I understand the folks have left, so we're going to make sure we get to everybody.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Eleanor Wong.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Eleanor here.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Carrie Flaherty.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Gorman Riley.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right, we have Gorman here.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Carlos, Elaine, Allie.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Sumana Hari Hari Swara.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right, Sumana's here.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We have space for a few more.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Chris Sanders.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We'll add you to the next panel.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I had a lot of people here have to go.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What's his name?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: There's an Avisa panel that's next, just so you're aware.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please.

chapters.summary: Jareth Swayze says illegal e-motos capable of 50 mph are sold as e-bikes, and supports banning Class 3 e-bikes, Intro 988, and a funded trade-in program.
chapters.title: Jareth Swayze of Upway testifies on illegal e-motos and Class 3 ban

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: My name is Jareth Swayze.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: I'm here on behalf of Upway.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: We're the Carvana of e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: We also co-chair the Next Mile Coalition, an industry group advocating for a sensible micromobility policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: Upway's U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: Headquarters is in Brooklyn, where we sell high-quality, safety-tested electric bikes, and we want more New Yorkers riding them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: E-bikes are a great equalizer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: They flatten hills, cost less than a car, reduce traffic, and cut pollution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: Upway is committed to connecting more New Yorkers to affordable street legal vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the market is currently flooded with a very different product.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: Illegal e-motos that can hit more than 50 miles an hour are being sold online as e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: These are not e-bikes, and they meet none of the safety standards that companies like Upway are committed to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: They invite people to ride recklessly and have been involved in a majority of fatal micromobility crashes in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: We're encouraged by positive movement at the state level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: Bill S-10700 would help

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: stop e-moto sales in New York by increasing penalties and enforcement in stores and online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: We strongly encourage the council to focus your attention on bills that will rein in these high-speed devices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: And to that end, Upway supports Intro 244, which ends the sale of Class 3 e-bikes in the city, which we believe 20 is plenty.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: Intro 988, which stops the sale from passing off registerable vehicles as e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: This bill, however, should be amended to also target e-motos, which cannot be registered and should not be sold in our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: Intro 985, which lets riders exchange illegal devices for legal e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: It needs real funding to work, but is essential to getting dangerous vehicles off of the road equitably.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jareth Swayze
utterances.text: Upway has a large warehouse with more than 1,000 high-quality, affordable bikes on hand, plus lithium-ion recycling capacity, and would be enthusiastic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daryl Reardon
utterances.text: Myra?

chapters.summary: Ira Gershenhorn, 74, says he relies on his bike for daily tasks, supports Intros 244, 988, and 950, and calls for infrastructure over registration laws.
chapters.title: Ira Gershenhorn testifies on cycling, affordability, and infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Ira Gershenhorn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: I am 74.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: I live on the Upper West Side in Sean Abrea's district, near Gail Brewer's district.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: I rely on my bike to go shopping, go swimming, and tend a community garden, and do many community-oriented tasks, like being a New York City Park super steward

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: and filling a community food fridge and being a cycling without age pilot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: Safety in numbers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: I don't love deliveryistas on their e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: I don't love bike clubs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: But safety in numbers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: They make my shopping rides safer, so that's more important than loving them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: Affordability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: Affordability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: I bike where I want.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: Getting rid of my car and using a bicycle saves me a ton of money and time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: It allows me to volunteer in my community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: I'm not sitting in a car or looking for a spot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: Infrastructure and not more laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: Infrastructure, infrastructure, infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: Do not create laws requiring registration of e-bikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: You will reduce safety, create complication, and greatly reduce affordability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: I support these bills, Intro 244, sponsored by Councilmember Hudson, Intro 988, sponsored by Councilmember Abrea, Intro 988,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: sponsored by Councilmember Abrea, Intro 950, sponsored by Councilmember Shulman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ira Gershenhorn
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Richard Easley says e-bike riders have become an elite class that cannot be held accountable, and calls for passage of Priscilla's Law and an end to campaign contributions from Transportation Alternatives.
chapters.title: Richard Easley testifies on lack of accountability for e-bike riders

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: My name is Richard Easley.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: Honorable Council members, today I want to congratulate you on an amazing accomplishment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: In the space of five, going on six years with truly little or no effort at all, you have created a whole new class of New York City citizens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: And what is remarkable is that this new elite class comes from all walks of life, a wide age range, and it encompasses the richest and the poorest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: Now, the new class doesn't have a name, but I can tell you who's in it and why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: They are both city and e-bike riders, pedicab drivers, e-bike delivery workers, and the vendors who hire those workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: And they are allowed to freely flaunt not only rules of the roads and lanes they ride on, but even the city laws governing those roads and lanes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: Why are they elite?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: Because they cannot be held accountable for any offense they commit or law they break.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: It would take too long to list all those offenses, but the worst of them includes endangering or physically injuring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: another human being.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: You want to take a look at your creation?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: Spend an afternoon walking in my neighborhood along 9th and 10th Avenues between 59th Street and 34th.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: A weekend would be the best.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: Or even an afternoon in Central Park and behold your creation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: Stop your safety lip service and stop accepting campaign financing from the wolf in sheep's clothing that is transportation alternatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: Pass Priscilla's law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: And I just want to quickly say you invited your constituency here to speak on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: And most of us who've been here since 10 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Richard Easley
utterances.text: This morning don't have the pleasure of speaking to even half the committee.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Next.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please, please don't start his time yet.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please put on the mic.

chapters.summary: Gorman Reilly supports Intros 244, 988, 985A, and 950, and proposes an amendment to Intro 1066 to include signage on bike paths prohibiting high-speed devices and setting a 20 mph speed limit.
chapters.title: Gorman Reilly of Civitas testifies on bike path signage

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: My name is Gorman Riley.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: I'm a member of the board of directors of Civitas Citizens, Inc.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: Civitas, a nonprofit community organization, was founded in 1981 and for the past 45 years has been working to improve quality of urban life in El Barrio, East Harlem,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: and the Upper East Side of Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: Civitas strongly supports

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: courts four of the pending bills under consideration today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: Intros 244, 988, 985A, and 950 for the persuasive and compelling reasons already set forth in testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: In addition, Civitas supports Intro 1066, but with a simple but helpful amendment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: Intro 1066 would require the city to study and install traffic calming devices in bike paths.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: The Civitas Amendment seeks to modify the term, quote, traffic calming device.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: To specifically include a program of signage at the bike paths with clear language that gives continuing notice to all

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: of, among other things, a prohibition against usage by motorcycles, mopeds, and other high-speed mobility devices, and a speed limit of 20 miles per hour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: Just having a law on the books is not enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: There has to be widespread notice and a continuing reminder of what is allowed and what is not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: Only a permanent program of signage at significant entry points along the bike path can bring about the necessary compliance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gorman Reilly
utterances.text: Saved by the bell.

chapters.summary: Sumana Harihareswara says street-legal e-bikes help her, a not-very-good cyclist, stop safely at intersections, and that 20 mph is plenty for sharing streets.
chapters.title: Sumana Harihareswara testifies on benefits of pedal-assist e-bikes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Sumana Harihareeshwara.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: I'm in my mid-40s.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: I live in Jackson Heights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: I'm here just as a volunteer, as a cyclist, but not a very good one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: And I want to tell you that street legal e-bikes help me, a not very good cyclist, bike more safely because they help me stop.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: So on a conventional bike, every time I come to a complete stop at a stop sign or a stoplight and then push off again, it uses a little energy and that adds up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: And let's say a 25-minute ride from Jackson Heights to Astoria to help a friend with child care or go to a doctor's appointment, that's maybe like nine stops at stoplights and stop signs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: And I am not very strong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: I do not have calves of steel, you know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: I'm jeans, not lycra, you know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: No matter how much I try to do like protein and carbs ahead of time, it is going to tire me to make all those stops, full stops, and then come, you know, rolling again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: And that tires me out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: But then on an e-bike, it's so much easier to start from a full stop.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: And if you've never ridden an e-bike, that is one of the game changers about it that we don't necessarily talk about enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: So for me, pedal assist bikes take away any temptation to just like roll through a stop sign at an empty intersection because I can stop as much as I need to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: and then still have the energy I need to do what I need to do when I get there, like help take care of my friend's five-year-old.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: I don't need illegal high-speed devices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: 20 is plenty to help me safely share our streets with pedestrians and drivers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: The only collision I've ever been in as a bicycle rider while cycling was that a driver of a car rear-ended me while I was stopped at a red light.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: Look, you know, of course, separated bike paths help, and that would help change this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: But most of my rides, most of my miles, I am sharing the road with cars.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: Street legal e-bikes help me do that safely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sumana Harihareswara
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you for that perspective.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Next.

chapters.summary: Chris Sanders supports Intros 244, 950, 985, 988, and 1004, and calls for a protected bike lane network and safe, low-speed e-bikes as the norm.
chapters.title: Chris Sanders of TA Manhattan testifies on e-bike safety and infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Sanders
utterances.text: All right, thank you Speaker Menon, thank you Council Member Abreu.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Sanders
utterances.text: I'm Chris Sanders, I live in Midtown Manhattan, City Council District 4.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Sanders
utterances.text: I'm here because I'm the recently elected co-chair of the unpaid volunteer-led TA Manhattan Activist Committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Sanders
utterances.text: I want to support e-bike safety and pedestrian safety with intros 244, 950, 985, 988, and 1004.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Sanders
utterances.text: The globally accepted standard speed for e-bikes is 20 miles per hour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Sanders
utterances.text: I support the City Council legislation that officially adopts this standard right here in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Sanders
utterances.text: I support pedestrian safety with improved look-up and other wayfinding signage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Sanders
utterances.text: Protecting pedestrians, getting dangerously fast e-bikes and other devices off the streets, and compelling DOT to complete an organized network of safe and protected bike lanes in every borough and every neighborhood

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Sanders
utterances.text: for the safety and benefit of pedestrians and bikes must be the outcome of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Sanders
utterances.text: Ridiculous and unworkable licensing schemes are a huge distraction that doesn't improve safety for people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Sanders
utterances.text: We need the legislation to streamline the process for building

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Sanders
utterances.text: out the cost-effective, safe, and protected bike lane network, add new signage that increases pedestrian safety, and ensure safe, low-speed e-bikes all become New York normal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Sanders
utterances.text: Thank you for letting me speak up for street safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Sanders
utterances.text: Speaker Menon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Sanders
utterances.text: Chairman Abreu, and shout out to Council Members Virginia Maloney, Harvey Epstein, Carl Wilson, and Chris Marte.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I appreciate your testimony and congrats on your new gig.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This panel is excused.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Sanders
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The next panel, we have Mary Allen.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Christina Hansen.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: But I'm glad that you're here.

utterances.text: Judy Kinberg.

utterances.text: Judy Kinberg.

utterances.text: Janine Uriel.

utterances.text: Susan Lee.

utterances.text: This is an EVSA panel.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I have a spot for one more for EVSA.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We may start with you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
